name: Abhinanda (Gauḍa Abhinanda)
summary: Kashmiri author to whom the Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha is ascribed.

name: Abhinavagupta
summary: The central figure of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism: author of the Tantrāloka, Tantrasāra, Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa, Mālinīślokavārttika, the two commentaries on the Īśvarapratyabhijñā, the Paramārthasāra, Gītārthasaṅgraha, devotional hymns, and of the Abhinavabhāratī and Locana in aesthetics. He integrated Trika, Kula, Krama, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā under the four upāyas.

scholarly.text: c. 975-1025 CE; dated works: Kramastotra (Laukika 66, c. 990/91), Bhairavastava (68, c. 992/93), Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (90, c. 1014/15)

realization_account.text: The Tantrāloka describes one born of a union of parents absorbed in the Kaula state as 'yoginībhū', by nature a vessel of knowledge, Rudra himself (TĀ 29.162-163), a description the tradition applies to Abhinavagupta. Later Kashmiri tradition relates that he entered the Bhairava cave near Bīrwa with many disciples and did not return (oral legend; low confidence).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Teacher ids tch:induraja and tch:bhatta-tauta (poetics, dramaturgy) belong to U31.
alt_summary: Author of the Gītārthasaṅgraha on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni
summary: Companion of Śaunaka Kāpeya in the saṃvarga episode (ChU 4.3.5-7).

name: Acyutaprekṣa
summary: The ascetic at Uḍupi from whom Madhva took renunciation; the Sumadhvavijaya calls him Acyutapramati. In the tradition's account his ascetic line had come under the teaching of māyā, and he later accepted his disciple's doctrine.
notes: The earlier names of his line (the 'Haṃsa paramparā' back to Nārāyaṇa as Haṃsa and Brahmā) are not listed; see lin:dvaita notes.

name: Adhokṣaja Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Pejavara maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Ādinātha
summary: Śiva as the first Nāth and first teacher of yoga; the Haṭhapradīpikā opens with homage to Śrī Ādinātha 'by whom the knowledge of haṭha yoga was taught' (HYP 1.1), and Nāth lineages begin with him. In Nāth accounts he taught Matsyendra, who overheard or received the teaching he gave to Pārvatī.

realization_account.text: The supreme Lord himself; the source of the teaching.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Aditi Dākṣāyaṇī
summary: Named as one possible seer of RV 10.72 on the birth of the gods (Aditi born of Dakṣa and Dakṣa of Aditi).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Āditya (the Sun as teacher)
summary: The Sun-god who instructs visitors to his world: Triśikhi (Triśikhibrāhmaṇa), Sāṅkṛti (Akṣi); in the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa Yājñavalkya goes to the solar world and is taught by the Person there (Nārāyaṇa).

name: Ādityanāth
summary: Present mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur (from 2014), also a political figure.
notes: Recorded only as head of the seat; no teachings attributed.

name: Ādivaṇ Śaṭhakopa Jīyar
summary: Founder of the Ahobila maṭha of the Vaṭakalai (traditionally 1398), who, the tradition says, received his renunciation from Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha of Ahobilam himself.

tradition.text: founded the Ahobila maṭha in 1398 CE

name: Advaita Ācārya
summary: Elder Vaiṣṇava scholar of Śāntipur whose prayers, the tradition says, called Caitanya down; one of the Pañca-tattva.

realization_account.text: Mahāviṣṇu and Sadāśiva combined; lived to a great age (tradition: 125 years).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Agasti (Pāśupata tīrthakara)
summary: Number 15 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Agastya
summary: In the Vīraśaiva tradition, the sage to whom Reṇuka taught the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi on the Malaya mountain (SSM 1.29; ch. 4–5).
notes: Contribution of U20 to a shared registry entity (Agastya is owned elsewhere).
alt_summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition, Akattiyar (Kuṟumuṉi, Kumpamuṉi) is the first and foremost of the Siddhars and the founder of Siddha medicine: sent south by Śiva to the Potiyil hills, he received Tamil from Śiva or Murukaṉ, composed the lost grammar Akattiyam, and is the author-authority of a large medical, alchemical and yogic corpus and of the vital-point (varmam) lore.

Agastya Maitrāvaruṇi, seer of RV 1.165–191; in 1.179 he answers his wife Lopāmudrā, reconciling long tapas with married life, and is said to have 'nourished both colours'. Born with Vasiṣṭha of Mitra-Varuṇa in the tradition; the Tamil tradition identifies him with the Siddhar Agastya (the Vedic contribution is recorded here).
In the Rāmāyaṇa the sage Agastya teaches Rāma the Āditya Hṛdaya before the final battle (Yuddhakāṇḍa 105/107).

In the Purāṇas the sage who, pilgrimaging with Lopāmudrā, receives the Lalitopākhyāna from Hayagrīva, and who in the Kāśī Khaṇḍa teaches Lopāmudrā the inner tīrthas (SkP 4.1.6.28-45); he also cursed Indradyumna to become the elephant Gajendra.
places: Anantaśayanam (Thiruvananthapuram) — samādhi in the popular list

realization_account.text: When all gods and sages gathered in the north for Śiva's wedding and the earth tilted, Śiva sent the diminutive Agastya south, where he balanced the world from the Potiyil hills; he is held to live there still as a Siddhar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_notes: U22 contribution (Tamil Siddha / Siddha medicine). Scholars do not assume the Vedic, epic and Tamil Agastyas are one person, and regard the Tamil medical works under his name as late. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.
Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). Scholars do not assume the Vedic and Tamil Agastyas are one person.
U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Agastya's sister (mother of the Gaupāyanas)
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 10.60.6; named among the brahmavādinīs of the Bṛhaddevatā.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Aghamarṣaṇa Mādhucchandasa
summary: Seer of RV 10.190 (ṛta and satya born of tapas), the 'sin-effacing' verses recited at the bath.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Aghoraśiva
summary: Twelfth-century Śaiva ācārya of Chidambaram (Āmardaka lineage — moderate confidence) whose ritual manual Kriyākramadyotikā (1157/58) and commentaries (on the Mṛgendravṛtti and six of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa treatises) fixed the dualist reading of the Siddhānta followed by South Indian temple priests.
notes: Corrected: his Aṣṭaprakaraṇa commentaries cover six treatises (not the Mokṣakārikā or Paramokṣanirāsakārikā).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08.
alt_summary: Saiddhāntika ācārya of Cidambaram whose ritual manual (Kriyākramadyotikā, 1157/58) became the standard for Tamil Śaiva temple and domestic ritual; he also wrote commentaries on the Mṛgendravṛtti, the Sarvajñānottara and works of Sadyojyoti and Bhoja.

name: Aitiśāyana
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, e.g. for the prima facie view that only men are eligible for rites because of the masculine gender in 'svargakāmo yajeta' (MS 6.1.6) and at MS 3.2.43.

name: Aiyaṭikaḷ Kāṭavarkōṉ Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Pallava king who gave up the throne and went on pilgrimage, singing a veṇpā at each shrine (the Kṣēttirat Tiruveṇpā).

realization_account.text: A Pallava king who gave up the throne and went on pilgrimage, singing a veṇpā at each shrine (the Kṣēttirat Tiruveṇpā).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ajagaṇṇa
summary: Muktāyakka's brother, a hidden devotee whose death occasions her meeting with Allama.

name: Ajātaśatru of Kāśī
summary: King of Kāśī who refutes Gārgya Bālāki's twelve (KauU: sixteen) identifications of brahman and teaches the self into which the sleeping person withdraws, from which all breaths, worlds and gods come forth like sparks (BAU 2.1; KauU 4). He notes it is against the natural order for a brahmin to come to a kṣatriya to learn brahman.
notes: Distinct from the Magadhan king of the Buddhist texts; id disambiguated.

name: Akappēyc cittar
summary: Siddhar poet named from his refrain addressing 'akappēy', the demon that is one's own mind.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

name: Akhaṇḍānanda
summary: Author of the Tattvadīpana on the Vivaraṇa.

name: Akka Mahādēvi
summary: Akka Mahādēvi (Mahādēviyakka) of Uḍutaḍi, the woman saint who took Śiva as Cennamallikārjuna for her only husband, left a royal household, wandered clad only in her hair, was examined by Allama at Kalyāṇa and ended at Kadaḷi on Śrīśaila; her vacanas of bridal devotion and fearless renunciation are the tradition's great witness to women's spiritual equality.

realization_account.text: Devoted from childhood to Cennamallikārjuna, she refused (or left) the king Kauśika, renounced even clothing, was tested and acknowledged by Allama and the śaraṇas at Kalyāṇa, and attained union in the Kadaḷi forest of Śrīśaila.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Whether she was married to Kauśika differs between sources; recorded as the sources' variance.

name: Akkamma
summary: A woman vacanakāra of the śaraṇa circle whose vacanas are included in the modern collections of the women śaraṇas; details of her life are not recorded here.

name: Akkanāgamma
summary: Basava's sister (Nāgalāmbike), mother of Cennabasava and a vacanakāra.

name: Akṛtavraṇa
summary: One of Romaharṣaṇa's disciples in both lists (VP 3.6.17; BhP 12.7.5), of the Kāśyapa lineage (VP 3.6.18 counts 'Kāśyapa' among the makers of saṃhitās; BhP 12.7.7 calls Akṛtavraṇa a disciple of Rāma Jāmadagnya).

name: Akṣobhya Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva, pontiff after Mādhava Tīrtha, and teacher of Jayatīrtha. The Mādhva tradition records his debate with the Advaitin Vidyāraṇya on 'tat tvam asi', with Vedānta Deśika as arbiter, and a verse it ascribes to Deśika declaring Akṣobhya the victor; the Advaita tradition does not accept this account.
notes: See dsp:tat-tvam-asi (historical_debates).

name: al-Bīrūnī
alt_names: Abū Rayḥān Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Bīrūnī
summary: Khwārazmian scholar who learned Sanskrit in India and rendered a Pātañjala yoga text with a commentary into Arabic (Kitāb Pātanǧal). He was not a member of the tradition; he is listed under this lineage only as the translator of its text.

name: Aḻagiya Maṇavāḷa Perumāḷ Nāyaṉār
summary: Younger brother of Piḷḷai Lokācārya, author of the Ācārya Hṛdayam, which presents Nammāḻvār's Tiruvāymoḻi as the Tamil Veda.

name: Alarka
summary: Youngest son of Madālasā and King Ṛtadhvaja (Kuvalayāśva); raised as a king, he received his mother's ring-instruction and, when defeated in war, went to Dattātreya, learned yoga and renounced (MkP 25-44).
alt_summary: A royal sage who first sought to conquer the mind and senses with arrows and then learned that they are conquered only by yoga (Anugītā 14.30).

name: Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa
notes: Role: commentator. Date not established.
summary: Commentator on the Sātvata Saṃhitā.

name: Ālekhana
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (MS 6.5.17).

name: Allama Prabhu
summary: Allama Prabhu (Prabhudēva), the mystic of the void (śūnya, bayalu) whose enigmatic vacanas, signed Guhēśvara, test every attainment; in the Śūnyasampādane he presides over the Anubhava Maṇṭapa on the 'throne of the void' and examines Basava, Cennabasava, Siddharāma, Akka Mahādēvi, Muktāyakka and Gorakṣa.

realization_account.text: Harihara: a temple drummer of Baḷḷigāve who, grieving the death of Kāmalate, came upon a buried shrine where the yogi Animiṣa placed a liṅga in his hand and passed away, and he awoke. Cāmarasa: Śiva's own descent, unmoved by Māyā sent by Pārvatī, whose body passes untouched by Gorakṣa's sword. He ended in Kadaḷi at Śrīśaila, merging into the liṅga.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Amalānanda
summary: Author of the Vedāntakalpataru on the Bhāmatī and of the Śāstradarpaṇa; 13th-century Advaitin at the Yādava court.

name: Amarnīti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who gave loincloths to devotees; a loincloth left with him by Śiva disguised as a celibate vanished, and he offered its weight in cloth, then all his wealth — the scale balanced only when he, his wife and son climbed on it, and they were taken to Śiva's world.

realization_account.text: A merchant who gave loincloths to devotees; a loincloth left with him by Śiva disguised as a celibate vanished, and he offered its weight in cloth, then all his wealth — the scale balanced only when he, his wife and son climbed on it, and they were taken to Śiva's world.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ambigara Cauḍayya
summary: The ferryman śaraṇa whose vacanas, signed with his own name, attack hypocrisy, ritualism and the pride of learning.

name: Ānanda (father of Somānanda)
summary: Son of Aruṇāditya and father of Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.120).
notes: Id disambiguated from tch:ananda (the Buddha's attendant).

name: Ānandabhaṭṭa (Bhaṭṭānanda)
summary: Author of the Vijñānakaumudī on the Vijñāna Bhairava; its opening honours Somānanda, Bhūtirāja, Utpala, Lakṣmaṇagupta and Abhinavagupta.

name: Ānandabodha (Bhaṭṭāraka)
summary: Dialectical Advaitin, author of the Nyāyamakaranda (and the Nyāyadīpāvalī and Pramāṇamālā).

name: Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Tātparyaprakāśa commentary on the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

name: Ānandagiri (Ānandajñāna)
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on many of Śaṅkara's works, including the Gītābhāṣya.
alt_summary: 13th-century glossator of nearly all of Śaṅkara's commentaries (Nyāyanirṇaya on the BSBh; ṭīkās on the Upaniṣad and Gītā bhāṣyas) and of Sureśvara's Vārttika; his glosses name Bhartṛprapañca as the opponent refuted there.

name: Anantadeva (author of the Padacandrikā)
summary: Author of the Padacandrikā, a short commentary on the Yoga Sūtra dedicated to Śiva.
notes: Whether he is identical with other authors named Anantadeva (e.g. the 17th-c. Mīmāṃsaka) is not established here; id disambiguated for that reason.

name: Anantāḻvāṉ
summary: Disciple of Rāmānuja sent to Tirumala to maintain a flower garden for Veṅkaṭeśvara.

name: Anantārya
summary: Author of the Sanskrit hagiography Prapannāmṛtam (Anantācārya; distinct from Prativādi Bhayaṅkaram Aṇṇaṉ).

name: Anantaśaktipāda
summary: Commentator on the Vātūlanāthasūtra.

name: Anasūyā
summary: Ascetic wife of the sage Atri, honoured for her austerities, who teaches Sītā the dharma of the devoted wife (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119).

name: Āṉāya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A cowherd who played the five-syllable mantra on his flute; Śiva appeared and took him to his world with his music.

realization_account.text: A cowherd who played the five-syllable mantra on his flute; Śiva appeared and took him to his world with his music.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Aṅgir
summary: Link in the Muṇḍaka's line: received brahmavidyā from Atharvan and taught Satyavāha Bhāradvāja (MuU 1.1.2).

name: Aṅgiras (teacher of Śaunaka)
summary: Teacher of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: answers Śaunaka's question 'by knowing what is all this known?' with the higher and lower knowledge (MuU 1.1.3-5); 'this truth the seer Aṅgiras declared of old' (MuU 3.2.11).
notes: Whether tradition identifies him with the Ṛgvedic seer-family ancestor Aṅgiras is not asserted here.
alt_summary: Eponymous ancestor of the Āṅgirasa priests; the Atharvaveda is 'the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases' (Atharvāṅgirasaḥ), the aṅgiras hymns being traditionally the fierce (ābhicārika) and the atharvan hymns the auspicious (bheṣaja) portion.
alt_notes: The division of the Atharvaveda into atharvan (auspicious) and āṅgirasa (fierce) portions is a traditional and scholarly account recalled with moderate confidence. The Aṅgiras who teaches Śaunaka in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad is a separate figure in U03's scope.

name: Animiṣayya
summary: The 'unblinking' yogi who, in Harihara's account, placed the liṅga in Allama's hand in a buried shrine and passed away, awakening him.

name: Aniruddha (Sāṃkhya commentator)
summary: Author of the earliest known commentary (vṛtti) on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra.

name: Annambhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tarkasaṅgraha and its Dīpikā, the most widely used primer of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, written 'for the easy understanding of beginners'; tradition makes him a scholar from the Andhra country who worked in Vārāṇasī.

name: Āpadeva
summary: Son of Anantadeva; author of the Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa ('Āpadevī'), a standard introduction to Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā that dedicates dharma to Govinda.

name: Apālā Ātreyī
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 8.91: a maiden who found soma on her way to the water, offered it to Indra and was freed by him of a skin affliction.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Apāntaratamas
summary: Born of Nārāyaṇa's word, the teacher of the Vedas (vedācārya), called by some Prācīnagarbha; Vyāsa says he himself was Apāntaratamas in a former birth (12.337.38–61).

name: Aparakuśika
summary: Number 10 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Aparārka (Aparāditya)
summary: Śilāhāra king and commentator on Yājñavalkya.

name: Āpastamba
summary: Founder (sūtrakāra) of the Āpastamba branch of the Taittirīya Black Yajurveda, to whom its whole Kalpasūtra is ascribed.

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE for the Dharmasūtra (estimates vary)

name: Appaṇṇācārya
summary: Disciple of Rāghavendra Tīrtha to whom the tradition ascribes the Rāghavendra-stotra recited by devotees.

name: Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar)
summary: One of the three Tēvāram poets (Tirumuṟai 4–6), a former Jain monk (Tarumacēṉar) who returned to Śaivism; exemplar of the servant's path (dāsa-mārga, caryā); famed for temple service (clearing the temple grounds) and hymns of defiance and surrender.

tradition.text: lived to 81 (tradition)

scholarly.text: 7th c.; contemporary of the Pallava Mahendravarman I (r. c. 600–630)

realization_account.text: Raised a Śaiva and cared for by his sister Tilakavati, he became a Jain monk; struck by an incurable colic he returned to Tilakavati at Tiruvatikai, received the sacred ash, and sang his first hymn, and the pain left him. The Jain-influenced Pallava king had him shut in a lime-kiln, fed poison, trampled by an elephant and thrown into the sea tied to a stone; he survived each by singing Śiva's names, floated ashore, and the king turned Śaiva. He died at Tiruppukalūr merging with Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Appayya Dīkṣita
summary: 16th-c. polymath of Adaippalam (Tamil country) who revived Śrīkaṇṭha's Śaiva Vedānta in the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā while holding Advaita as final (Śivādvaitanirṇaya).

realization_account.text: Tradition says the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā was written under the patronage of Cinna Bomma of Vellore.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Polymath of Tamil Nadu, author of the Siddhāntaleśasaṅgraha, the Kalpataruparimala (completing the Bhāmatī chain), the Nyāyarakṣāmaṇi, works in Mīmāṃsā and poetics, and the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā on Śrīkaṇṭha's Śaiva Vedānta; an Advaitin devoted to Śiva.
For Mīmāṃsā: author of the Vidhirasāyana (on the kinds of injunction) and the Upakramaparākrama (on the priority of the opening statement), among other works.

name: Appūti Aṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who, without having met Appar, named his sons, water-sheds and alms-houses after him; when Appar visited, a son died of snakebite and the parents hid it to feed their guest; Appar sang and the boy revived.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who, without having met Appar, named his sons, water-sheds and alms-houses after him; when Appar visited, a son died of snakebite and the parents hid it to feed their guest; Appar sang and the boy revived.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Arivāṭṭāya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He offered red rice, greens and tender mango daily; impoverished and faint, he stumbled and the offering fell into a crack in the earth, and he began to cut his throat with a sickle (arivāḷ) — Śiva's hand rose from the crack to stop him.

realization_account.text: He offered red rice, greens and tender mango daily; impoverished and faint, he stumbled and the offering fell into a crack in the earth, and he began to cut his throat with a sickle (arivāḷ) — Śiva's hand rose from the crack to stop him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Arjuna (Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The third Pāṇḍava, the archer, whose refusal to fight his kinsmen occasions the Gītā; he declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and takes refuge in him (2.7), receives the divine eye and the vision of the universal form (11.8ff), and after the war asks Kṛṣṇa to repeat the teaching (Anugītā 14.16).

name: Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga
summary: Questions Yājñavalkya on the eight graspers and over-graspers and on what remains of a person at death; they go aside and speak of karma (BAU 3.2).

name: Aruḷāḷa Perumāḷ Emperumāṉār
summary: Formerly the Advaita renouncer Yajñamūrti who, the tradition says, debated Rāmānuja for eighteen days, conceded, and became his disciple; author of the Tamil Jñānasāram and Prameyasāram.

name: Ārumuka Nāvalar
summary: Jaffna Śaiva reformer and scholar: prose catechisms of Śaiva Siddhānta, printed editions of Tamil Śaiva texts, schools, and polemic against Christian missionaries.

name: Aruṇāditya
summary: Son of Varṣāditya in Somānanda's lineage (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.119).

name: Aruṇanti Civācāriyār
summary: Author of the Civañāṉa Cittiyār and Irupā Irupatu; a learned brahmin, family preceptor of Meykaṇṭār's father, who became Meykaṇṭār's chief disciple.

name: Asita Devala
summary: Sage named in the Gītā among those who proclaim Kṛṣṇa supreme (10.13); he teaches Nārada the five eternal elements with time as the sixth (12.267.1–6), and learns equanimity from the yogin Jaigīṣavya (12.222; 9.49).

name: Āśmarathya
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra on a ritual detail of the new-moon rite (MS 6.5.16); also cited in the Brahma Sūtra.
alt_summary: Early Vedāntin cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.20; 1.2.29): the self's identity with Brahman is stated in view of the promise that by knowing one all is known — later read as an early difference-and-non-difference view.

Early Vedāntin named in the Brahma Sūtras (1.2.29; 1.4.20). On the self and Brahman he held that the Upaniṣads' promise ('by knowing one, all is known') indicates non-difference; Śaṅkara glosses his view as difference-and-non-difference, like sparks and fire.
notes: Known only from the Brahma Sūtra and its commentators.

name: Aṣṭāvakra
summary: A sage born bent in eight places by his father Kahoḍa's curse; as a boy he defeated Bandin at Janaka's court (Mahābhārata 3.132-134). The Aṣṭāvakra Gītā presents him as Janaka's teacher of non-dual knowledge.

name: Āsuri
alt_names: the brahmin of the Āsuri clan (āsurisagotra)

realization_account.text: A brahmin devoted to sacrifice for a thousand years; Kapila asked him three times, at thousand-year intervals, whether he delighted in the householder's life; the third time he answered that he did not, renounced, and became Kapila's disciple (Māṭhara). His dispassion arose from the presence of the supreme sage (Yuktidīpikā on SK 43).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Kapila's disciple and Pañcaśikha's teacher (SK 70). The commentaries describe him as a brahmin of the Āsuri clan who renounced householder life after Kapila's repeated questioning. A person named Āsuri also appears in Vedic ritual literature; identity with the Sāṃkhya Āsuri is uncertain.
alt_summary: Named in the Mokṣadharma as the teacher of Pañcaśikha in Kapila's line (12.211.10).

name: Aśvala
summary: Janaka's hotṛ priest, the first to question Yājñavalkya at the court debate, on how the sacrificer is freed from death, day and night, the fortnights (BAU 3.1).

name: Āśvalāyana
summary: Ṛgvedic sūtrakāra, pupil of Śaunaka by tradition, author of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta- and Gṛhyasūtras (he has no surviving Dharma- or Śulbasūtra).
alt_summary: Ṛgvedic sage who approaches Parameṣṭhin for brahmavidyā (Kaivalya 1.1) and who teaches the sages the Sarasvatī-vidyā (Sarasvatīrahasya). Identity with the Kausalya Āśvalāyana of the Praśna not asserted.

name: Aśvapati Kaikeya
summary: King of the Kekayas who teaches five great householders and Uddālaka Āruṇi the vaiśvānara self as a whole, correcting each one's partial view (ChU 5.11-18); he claims there is no thief, miser, drunkard, man without a sacred fire, ignorant or adulterer in his kingdom (ChU 5.11.5).
alt_summary: King who taught the Vaiśvānara self to brāhmaṇa householders led by Aruṇa Aupaveśi (ŚB 10.6.1; ChU 5.11–18).

name: Atharvan
summary: Eldest son of Brahmā, who received brahmavidyā and passed it to Aṅgir (MuU 1.1.1-2).
alt_summary: The primordial fire-priest: 'you, Agni, Atharvan churned forth from the lotus' (RV 6.16.13); eponym and seer of many Atharvaveda hymns (e.g. AVŚ 1.1, 3.30, 10.7, 11.7, 12.1, 15).

U04 contribution: teaches Śāṇḍilya the eight-limbed yoga and brahmavidyā (Śāṇḍilya) and teaches Pippalāda, Aṅgiras and Sanatkumāra the meditation on Oṃ (Atharvaśikhā); speaker of the short Mahā Upaniṣad.

name: Atipatta Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Head of a fishing community who released the first fish of every catch for Śiva; in lean days he caught only one fish and released it, and when a golden fish set with gems came into his net he released that too; Śiva appeared.

realization_account.text: Head of a fishing community who released the first fish of every catch for Śiva; in lean days he caught only one fish and released it, and when a golden fish set with gems came into his net he released that too; Śiva appeared.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ātmasukha
summary: Recalled as author of the Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā on the Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

name: Ātreya (of the Brahma Sūtras)
summary: Early teacher cited in BS 3.4.44: the fruit of meditations connected with ritual goes to the sacrificer (as owner), against Auḍulomi's view that it goes to the priest.

name: Ātreya (Mīmāṃsā teacher)
notes: Disambiguated from other Ātreyas (e.g. of Āyurveda).
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: the fruit stated for a rite is real, not mere praise (MS 4.3.18); only the three higher varṇas are eligible because the setting-up of the fires names only them (MS 6.1.26).

name: Ātreya Rāmānuja
summary: Kiḍāmbi Appuḷḷār, maternal uncle and teacher of Vedānta Deśika, disciple of Naḍādūr Ammāḷ; the Nyāyakuliśa is attributed to him.

name: Atri
summary: Atri Bhauma, founder of the Ātreya family whose hymns form Ṛgveda book 5 (e.g. 5.85, Varuṇa's great māyā); one of the seven seers of RV 10.137. Later tradition makes him husband of Anasūyā and father of Dattātreya.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
alt_summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Samūrtārcanādhikaraṇa.
Vedic seer who questions Yājñavalkya about Avimukta and the sacred thread (Jābāla 2, 5; Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad); father of Dattātreya.

name: Atri (Pāśupata tīrthakara)
summary: Number 11 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Auḍulomi
summary: Early Vedāntin cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.21; 3.4.45; 4.4.6): the soul is different from Brahman while embodied and becomes one with it on departing — an early form of difference-and-non-difference.
alt_summary: Early Vedāntin named in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.21; 3.4.45; 4.4.6): the individual self becomes one with Brahman when it departs (in liberation), being different while bound; the liberated self exists as pure consciousness alone.

name: Aupamanyava
summary: Early etymologist cited by Yāska, e.g. for 'ṛṣi from seeing: he saw the hymns' (Nirukta 2.11).

name: Avaidyanāth
summary: Mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, in the later 20th century.

name: Āvaṭya
summary: Sage, 'bearer of a body' (tanudhara), who questions Jaigīṣavya in YBh 3.18 about whether the happiness of contentment too belongs to suffering.

name: Aviddhakarṇa
summary: Early Naiyāyika known only from citations in Buddhist works (Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha and Kamalaśīla's commentary), among them arguments for Īśvara.
notes: Known only through opponents' reports; details unverified.

name: Auvaiyār (of the Vināyakar akaval)
summary: The poetess to whom the Vināyakar akaval, a Siddha-revered hymn of the inner yoga, is ascribed; several Tamil poetesses of different centuries bear the name.

name: Ayāsya Āṅgirasa
summary: Identified with the breath in the mouth, the essence (rasa) of the limbs, in the udgītha passages (BAU 1.3.8, 1.3.19; ChU 1.2.12).

name: Āydakki Lakkamma
summary: Mārayya's wife, a vacanakāra remembered for sending back rice gathered beyond the day's need, teaching that kāyaka and dāsōha exclude hoarding.

name: Āydakki Mārayya
summary: The śaraṇa who lived by gleaning rice grains fallen in the market; his vacana declares that kāyaka is Kailāsa.

name: Aḻukaṇṇi (Aḻukaṇic cittar)
summary: Siddhar poet of forty stanzas in veiled imagery of the root, the six supports and the ninety-six principles, addressed to 'my Kaṇṇammā'; he tells how the guru came, showed his own form and burnt the supports and letters.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Nothing is recalled of his life. The name means 'weeping-eyed'; whether the poet is a man or a woman is not settled here.

name: Bādarāyaṇa

tradition.text: identical with Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

notes: The identification with Vyāsa (tch:vyasa) is the tradition's; Śaṅkara refers to the sūtrakāra as Vyāsa in places. Scholars treat them as distinct.
summary: Author (tradition) or final redactor (scholarly) of the Brahma Sūtras; he states his own view by name at several points (e.g. BS 1.3.33, 3.4.1, 4.4.7, 4.4.12) against Jaimini, Bādari and others.
alt_notes: Identified with Vyāsa in Vedānta tradition; Mīmāṃsā contribution only here.
alt_summary: Cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra as an authority: the injunction is valid 'in Bādarāyaṇa's view' because it depends on nothing else (MS 1.1.5); women are eligible for rites because the class is meant (MS 6.1.8); also MS 5.2.19, 10.8.44, 11.1.63. Author of the Brahma Sūtra.

name: Bādari
summary: Early Mīmāṃsā teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: holds that only substances, qualities and purificatory acts are subsidiaries (MS 3.1.3) and that the injunctions are for all four varṇas (MS 6.1.27, a view rejected); also cited at MS 8.3.6 and in the Brahma Sūtra.
alt_summary: Early teacher cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.2.30; 3.1.11; 4.3.7; 4.4.10) and in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: the path of the gods leads to the conditioned (kārya) Brahman; the liberated has no body.

name: Bāl Gaṅgādhar Tilak
summary: Scholar and political leader whose Gītā Rahasya (1915) argues that the Gītā teaches action (karma-yoga) by the enlightened rather than renunciation.
notes: Recent (post-1800); no initiatory lineage — lineage field records the text-tradition he interpreted.

name: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
summary: Orissan scholar trained in Madhva's school who joined the Gauḍīyas; wrote the Govinda-bhāṣya (the school's Brahma Sūtra commentary), Prameyaratnāvalī, Siddhāntaratna and Gītābhūṣaṇa, defending the Gauḍīyas at Jaipur.
alt_summary: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Gītābhūṣaṇa (and the Govinda-bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra).

name: Bālakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Later Śuddhādvaita author to whom the Prameyaratnārṇava is attributed.

name: Bālarāma Udāsīna
summary: Modern scholar of the Udāsīna order to whom the Vidvattoṣiṇī on the Tattvakaumudī is ascribed.

name: Bali
summary: In the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (5.22-29), the asura king who remembers his father Virocana's teaching on the realm beyond the worlds, inquires, and attains self-knowledge while continuing to rule.
alt_summary: The defeated Daitya king who tells Indra that Time takes and gives all, and bears his fall without grief (12.216–218).

name: Bālnāth
summary: Nāth yogī associated with Tilla Jogian (Gorakh Ṭillā) in the Salt Range; in Wāris Shāh's Hīr he gives Rāñjhā the split-ear initiation.
notes: Distinct from the Himachali folk deity Bābā Bālaknāth (U59), with whom he is sometimes confused.

name: Barku Vārṣṇa
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is sight (BAU 4.1.4); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

name: Basava
summary: Basava (Basavaṇṇa, Basaveśvara), minister at the Kalacuri court of Bijjala in Kalyāṇa, the central figure of the twelfth-century śaraṇa movement; his vacanas, signed Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, teach devotion, humility before devotees, work as worship, sharing, and the equality of all who wear the liṅga.

realization_account.text: Born to a brāhmaṇa family, he refused the sacred-thread initiation, took refuge at Kūḍalasaṅgama where Śiva as Saṅgamadēva became his lord, and was sent to Kalyāṇa, where as treasurer and minister he served the devotees, gathered the śaraṇas and founded the Anubhava Maṇṭapa; after the upheaval that followed an intercaste marriage among the śaraṇas he returned to Kūḍalasaṅgama and became one with the liṅga there.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Parents in the hagiographies: Mādarasa and Mādalāmbike (moderate). In the Pañcācārya account he is a great devotee within an older stream; in the śaraṇa account the founder. A Jaina narrative of Bijjala's reign gives a hostile account of these events (low confidence).

name: Bāṣkala
summary: Eponym of the Bāṣkala recension of the Ṛgveda, named in the Purāṇic accounts among the pupils in Paila's line.
notes: Position in the pupil lists recalled from memory (low).

name: Baudhāyana
summary: Founder (sūtrakāra) of the Baudhāyana branch of the Taittirīya school; its Kalpasūtra is ascribed to him.

scholarly.text: Śrautasūtra among the oldest sūtras (mid-1st millennium BCE); Dharmasūtra core c. 2nd c. BCE

name: Pattirakiriyār (Bhadragiri)
summary: King of Ujjain turned renouncer and disciple of Paṭṭiṉattār; his 'Lament for true knowledge' asks, in 231 couplets, 'when will the day come' of renunciation, inner yoga and knowledge. The tradition identifies him with Bhartṛhari, king of Ujjain.

realization_account.text: Seeing the stake burn when Paṭṭiṉattār was wrongly condemned, and learning the truth about his court, the king renounced and followed him; living on alms at Tiruviṭaimarutūr, he was chided by his guru for keeping a begging-bowl and a dog ('a householder!'), cast both away, and attained release before his guru.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The identification with Bhartṛhari (tch:bhartrhari) is the tradition's; scholars do not accept it. Story recalled at low–moderate confidence.

name: Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām
summary: Aghora teacher of Varanasi who founded the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh (1961) and a leprosy service ashram, taught Aghora as naturalness, service and the rejection of caste and social evils, and travelled abroad; he died in 1992.

name: Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī
summary: Son of Bhaktivinoda; founder of the Gauḍīya Maṭha (1920s), who gave renunciation (sannyāsa) a missionary form and criticised premature esoteric practice and caste-based guru lineages.

name: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
summary: Disciple of Bhaktisiddhānta; founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (1966), which spread the chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahāmantra worldwide.

name: Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura (Kedarnath Datta)
summary: Magistrate and writer who revived Gauḍīya learning in the 19th c. (Jaiva Dharma and many works) and identified Māyāpur as Caitanya's birthplace.

name: Bharadvāja
summary: Bharadvāja Bārhaspatya, founder of the family of Ṛgveda book 6, whose vision of the light set in the heart (6.9.5–6) is among the Veda's inner experiences; one of the seven seers of RV 10.137.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).
alt_summary: Seer who questions Bhṛgu in the Mokṣadharma (12.175–185), raising doubts about the existence of a living self in a body made of elements.
U02 contribution: in TB 3.10.11.3–5 he spends three lives as a Vedic student and is shown by Indra that the Vedas are endless, then taught the Sāvitra fire as 'all knowledge'.
Vedic seer who asks Yājñavalkya about the tāraka (Rāmottaratāpanī; Tārasāra) and is among the rudrākṣa-wearing sages (Rudrākṣajābāla); named among the kuṭīcaka renouncers (Bhikṣuka).

name: Bharata (Rāma's brother)
summary: Rāma's brother, who refuses the throne and rules as Rāma's regent; Rāma's teachings on impermanence and kingship are addressed to him (2.100–105).
notes: Disambiguated from Bharata Muni (tch:bharata-muni).

name: Bhāratītīrtha
summary: Śṛṅgeri pontiff of the 14th century, associate of Vidyāraṇya; credited with part of the Pañcadaśī, the Vaiyāsikanyāyamālā and (by some) the Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka.

name: Bhārgava (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others.

name: Bhārgava Vaidarbhi
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks how many deities support a being (PrU 2).
alt_summary: The seer to whom the Prāṇa hymn of the Atharvaveda (AVŚ 11.4) is ascribed.
notes: Ascription taken from the hymn header of the local Atharvaveda text (checked).

name: Bhartṛhari (Bharthari, the Nāth king-yogī)
summary: King of Ujjain in Nāth legend who renounced his throne — in the best-known telling after the fruit of immortality he gave his queen returned to him through her lover — and became a disciple of Gorakh; founder of the Bharthari (Vairāg) panth; hero of sung sagas; counted among the Marathi nine Nāths. Tradition often identifies him with the poet of the three śatakas and with Bhartṛhari the grammarian.
notes: Distinct id from tch:bhartrhari (the grammarian of the Vākyapadīya, U31). The tradition's identification of the three is not accepted by scholars.

name: Bhartṛmitra
summary: Pre-Kumārila Mīmāṃsaka whom the Nyāyaratnākara names among those who had made Mīmāṃsā 'Lokāyata' (ŚV pratijñā 10) — by the commentators' account, by denying that obligatory and prohibited acts bear fruit. His work is lost.

name: Bhartṛprapañca
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin and commentator on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (and reportedly the Kaṭha) Upaniṣad; taught that Brahman is both one and many like the ocean and its waves, that the world is its real modification, and that liberation needs knowledge combined with works. Known only from his critics Śaṅkara, Sureśvara and Ānandagiri.

scholarly.text: before Śaṅkara (6th–7th c. CE or earlier)

notes: The list of eight 'states' (avasthā) of Brahman ascribed to him by Sureśvara is recalled with low confidence and not recorded as a teaching.
alt_notes: Views reported by opponents (reported_by_opponent).
alt_summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin who held difference-and-non-difference between Brahman and the world/selves and taught that liberation requires knowledge combined with works; known through Śaṅkara's and Sureśvara's refutations in their Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentaries.

name: Bharuci
summary: Ancient Vedāntin named by Rāmānuja among the earlier teachers; possibly the same as the Dharmaśāstra commentator Bhāruci (uncertain).

name: Bhāsarvajña
summary: Kashmiri Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyasāra and its auto-commentary Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, known for independent positions: only three means of knowledge, and liberation as the cessation of pain qualified by the experience of eternal bliss. A Śaiva of Pāśupata orientation.
notes: The Ratnaṭīkā on the Pāśupata Gaṇakārikā is also attributed to him (attribution recalled, not checked).
alt_summary: Naiyāyika author of the Nyāyasāra (with its self-commentary Nyāyabhūṣaṇa) and a Pāśupata: the Ratnaṭīkā on the Gaṇakārikā is ascribed to him, and Dalal's edition ascribes the Gaṇakārikā verses to him too.

name: Bhāskara (Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, the Vedāntin)
summary: Author of the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya that is the classic statement of aupādhika bhedābheda: Brahman really transforms through its power; souls are its parts, distinguished by real adjuncts; liberation after death through knowledge combined with lifelong duty. He attacked Śaṅkara's māyāvāda as Mahāyāna Buddhism in Vedic dress; Vācaspati Miśra and later Advaitins answer him.
notes: Often described as a tridaṇḍin (Vaiṣṇava-style renouncer) — low confidence. Distinct from the mathematician Bhāskara and from Bhāskararāya.
alt_summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin credited with a Gītā commentary defending the combination of knowledge and works.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Bhāskara (author of the Śivasūtravārttika)
summary: Kashmiri teacher, 'son of Bhaṭṭa Divākara', who wrote the Śivasūtravārttika on the teaching received from Śrīkaṇṭhabhaṭṭa, giving an account of the Śiva Sūtra's revelation and lineage that differs from Kṣemarāja's.

scholarly.text: c. 10th-11th c. CE; relation to Kṣemarāja debated

notes: Id disambiguated from tch:bhaskara (the Bhedābheda Vedāntin) and tch:bhaskarakantha.

name: Bhāskarakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmiri Paṇḍit, author of the Mokṣopāyaṭīkā and (outside U06) of the Bhāskarī commentary on Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī.
alt_summary: 18th-century Kashmiri scholar, author of the Bhāskarī on Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and of a commentary on the Mokṣopāya (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha); identified by many with the Rājānaka Bhāskara who rendered Lal Ded's vākhs into Sanskrit verse.
notes: Identification with the Lallāvākyāni translator is low confidence.

name: Bhāskararāya
summary: In this unit: author of the Guptavatī commentary on the Devī Māhātmya (his Śrīvidyā works belong to U23).
alt_summary: U04 contribution: commented on the Tripurā, Bhāvanā and Kaula Upaniṣads.

name: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara Miśra
summary: Author of the Jñānayajña, commentary on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka.
alt_summary: Commentator on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka (Jñānayajña).

name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa
summary: Author of the Stavacintāmaṇi, a hymn to Śiva quoted in Utpaladeva's commentary on the Śivadṛṣṭi as the work of a 'former teacher' (pūrvaguru).

name: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Siddhāntakaumudī and other Pāṇinian works.

name: Bhāva Bṛhaspati
summary: Pāśupata ācārya who, according to the Prabhāsa (Bhadrakālī) inscription of 1169 CE, became head of Somanātha and directed its restoration under the Caulukya king Kumārapāla.

name: Bhavadāsa
summary: Commentator on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra before Kumārila, who mentions him (ŚV pratijñā 63); the Nyāyaratnākara reports that he split MS 1.1.4 into two sūtras. His work is lost.

name: Bhavadeva Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tautātitamatatilaka, an exposition of Kumārila's doctrine.

name: Bhāvāgaṇeśa
summary: Pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu; author of the Tattvayāthārthyadīpana on the Tattvasamāsa.
alt_summary: Pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu and author of a Dīpikā on the Yoga Sūtra that condenses his teacher's Vārttika.

name: Bhavānanda Siddhāntavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Bhavānandī sub-commentary on the Dīdhiti.

name: Bhavanātha
summary: Prābhākara author of the Nayaviveka.

name: Bhikṣu Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 10.117 on the giving of wealth and food ('he who eats alone has only sin').
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Bhīma (Bhīmasena)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Second Pāṇḍava; argues for artha and action against Yudhiṣṭhira's forbearance (3.34; 12.10); instructed by Hanumān on the ages and the duties of the varṇas (3.147–150).

name: Bhīmakavi
summary: Kannada poet who rendered the Basava Purāṇa into ṣaṭpadi verse in 1369.

name: Bhiṣag Ātharvaṇa
summary: The 'physician, son of Atharvan', seer of the hymn to healing plants RV 10.97.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Bhīṣma (Devavrata, Gāṅgeya)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Son of Śaṃtanu and Gaṅgā, the Kuru elder who vowed celibacy; granted mastery over the moment of his death, he lies on a bed of arrows waiting for the sun's northern course (6.114.89–98) and instructs Yudhiṣṭhira in Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma (Śāntiparvan) and in the Anuśāsana, including the thousand names of Viṣṇu; at death his self, restrained in all the openings, pierces the crown and rises to heaven (13.154.5).

name: Bhoja
summary: Paramāra king of Dhārā and polymath, author of the Rājamārtaṇḍa, a concise vṛtti on the Yoga Sūtra; its introductory verses praise him for works on grammar, on the Pātañjala (yoga) and on medicine.
alt_summary: Scholar-king of Mālava, author of the Siddhānta manual Tattvaprakāśa and (attributed) the ritual Siddhāntasārapaddhati, as well as the Yoga commentary Rājamārtaṇḍa.
Paramāra king of Dhārā, author of a Siddhānta ritual manual (Siddhāntasārapaddhati) and of the doctrinal Tattvaprakāśa, besides works in other fields.
notes: Contribution from U08; registry id shared with U10 (Rājamārtaṇḍa).

name: Bhṛgu Vāruṇi
summary: Son of Varuṇa who asks his father to teach him brahman and, by repeated tapas, realizes in turn that food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss are brahman (TU 3.1-6: 'the knowledge of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa').
notes: Contribution of lin:upanisadic; other units record the Purāṇic and astrological Bhṛgu.
alt_notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
alt_summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes several adhikāras on temple ritual (Kriyādhikāra, Khilādhikāra, Prakīrṇādhikāra and others).

Seer who recites Manu's teaching in the Manusmṛti (1.59–60), one of Manu's ten mind-born sons (1.35); as Bhṛgu Vāruṇi, son of Varuṇa, he journeys through the other world in ŚB 11.6.1 and JB 1.42–44 (and learns Brahman in TU 3).
Ancient seer who answers Bharadvāja on creation, the elements, the self, the varṇas and the āśramas (12.175–185).
Eponymous ancestor of the Bhārgava priests; with the Aṅgirases the source of the Atharvaveda (Bhṛgvaṅgirasaḥ); in the Ṛgveda the Bhṛgus are among those who brought fire to men.

name: Bhujyu Lāhyāyani
summary: Asks Yājñavalkya where the descendants of Parikṣit went (BAU 3.3); he had heard of it in Madra from a gandharva.

name: Bhuśuṇḍa
summary: The ancient crow living on a wish-fulfilling tree on a peak of Meru, who tells Vasiṣṭha how contemplation of the breath (prāṇa-cintā) made him outlive many world-ages (Mokṣopāya 6.14-27; Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Nirvāṇa, pūrvārdha). The Rāmcaritmānas's Kāk Bhuśuṇḍi is a related figure.

realization_account.text: Resting in the Self through contemplation of the breath, he remains unaffected by the dissolutions of the worlds he has witnessed.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Questioner in the Bṛhajjābāla (of Kālāgnirudra) and Bhasmajābāla (of Mahādeva) on sacred ash.

name: Bhūtirāja
summary: A Kashmiri Śaiva teacher named among Abhinavagupta's teachers and praised by Ānandabhaṭṭa (Vijñānakaumudī, opening) with Somānanda and Utpala among those who descended to restore the Śaiva teaching.
notes: Subject taught to Abhinavagupta not verified here.

name: Bījārām
summary: Disciple and successor of Kīnārām at Krīm Kuṇḍ (tradition).
notes: The full succession list of Krīm Kuṇḍ heads is not reproduced (gap); only names recalled with some confidence are given.

name: Bilvamaṅgala (Līlāśuka)
summary: Poet of the Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta, revered by Caitanya; placed by the Vallabha tradition in Viṣṇusvāmin's line.

name: Bodhāyana (the Vṛttikāra)
summary: Author of an extensive vṛtti on the Brahma Sūtras which Rāmānuja says earlier teachers abridged and which he follows; claimed as a precursor of Viśiṣṭādvaita.

name: Bodhya
summary: A tranquil sage who, questioned by King Nahuṣa, names six teachers: Piṅgalā, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden (Mahābhārata 12.171.57-61).

name: Bogar (Pōkar)
summary: Siddhar of Palani, alchemist and physician: the tradition says he made the image of Murukaṉ as Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi at Palani from nine poisonous minerals (navapāṣāṇam), travelled to China (Cīṉam) and flew through the air, and recorded medicine, alchemy and kāya kaṟpam in the 'Seven Thousand' (Pōkar ēḻāyiram). Disciple of Kālāṅki Nātar; teacher of Pulippāṇi, Koṅkaṇar and Karuvūrār.
places: Palani — samādhi within the hill temple (tradition)

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

realization_account.text: Bogar is said to have consecrated the navapāṣāṇa image at Palani and to have entered samādhi beneath the shrine, where he abides; his own verses describe journeys to China and flights by the power of kaḷikai pills (recorded as his claim).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The Chinese connection is the text's and tradition's claim; modern theories identifying him with a Chinese Taoist are outside the tradition and not recorded. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Bopadeva
summary: Author of the Mugdhabodha grammar.

name: Brahmā (as first teacher)
summary: The first of the gods, maker and protector of the world, who taught the knowledge of brahman to his eldest son Atharvan (MuU 1.1.1); the first link of teacher-lines (ChU 3.11.4, 8.15.1); in KauU 1.5-7 he questions the knower arriving in the brahma-world.
alt_summary: U04 contribution: answers Nārada (Kalisantaraṇa, Nāradaparivrājaka 2), Vaiśravaṇa (Pāśupatabrahma), Paippalāda (Śarabha); taught by Viṣṇu (Yogatattva) and Śiva (Yogaśikhā); as Parameṣṭhin teaches Āśvalāyana (Kaivalya).

name: Brahmadatta
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara (or early) Vedāntin reported to have held that the knowledge from the Upaniṣads must be meditated upon throughout life (knowledge as an injunction to meditation) and that the individual self is not eternal; known through reports by Sureśvara and Yāmuna.

name: Brahmānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Advaita scholar who wrote the Laghucandrikā on Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi, answering the Mādhva Rāmācārya's Taraṅgiṇī.
alt_summary: Author of the Laghucandrikā ('Gauḍa-Brahmānandī') on the Advaitasiddhi and of the Nyāyaratnāvalī on the Siddhāntabindu.

name: Brahmanandin (Ṭaṅka)
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin, the 'Vākyakāra', author of the Vākya cited by Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and others.

name: Brahmaṇya Tīrtha
summary: The ascetic of Abbūr who gave renunciation to Vyāsatīrtha; the colophons of the Nyāyāmṛta name Vyāsatīrtha as his disciple.
notes: Discipleship stated in the Nyāyāmṛta colophons checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

name: Brahmatantra Svatantra Jīyar
summary: Disciple of Vedānta Deśika and first head of the Parakāla maṭha (later at Mysore) in the Vaṭakalai line.

name: Bṛhadārya
summary: Number 14 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Bṛhadratha
summary: A king of the Ikṣvāku line who, having installed his son and renounced his kingdom, practised austerities in the forest and asked Śākāyanya about the self, lamenting the foulness of the body and the transience of all things (MaiU 1.2-4).

name: Bṛhaspati
summary: Preceptor of the gods who asks Yājñavalkya about Kurukṣetra/Avimukta (Jābāla 1; Rāmottaratāpanī).
alt_summary: Preceptor of the gods; he officiates at Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice (12.323) and questions Prajāpati Manu on the highest knowledge (12.194).
U02 contribution: the preceptor of the gods, to whom the Bṛhaspatismṛti is ascribed; in the Mahābhāṣya he teaches Indra words one by one. The Lokāyata tradition's Bṛhaspati is treated by U33.

name: Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of the hymn on knowledge and speech (RV 10.71) and, with alternatives, of the hymn on the birth of the gods (10.72).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Bṛhaspati (Saiddhāntika)
summary: An early Siddhānta authority cited by later exegetes (Rāmakaṇṭha, Abhinavagupta) as pre-dating or contemporary with Sadyojyoti; his work is lost except in citations (a title Śivatanu(śāstra) is associated with him — low confidence).
notes: Distinct from the Vedic Bṛhaspati and from the Lokāyata founder of the same name.

name: Buddhamitra
summary: Buddhist teacher of Vasubandhu according to Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu, which tells that he was defeated in debate by the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa before a king at Ayodhyā; Vasubandhu is said to have answered with his (lost) Paramārthasaptati.
notes: Lineage assignment follows the biography's setting; verify.

name: Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi
summary: One of the five great householders and great Vedic scholars who asked 'what is our self, what is brahman?' and, with Uddālaka Āruṇi, went to Aśvapati Kaikeya; each had venerated only one part of the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11-17).

name: Caikitāyana Dālbhya
summary: One of three experts on the udgītha who discuss the support of the sāman (ChU 1.8).

name: Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya (Viśvambhara Miśra, Nimāi, Gaurāṅga, Mahāprabhu)
summary: Founder figure of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism: Navadvīpa scholar who after initiation at Gayā led nocturnal congregational chanting, took renunciation, travelled to south India and Vṛndāvana, and lived his last eighteen years at Purī absorbed in Rādhā's love for Kṛṣṇa. His only writing is the Śikṣāṣṭaka; his teaching was given to Rūpa, Sanātana, Rāmānanda and others and recorded by his biographers.

realization_account.text: Kṛṣṇa himself, appearing with the mood and golden complexion of Rādhā to taste her love (CC 1.1.5–6); the hidden (channa) avatāra and yuga-avatāra of Kali who inaugurated the chanting of the name; in his last years he passed through states of divine madness (divyonmāda); he disappeared at Purī in 1533 (accounts differ on how).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cākkiya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Buddhist who became Śiva's devotee while keeping the Buddhist robe; the first day, seeing a liṅga, he threw a stone at it in ecstasy and made that his daily worship; one day he forgot and ran back without eating, and Śiva appeared to him.

realization_account.text: A Buddhist who became Śiva's devotee while keeping the Buddhist robe; the first day, seeing a liṅga, he threw a stone at it in ecstasy and made that his daily worship; one day he forgot and ran back without eating, and Śiva appeared to him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cāmarasa
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet at the court of Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara, author of the Prabhuliṅgalīle on Allama Prabhu.

name: Tiruñāṉacampantar
summary: Child-saint and the most prolific Tēvāram poet (Tirumuṟai 1–3); exemplar of the son's path (satputra-mārga, kriyā); champion of Śaivism against the Jains at Madurai.

tradition.text: lived sixteen years

scholarly.text: 7th c.; contemporary of Appar, the Pāṇṭiya Neṭumāṟaṉ and Ciṟuttoṇṭar (Vātāpi, 642)

places: Nallūr Perumaṇam (union with Śiva at his wedding)

realization_account.text: At three, left on the tank's edge at Cīkāḻi, he cried and Umā fed him the milk of divine knowledge in a golden cup; asked who had fed him, he sang his first hymn pointing to Śiva and Umā. He went on pilgrimage with the bard Tirunīlakaṇṭa Yāḻppāṇar, was invited to Madurai by the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār and the minister Kulacciṟaiyār, cured the king's fever with sacred ash, and won the fire and water ordeals against the Jains. At sixteen, at his wedding at Nallūr Perumaṇam, he entered a divine light with his bride and all the guests.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Candragomin
summary: Buddhist lay scholar, author of the Cāndra grammar (his Buddhist works belong to other units).

name: Candramati
summary: Author of the Daśapadārthaśāstra, a Vaiśeṣika treatise of ten categories preserved only in Xuanzang's Chinese translation.
notes: The alternative name form is recalled with low confidence.

name: Candrānanda
summary: Author of the Vṛtti on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra that transmits the older recension of the sūtras.

name: Candraśekhara Bhāratī III
summary: Pontiff of Śṛṅgeri (1892–1954), revered in the tradition as a jīvanmukta given to long absorption.

name: Candraśekharendra Sarasvatī
summary: Pontiff of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi pīṭha (1894–1994), teacher of Advaita and Vedic dharma.

name: Caṇṭēcura Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin boy who, tending the village cows, made a sand liṅga and bathed it with their milk; when his father kicked over the milk pots he struck at his father's legs with the staff, which became an axe; Śiva made him Caṇṭēcuran, chief of his attendants, heir to his leftover garlands and offerings.

realization_account.text: A brahmin boy who, tending the village cows, made a sand liṅga and bathed it with their milk; when his father kicked over the milk pots he struck at his father's legs with the staff, which became an axe; Śiva made him Caṇṭēcuran, chief of his attendants, heir to his leftover garlands and offerings.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Carpaṭanātha
summary: A Nāth siddha (Carpaṭi in HYP 1.6) to whom Hindi sayings are ascribed (Nāth Siddhoṁ kī Bāniyāṁ); in Chamba tradition the guru of the founder-king of Chamba; also named among alchemical siddhas; one of the Marathi nine Nāths (Carpaṭnāth).

name: Caṭaiya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Cuntarar's father, an Ādiśaiva brahmin.

realization_account.text: Cuntarar's father, an Ādiśaiva brahmin.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Catti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He cut out the tongues of those who reviled Śiva's devotees.

realization_account.text: He cut out the tongues of those who reviled Śiva's devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Caturbhujdās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, son of Kumbhandās.

name: Cauraṅgīnātha
summary: A Nāth siddha (Cauraṅgī in HYP 1.5): a prince whose hands and feet were cut off at a stepmother's false accusation and who was restored by the Nāth gurus — known in Punjab as Pūraṇ Bhagat and in Telugu as Sāraṅgadhara. The Prāṇ Saṅkalī is ascribed to him.

realization_account.text: Restored in body by the guru's grace after twelve years of practice (the tradition's story in its several versions).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cēkkiḻār
summary: Minister of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (Anapāyaṉ), author of the Periya Purāṇam, the twelfth Tirumuṟai.

realization_account.text: Seeing the king delight in the Jain epic Cīvakacintāmaṇi, he turned him to the lives of Śiva's devotees; at Chidambaram Śiva gave him the first word 'ulakelām' and he completed the work in a year.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cennabasava
summary: Cennabasava (Cennabasavaṇṇa), Basava's nephew, honoured as the master of ṣaṭsthala doctrine; his vacanas are signed Kūḍalacennasaṅgamadēva, and after the Kalyāṇa upheaval he led the śaraṇas with the vacana manuscripts to Uḷavi.

realization_account.text: Son of Basava's sister Akkanāgamma; the Śūnyasampādane has Allama acknowledge his knowledge of the sthalas, and he gives liṅga-initiation to Siddharāma; he attained union at Uḷavi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan Nampūtirippāṭ
summary: Kerala brahmin of the Cēnnās family — hereditary tantris of the Guruvāyūr temple — and author of the Tantrasamuccaya, the standard manual of Kerala temple ritual.

name: Cēntaṉār
summary: Poet of the Tiruvicaippā and of the benedictory Tiruppallāṇṭu (Tirumuṟai 9).

name: Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Cēra king who heard the anklets of Naṭarāja's dance at the end of his daily worship; friend of Cuntarar, he rode with him to Kailāsa on a horse into whose ear he whispered the five syllables, and recited his Ulā there.

realization_account.text: A Cēra king who heard the anklets of Naṭarāja's dance at the end of his daily worship; friend of Cuntarar, he rode with him to Kailāsa on a horse into whose ear he whispered the five syllables, and recited his Ulā there.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ceruttuṇai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He cut the nose of the Pallava queen who smelled a flower meant for Śiva in the temple at Tiruvārūr.

realization_account.text: He cut the nose of the Pallava queen who smelled a flower meant for Śiva in the temple at Tiruvārūr.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Swami Chinmayananda
summary: Advaita teacher (1916–1993), disciple of Sivananda and Tapovan Maharaj, founder of the Chinmaya Mission, who taught the prasthāna-traya and prakaraṇas in English.

name: Chītsvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a Caube of Mathurā.

name: Cinnambhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tarkabhāṣāprakāśikā on Keśava Miśra's Tarkabhāṣā.

name: Ciṟappuli Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who fed devotees and performed sacrifices for Śiva.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who fed devotees and performed sacrifices for Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Citra Gāṅgyāyani
alt_names: Citra Gārgyāyaṇi (reading of the Advaita-Śāradā text)
summary: A king who, about to sacrifice, questions Śvetaketu on the closed place of the world, then teaches Āruṇi (who comes fuel in hand) the path to the world of brahman (KauU 1.1-7).

name: Citsukha
summary: Dialectical Advaitin, author of the Tattvapradīpikā and of commentaries on the Khaṇḍana, the Brahmasiddhi and the Nyāyamakaranda; pupil of Jñānottama.

name: Civañāṉa Muṉivar
summary: Monk of the Tiruvāvaṭuturai ātīṉam, the classical scholastic of Tamil Siddhānta: the Civañāṉa Māpāṭiyam and Ciṟṟurai on the Civañāṉa Pōtam, a commentary on the Cittiyār, the first part of the Kāñci Purāṇam, grammatical works and a Tamil rendering of the Tarkasaṅgraha.

name: Cōmāci Māṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who performed Vedic sacrifices dedicated to Śiva and was a friend of Cuntarar.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who performed Vedic sacrifices dedicated to Śiva and was a friend of Cuntarar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cūḍālā
summary: Queen of Mālava who attained self-knowledge by her own inquiry and powers through breath-discipline; unable to teach her husband Śikhidhvaja as herself, she came to him in the forest disguised as the young brāhmaṇa Kumbha and led him to realization (Mokṣopāya 6.81-114; Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Nirvāṇa, pūrvārdha).

realization_account.text: Through daily inquiry into what the self is she found the Self and 'shone' so that her husband remarked on her changed radiance (MU 6.82-83 'cūḍālā-prabodha', 'cūḍālātmalābha').
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cuntaramūrtti (Cuntarar)
summary: Third Tēvāram poet (Tirumuṟai 7); exemplar of the friend's path (sakhā-mārga, yoga); author of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai, the list of devotees on which the cult of the sixty-three rests.

realization_account.text: An Ādiśaiva boy of Tirunāvalūr adopted by the chieftain Naracinka Muṉaiyaraiyar; on his wedding day an old brahmin produced a deed showing Cuntarar's grandfather had pledged his line as the brahmin's slaves; followed to Tiruveṇṇeynallūr, the old man vanished into the temple — Śiva himself — and Cuntarar sang 'Pittā' ('Madman!'). Śiva later acted as his messenger to his wife Paravai. With Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ he rode to Kailāsa on a white elephant sent by Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa
summary: Seer who taught the honey-doctrine (madhu-vidyā) to the two Aśvins through a horse's head, as recounted with Ṛgvedic verses at BAU 2.5.16-19.

name: Daivarāti Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā instructed by Yājñavalkya in the Mokṣadharma (12.298–306).
notes: Whether he is the Upaniṣadic Janaka (tch:janaka) is not asserted.

name: Dakṣiṇā Prājāpatyā
summary: Named (beside Divya Āṅgirasa) as ṛṣikā of the hymn in praise of the sacrificial gift, RV 10.107.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Dāmodaradās Harsānī
summary: Vallabha's first disciple, initiated with brahmasambandha the morning after the Gokul revelation (tradition).

name: Dārā Shikoh
summary: Mughal prince (1615–1659) who with pandits translated some fifty Upaniṣads into Persian (Sirr-i Akbar, 1657).

name: Dāruka
summary: A gaṇa dear to Śiva, paired with Reṇuka among the pramathas; Reṇuka's leap over him in Śiva's assembly is the occasion of Reṇuka's descent (SSM 2.27; 3.67–77).
notes: In Pañcācārya yuga-lists Dāruka is also named among the ācāryas of an earlier age (low confidence).

name: Dattātreya
summary: Son of Atri and Anasūyā, counted the sixth avatāra in the Bhāgavata (1.3.11: he taught ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda and others); Yadu and the Haihayas gained yogic powers from him (2.7.4). The tradition identifies him with the unnamed avadhūta who teaches King Yadu his twenty-four teachers (Bhāgavata 11.7-9), and ascribes to him the Avadhūta Gītā and the Jīvanmukta Gītā. Revered as the ādiguru of the Datta tradition and in the Nāth lineages.

realization_account.text: Son of Atri and Anasūyā (a portion of Viṣṇu; in some accounts of the Trimūrti), the sixth avatāra who 'taught ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda and others' (BhP 1.3.11); an avadhūta who hid his yoga under outward impurity (MkP 16-19); in the Bhāgavata he tells of his twenty-four teachers (BhP 11.7-9, U06).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: The avadhūta yogin of the Purāṇas whose teaching to Alarka (MkP 37-43) is the Mārkaṇḍeya's yoga: discrimination of self and body, posture, breath, dhāraṇā, obstacles, powers, Oṃ and the signs of death.

Son of Atri and Anasūyā, regarded as a form of Viṣṇu (or of the trimūrti) who 'gave himself' (datta) to Atri; in the minor Upaniṣads he teaches Sāṅkṛti the eightfold yoga (Darśana) and the nature of the avadhūta (Avadhūta), is named among the paramahaṃsas who live with unmanifest marks (Jābāla 6, Bhikṣuka, Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86), and is the 'most manifest' form of Brahman in Śāṇḍilya 3.

U21 contribution: in Marathi Nāth tradition Dattātreya instructs the Nāths (Navanātha Bhaktisāra) and appears with Gorakṣa (Gorakṣaguṭikā 1.24); Aghora regards him as ādiguru, who appeared to Kīnārām at Girnar and whose form was Bābā Kālūrām.

name: Dayānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Founder of the Ārya Samāj (1875); commented on the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda and wrote the Ṛgvedādibhāṣyabhūmikā, teaching that the Saṃhitās alone are revelation, that they teach one God under many names, and that Vedic study is open to all.

name: Swami Dayananda Saraswati (Arsha Vidya)
summary: Advaita teacher (1930–2015) of the traditional method of teaching (sampradāya) through the texts; founder of the Arsha Vidya Gurukulam. Distinct from the 19th-c. founder of the Ārya Samāj.

name: Devabodha
summary: Early commentator on the Mahābhārata (Jñānadīpikā).

name: Devācārya
summary: Nimbārka scholar, author of the Brahma Sūtra commentary Siddhāntajāhnavī.

name: Devahūti
summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of the sage Kardama and mother of Kapila; the questioner of the Kapila Gītā, who asks for a devotion suited to her and attains liberation.

realization_account.text: Following her son's instruction she practised devotional yoga at Bindusaras, her body withered unnoticed, and she attained the Lord; the place became Siddhapada (Bhāgavata 3.33).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of Kardama and mother of Kapila, who asked her son for the path to liberation, received the Kapila Gītā and attained perfection through its yoga (BhP 3.25-33).

name: Devala (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others. The Mahābhārata presents an Asita Devala as teacher of related doctrines; the identity is uncertain.

name: Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Smṛticandrikā.

name: Dēvara Dāsimayya
summary: The weaver-saint (Jēḍara Dāsimayya) of Muddanūru, reckoned by the tradition among the earliest vacanakāras, before Basava; his vacanas, signed Rāmanātha, deny that the self is male or female.

tradition.text: before Basava

scholarly.text: 10th–11th c. (debated; some place him closer to Basava)

notes: Whether 'Dēvara' and 'Jēḍara' Dāsimayya are one person is debated.

name: Devarāja Yajvan
summary: Commentator on the Nighaṇṭu.

name: Devasvāmin
summary: Author of a bhāṣya on the Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa.

name: The Goddess (Devī)
summary: The supreme Goddess, appearing as Bhuvaneśvarī, who teaches Himālaya and the gods in the Devī Gītā (Devī Bhāgavata 7.31-40): she is consciousness, supreme Brahman, whose power is māyā.

name: Dhanapati Sūri
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on Śaṅkara's Gītābhāṣya.

name: Piḷḷai Uṟaṅgāvilli Dāsar
summary: Wrestler of Uṟaiyūr whom, the tradition says, Rāmānuja turned from infatuation with his wife's eyes to the eyes of Raṅganātha; an exemplar of devotion regardless of birth.

name: Dhanvantari (Taṉvantiri)
summary: The physician of the gods, counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars in the popular list, with a samādhi place at Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil, the shrine of Śiva as the divine physician.
places: Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; the Āyurvedic account belongs to U30. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Dharma (the god; Yama Dharmarāja)
summary: The deity Dharma, father of Yudhiṣṭhira; he tests his son as the Yakṣa at the lake (3.297–298) and as the dog on the great departure (17.3); Vidura is his incarnation (1.100.28).

name: Dharmadhvaja Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā who claims to be liberated while ruling and is tested by the ascetic Sulabhā (12.308).

name: Dharmamegha Āraṇya
summary: Successor of Hariharānanda Āraṇya at the Kāpil Maṭh, Madhupur (recalled; verify).

name: Dharmanātha
summary: Nāth yogī regarded as founder of the Dharamnāthī panth; tradition says he performed austerities on Dhinodhar hill in Kutch, where his seat remains.

name: Dharmarāja Adhvarīndra
summary: Author of the Vedāntaparibhāṣā, manual of Advaita epistemology.

name: The righteous meat-seller of Mithilā (dharmavyādha)
summary: A meat-seller who, living by his inherited work, serving his parents and speaking truth, teaches the brāhmaṇa Kauśika dharma, karma and liberation (3.198–206).
alt_summary: The righteous meat-seller of Mithilā who teaches the proud brāhmaṇa Kauśika the dharma of one's own station and of service to parents (Mahābhārata 3.198-206).

name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The blind Kuru king, father of Duryodhana; hearer of the Gītā through Sañjaya, of Vidura's counsel (5.33–40), Sanatsujāta's teaching (5.41–45) and Vidura's consolations (11.2–7); he later retires to the forest (Āśramavāsika).

name: Dhruva
summary: Son of King Uttānapāda; slighted by his stepmother, he went to the forest as a child, was initiated by Nārada (BhP 4.8) - or taught by the seven sages (VP 1.11-12) - and by austere meditation on Vāsudeva won the vision of Viṣṇu and the eternal position of the pole-star (dhruva-sthāna).

name: Dhuṇḍisuta Mālu (Narahari Mālu)
summary: Marathi author of the Navanātha Bhaktisāra.

name: Digvijaynāth
summary: Mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, in the mid-20th century.
notes: Listed only as a head of the Gorakhpur seat; succession Digvijaynāth → Avaidyanāth → Ādityanāth as commonly reported.

name: Dinakara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Dinakarī, a commentary on Viśvanātha's Siddhāntamuktāvalī.

name: Dīrghatamas
summary: Dīrghatamas Aucathya (Māmateya), seer of RV 1.140–164, including the riddle hymn 1.164 (the two birds, the four quarters of speech, 'the One Being the inspired call by many names'), the Viṣṇu hymn 1.154 and the horse-sacrifice hymns 1.162–163. The tradition remembers him as born blind.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). 'Born blind' and 'father of Kakṣīvant' are traditional (Bṛhaddevatā/epic) reports recalled with moderate confidence.

name: Doḍḍayācārya
summary: Mahācārya of Ghaṭikāśatam, a Vaṭakalai polemicist who continued Deśika's attack on Advaita in the Caṇḍamāruta; the tradition sets him against Appayya Dīkṣita.

name: Dōhara Kakkayya
summary: A leather-worker śaraṇa of 'untouchable' birth honoured among the devotees.

name: Drāhyāyaṇa
summary: Author by tradition of the Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda Śrautasūtra.

name: Dramiḍa (Draviḍācārya)
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin who commented on Brahmanandin's Vākya; cited by Rāmānuja as an authority.

name: Draupadī (Kṛṣṇā, Pāñcālī)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Wife of the Pāṇḍavas; in the forest she questions divine justice and argues for human effort against Yudhiṣṭhira (3.28–33), and after the war urges him to rule (12.14).

name: Duggaḷe
summary: Wife of Dēvara Dāsimayya and a vacanakāra.

name: Durga (Durgācārya)
summary: Commentator on the Nirukta; date uncertain.

name: Durvāsas
summary: The celibate sage whom Śrīkaṇṭha commanded to preserve the Śaiva scripture; he created a mind-born son, Tryambakāditya, and transmitted the secrets to him (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.110-112). Later Kashmirian accounts (Tantrāloka 36; Jayaratha) speak of his three mind-born sons for the non-dual, dual and dual-non-dual teachings, and a 'half' Kaula line - hence the 'three and a half maṭhikās' (TĀ 4.266).
notes: The three-sons account (Tryambaka, Āmardaka, Śrīnātha, plus Ardhatryambaka) is from memory of TĀ 36 and Jayaratha; TĀ 4.266 itself names the Śrī-, Tryambaka-, Ardha- and Āmarda- maṭhikās (confirmed).
alt_summary: Irascible sage named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86); in the Gopālottaratāpanī he teaches the gopīs.

name: Ēkānta Rāmayya
summary: The Śaiva devotee of Abalūr who, according to an inscription there, staked his head in a contest with the Jainas, cut it off, offered it to Śiva and received it back.

name: Eknāth
summary: In U06's texts: author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata, the Marathi commentary on the Uddhava Gītā (Bhāgavata Book 11).

name: Ēkōrāmārādhya
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Kedāra pīṭha (Kedārnāth).

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Emergence from the Rāmanātha liṅga at Drākṣārāma and seat name Vairāgya-siṃhāsana: low confidence.

name: Embār
summary: Rāmānuja's cousin Govinda, once a Śaiva at Kāḷahasti, brought back by Periya Tirumalai Nambi; Rāmānuja's successor at Śrīraṅgam and teacher of Parāśara Bhaṭṭar, in the line the Teṅkalai follow.

name: Ēṉātinātar Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A master of swordsmanship whose defeated rival Atisūraṉ smeared sacred ash on his forehead before their duel; seeing the ash, Ēṉātinātar lowered his guard and let himself be killed rather than strike a wearer of Śiva's sign.

realization_account.text: A master of swordsmanship whose defeated rival Atisūraṉ smeared sacred ash on his forehead before their duel; seeing the ash, Ēṉātinātar lowered his guard and let himself be killed rather than strike a wearer of Śiva's sign.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Eṟipatta Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He cut down the royal elephant that had scattered the flowers gathered for Śiva by the devotee Civakāmi Āṇṭār, and its keepers; the king Pukaḻccōḻar offered his own life in atonement and Eṟipattar tried to take his own, until Śiva intervened and restored all.

realization_account.text: He cut down the royal elephant that had scattered the flowers gathered for Śiva by the devotee Civakāmi Āṇṭār, and its keepers; the king Pukaḻccōḻar offered his own life in atonement and Eṟipattar tried to take his own, until Śiva intervened and restored all.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ēyarkōṉ Kalikkāma Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Angered that Cuntarar made the Lord his messenger to Paravai, he was struck by colic that only Cuntarar could cure; rather than be cured by him he tore out his own bowels; Cuntarar, arriving, was about to die with him, when Śiva revived Kalikkāmar and the two became friends.

realization_account.text: Angered that Cuntarar made the Lord his messenger to Paravai, he was struck by colic that only Cuntarar could cure; rather than be cured by him he tore out his own bowels; Cuntarar, arriving, was about to die with him, when Śiva revived Kalikkāmar and the two became friends.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya
