summary: The most prolific Navadvīpa Naiyāyika: the Gādādharī on the Dīdhiti and many vāda treatises, including the Vyutpattivāda and Śaktivāda on verbal cognition.
notes: Teacher relation to Harirāma Tarkavāgīśa is the tradition's account (low confidence).

name: Gadādhara Paṇḍita
summary: Caitanya's lifelong companion at Navadvīpa and Purī, identified in the tradition with Rādhā's śakti; one of the Pañca-tattva.

name: Gāgā Bhaṭṭa
notes: His role in Śivājī's coronation (1674) is well known; not a Mīmāṃsā teaching.
summary: Vārāṇasī scholar (Viśveśvara Bhaṭṭa) of the Bhaṭṭa family; author of the Bhāṭṭacintāmaṇi.

name: Gahinīnātha
summary: Nāth guru of Nivṛttināth in the Marathi tradition, counted among the nine Nāths (the Marathi list); tradition places his meeting with Nivṛtti at the Brahmagiri near Tryambakeśvar and a samādhi at Gahinīnāthgaḍ.

name: Gambhīrnāth
summary: Nāth yogī of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, revered as a realised yogī in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

name: Gaṇeśa (Gajānana)
summary: The elephant-faced lord who, in the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, teaches King Vareṇya the Gaṇeśa Gītā.

name: Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Svārājyasiddhi.

name: Gaṅgāmbike
summary: Basava's wife, daughter of the minister Baladēva; a vacanakāra.

name: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya

scholarly.text: first half of the 14th c. CE

summary: Founder of Navya-Nyāya: his Tattvacintāmaṇi in four books on the four means of knowledge recast Nyāya in a precise technical language.

name: Gardabhīvipīta Bhāradvāja
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is hearing (BAU 4.1.5); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

name: Garga Bhāradvāja
summary: Seer of RV 6.47, including 'Indra goes in many forms by his māyās' (6.47.18).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Garga (Pāśupata)
summary: The second of Lakulīśa's four disciples in the Purāṇic lists (Liṅga P. 1.24.131; Kūrma P. 1.51.26) and third in the Jain lists of eighteen tīrthakaras (as Gārgya); a Pāśupata line was traced to him.

name: Gārgī Vācaknavī
summary: Woman participant in the debate at Janaka's court: she questions Yājñavalkya on what the worlds are woven upon, is warned not to ask too much lest her head fall off (BAU 3.6), returns with two questions 'like two arrows', hears the teaching of the imperishable (akṣara) and declares that no one will defeat him (BAU 3.8).

name: Gārgya
summary: Early grammarian cited by Yāska and Pāṇini; held that not all nouns derive from verbs (Nirukta 1.12).

name: Gārgya Bālāki
summary: A proud (dṛpta) learned brahmin who offers to explain brahman to Ajātaśatru, proposes a series of persons in the sun, moon and other phenomena, is refuted and becomes his pupil (BAU 2.1; KauU 4).

name: Garuḍa
summary: The eagle-mount of Viṣṇu to whom Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa teaches the Garuḍa Purāṇa; his questions in the Pretakalpa frame the teaching on death and the dead.

name: Garuḍavāhana Paṇḍita
summary: Author, by tradition a contemporary of Rāmānuja, of the Sanskrit Divyasūricaritam on the lives of the Āḻvārs and Rāmānuja.

name: Gauḍapāda

tradition.text: disciple of Śuka; paramaguru of Śaṅkara

notes: Also credited (traditional) with Śākta works (Subhagodaya, Śrīvidyāratnasūtras) and an Uttaragītā commentary. Whether he is the same person as the author of the commentary on the Sāṃkhya Kārikā (src:samkhya-karika-bhasya-gaudapada) is doubted by most scholars.
summary: Author of the Māṇḍūkya Kārikā; teacher of Govinda, Śaṅkara's teacher, and in the paramparā disciple of Śuka; first systematic exponent of non-origination (ajātivāda) and asparśa-yoga.
alt_summary: U09 contribution: a Gauḍapāda is named in the closing verse of the bhāṣya on SK 1–69. Whether he is the Advaita teacher Gauḍapāda (author of the Māṇḍūkya-kārikā, Śaṅkara's paramaguru) is disputed; many scholars regard them as different persons.
In U06's context: a commentary on the Uttara Gītā is ascribed to him (attribution doubtful).
alt_notes: Registry id used as mandated; if the merge keeps the two persons apart, the Sāṃkhya commentator should be split out (e.g., tch:gaudapada-samkhya).

name: Gaura Kiśora Dāsa Bābājī
summary: Renunciate bābājī of Navadvīpa, guru of Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī.

name: Gauraṇa
summary: Telugu poet, author of the Navanāthacaritramu.

name: Gautama Akṣapāda

tradition.text: an ancient ṛṣi

scholarly.text: the Nyāya Sūtra is usually dated c. 2nd–3rd c. CE; nothing is known of its author(s)

realization_account.text: Called 'the best of sages' (Nyāyavārttika maṅgala) and 'the supremely compassionate sage' who composed the śāstra wishing to lift the world sunk in the mire of pain (Vācaspati, Tātparyaṭīkā on NS 1.1.1).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The sage to whom the Nyāya Sūtra is attributed, the founder of Nyāya. The commentators call him the best of sages who taught the śāstra for the peace of the world.
notes: Popular legends explain 'Akṣapāda' ('eyes in the feet'); not recorded here because the versions could not be checked.

name: Gautama (author of the Dharmasūtra)
summary: The Gautama of the Gautama Dharmasūtra, cited by Baudhāyana (BDh 1.1.2.7) and assigned by Parāśara to the Tretā age; distinct from Gautama Akṣapāda of Nyāya.

name: Gautama (questioner of the Haṃsa)
summary: Sage who asks for the means to brahmavidyā in the Haṃsa Upaniṣad; Brahmavidyā 53 also addresses a Gautama. Identity with other Gautamas not asserted.

name: Gautamī
summary: An aged brāhmaṇī whose son dies of snakebite; she refuses the vengeance a hunter offers, and in the ensuing debate the serpent, Death and Time each disclaim the cause until karma is named (Anuśāsana 13.1).

name: Ghora Āṅgirasa
summary: Teacher who taught Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, the doctrine of the person as sacrifice and the three sayings to be taken as refuge at death (ChU 3.17.6).

name: Ghoṣā Kākṣīvatī
summary: Daughter of Kakṣīvant, ṛṣikā of RV 10.39–40 to the Aśvins; the tradition says she remained unmarried in her father's house through a skin disease until the Aśvins healed her.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The illness story is the commentarial account (moderate confidence).

name: Giridhara (Giridharajī, of the Vallabha line)
summary: Later Śuddhādvaita author to whom the Śuddhādvaitamārtaṇḍa is attributed.

name: Gobhila
summary: Author by tradition of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda Gṛhyasūtra.

name: Godhā
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 10.134.6b–7.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Gokulnāth
summary: Fourth son of Viṭṭhalanātha, to whom the Caurāsī and Do Sau Bāvan Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā are attributed; head of one of the seven houses.

name: Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of Veṅkaṭa Bhaṭṭa of Śrīraṅgam, where Caitanya spent the rainy season (1511 per tradition); in Vṛndāvana served the Rādhāramaṇa deity (manifested from a śālagrāma); named compiler of the Haribhaktivilāsa and drafter of the Sandarbhas completed by Jīva.

name: Gopīcandra (Gopīcand)
summary: King of Bengal in the Nāth cycle, son of Mayanāmatī, who at his mother's insistence renounced his kingdom and queens and took initiation from Hāḍipā (Jālandhara) to escape an early death; hero of Bengali, Hindi and Rajasthani sagas.

name: Gopīnātha (elder son of Vallabha)
summary: Vallabha's elder son and first successor, who died young.

name: Gorakṣanātha
summary: Disciple of Matsyendra and the great organiser of the Nāth order, to whom the Nāths trace their panths, insignia and yoga; the Gorakṣaśataka, Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati, Amaraughaprabodha, Amaraughaśāsana and the Hindi Gorakh Bānī are ascribed to him. The tradition holds him immortal, appearing in every age; he rescues Matsyendra from the Kadalī kingdom, initiates Gopīcand, Bharthari and Pūraṇ Bhagat (Cauraṅgī), and in Vīraśaiva accounts meets Allama Prabhu. The Gorakhnāth Maṭh at Gorakhpur is his principal seat; Gorkha and the Gurkhas take their name from him.

tradition.text: immortal; appears in all four ages (tradition)

realization_account.text: Born by the power of Matsyendra's ash (vibhūti) — in the common north Indian and Marathi telling, the ash given to a childless woman was thrown on a dung-heap, and Matsyendra later called forth the boy from it; the Gorakṣaguṭikā gives a different origin. Perfected in body, deathless, master of all siddhis.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Gotama Rāhūgaṇa
summary: Seer of RV 1.74–93, including 1.89 ('let auspicious intentions come to us from every side') and 1.90.9 ('may Mitra be propitious to us…').
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Govinda Bhagavatpāda
summary: Śaṅkara's guru, disciple of Gauḍapāda; the Śaṅkaradigvijaya places him in a cave on the Narmadā where he initiated Śaṅkara into sannyāsa, and identifies him with Patañjali/Ādiśeṣa.

name: Govindānanda
summary: Author of the Ratnaprabhā gloss on Śaṅkara's BSBh.

name: Govindarāja
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava commentator on the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (the Bhūṣaṇa).

name: Govindasvāmin
summary: Commentator on the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

name: Govindsvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and musician.

name: Gṛtsamada
summary: Seer of most of Ṛgveda book 2 (e.g. 2.12 on Indra, whom some say 'does not exist' — 'have faith in him'; 2.33 to Rudra the best of physicians). The Anukramaṇī calls him formerly Āṅgirasa Śaunahotra, later Bhārgava Śaunaka.

realization_account.text: The tradition counts him among the seers who 'saw' the hymns of the second maṇḍala.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Gūgā (Gogā, Jāhar Pīr)
summary: Warrior-saint of Rajasthan and Punjab, revered by Hindus and Muslims as a snake-protector; in the legend a disciple of Gorakhnāth, born through Gorakh's blessing to his mother Bāchal.

name: Guhadeva
summary: Ancient Vedāntin named by Rāmānuja (Vedārthasaṅgraha) among the earlier teachers (with Bodhāyana, Ṭaṅka, Dramiḍa, Kapardin and Bharuci).

name: Gūḷūra Siddhavīraṇṇoḍeya
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Gummaḷāpurada Siddhaliṅgayati
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Gurupad Sambhav Rām
summary: Disciple of Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām associated with the leadership of the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh.

name: Haḍapada Appaṇṇa
summary: The barber śaraṇa, Basava's personal attendant.

name: Haḍapada Liṅgamma
summary: Wife of Haḍapada Appaṇṇa and a vacanakāra.

name: Halageyārya
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: P. G. Halakatti
summary: Phakīrappa Gurubasappa Halakatti, who collected palm-leaf vacana manuscripts and printed the vacanas from the 1920s, beginning their modern revival ('father of vacana literature' in popular usage).
notes: An editor-publisher rather than a teacher; included as a transmitter of the texts.

name: Halāyudha
summary: Author of the Mṛtasañjīvanī commentary on Piṅgala's Chandaḥśāstra.

name: Haṃsa (the Lord as swan)
summary: The form of a swan in which the Lord appeared before Brahmā and the Kumāras to answer their question (Bhāgavata 11.13.19-42).

name: Hānagal Kumāra Svāmi
summary: Vīraśaiva renunciant who founded the Śivayōga Mandira near Bādāmi (1909) to train virakta ascetics in iṣṭaliṅga yoga, and worked for the community's unity and education.

name: Hanumān
summary: Son of the Wind, Rāma's devoted servant in the Rāmāyaṇa; in the Mahābhārata he meets his brother Bhīma and teaches him the ages of the world and the four sciences — the Veda, economics (vārtā) and polity (daṇḍanīti) (3.147–150).
alt_summary: In the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa the devoted servant judged fit for knowledge, to whom Sītā and Rāma teach the Rāma-hṛdaya (1.1.29-52).
Rāma's devotee, the questioner of the Muktikā; in the Rāmarahasya he teaches Sanaka, Prahlāda and others that Rāma is the supreme Brahman.

name: Haradatta
summary: Commentator on the Āpastamba and Gautama Dharmasūtras; possibly (uncertain) the author of the Padamañjarī.

name: Haradatta (Pāśupata ācārya)
summary: Pāśupata teacher whom the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha (ch. 6) quotes as the author of the Gaṇakārikā verses on the gains and impurities. Not to be confused with other Haradattas (the Dharmasūtra commentator; Haradatta Śivācārya).

name: Haridāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Devotee born in a Muslim family (tradition) who chanted three hundred thousand names daily, endured beating in twenty-two marketplaces without abandoning the name, and taught that even the semblance of the name (nāmābhāsa) gives liberation; honoured as the teacher of the name (nāmācārya); died at Purī in Caitanya's presence.

name: Hāridrumata Gautama
summary: Teacher who accepts Satyakāma Jābāla because 'no non-brahmin could speak thus' and initiates him (ChU 4.4.3-5).

name: Harihara (Kannada poet)
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet of Hampi who created the ragaḷe form for lives of the śaraṇas and of the ancient Śaiva devotees (purātanas), and wrote the Girijākalyāṇa.

name: Hariharānanda Āraṇya
summary: Renunciant who founded the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur as a monastery of Sāṃkhya-Yoga and lived much of his life in seclusion in a cave there; author of the Bhāsvatī on the Yoga Bhāṣya and of works on Sāṃkhya (e.g., Sāṃkhyatattvāloka), and of the commentary rendered in English as 'Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali'.
notes: Dates, titles and the Maṭh's founding recalled, not checked.
alt_summary: Sāṃkhya-Yoga monk who spent long years in retreat, founded the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur, and wrote the Bhāsvatī on the Yoga-bhāṣya and a Bengali exposition of Patañjali's Yoga later published in English.

name: Harirāy (Harirāyajī)
summary: Puṣṭimārga scholar and poet, commentator (Bhāvaprakāś) on the Vārtā literature and author of many Sanskrit and Braj works.

name: Harirāma Tarkavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika of the 17th c., remembered as the teacher of Gadādhara.

name: Harisvāmin
summary: Commentator on the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (partly surviving).

name: Hārīta (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Also named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others.

name: Hārītaka
summary: Named among the paramahaṃsas in the Bhikṣuka and Yājñavalkya Upaniṣads.

name: Haritāyana
summary: Narrator of the Tripura Rahasya, conveying Dattātreya's teaching to Paraśurāma.

name: Harivyāsadeva
summary: Disciple of Śrī Bhaṭṭa; author of the Mahāvāṇī (Braj songs of the eternal love-play in the sakhī mood) and the Siddhāntaratnāñjali; his disciples spread the school through twelve branches.

name: Hastāmalaka
summary: Disciple of Śaṅkara; in the tradition's account a seemingly dull boy who, asked 'who are you?', answered with the verses of the Hastāmalakīya, knowing the self as clearly as 'an āmalaka fruit in the hand'; first head of the Dvārakā (Śāradā) maṭha.

name: Hayagrīva
summary: The horse-headed form of Viṣṇu (BhP 2.7.11), who in the Lalitopākhyāna is sent as a portion of Viṣṇu to teach Agastya the story and worship of Lalitā.

name: Hemacandra
summary: Śvetāmbara polymath; U02 adds only his grammar, the Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana.

name: Hemādri

scholarly.text: 13th c. CE, minister at the Yādava court

summary: Author of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi, whose volumes on vows and gifts are the fullest compilation of Purāṇic vrata and dāna.
alt_summary: Minister of the Yādava kings, author of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi.

name: Himavat (Himālaya)
summary: King of the mountains and father of Pārvatī, who asks the Goddess for the yoga, devotion and knowledge that lead to her (Devī Gītā).

name: Hiraṇyadāma

scholarly.text: early 9th c. (as narrated in an inscription of 1052 CE)

summary: Brahmin who, according to the Khmer Sdok Kak Thom inscription (1052 CE), performed rites for King Jayavarman II and taught four Vāma tantras — Vīṇāśikha, Nayottara, Sammoha and Śiraścheda — to the royal priest.

name: Hiraṇyagarbha
alt_names: Pitāmaha (Brahmā) as first teacher of yoga

realization_account.text: The first and most ancient teacher of yoga: 'Hiraṇyagarbha is the speaker of yoga, no other is ancient' (verse cited by Vijñānabhikṣu from the Yoga-Yājñavalkya, YV 1.1). Commentators read 'anuśāsana' in YS 1.1 as Patañjali's re-teaching of the yoga Hiraṇyagarbha taught; Nārāyaṇatīrtha: 'Pitāmaha taught yoga, then Śeṣa'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The tradition's founder of yoga. The Yoga commentators (Vācaspati, Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nāgeśa) name Hiraṇyagarbha as the original teacher and treat Patañjali's śāstra as a re-teaching; the Mahābhārata's Nārāyaṇīya likewise pairs Kapila as the teacher of Sāṃkhya with Hiraṇyagarbha as the knower of yoga.
notes: The Mahābhārata reference (Nārāyaṇīya, c. MBh 12.337 CE) and a reported Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā passage on a Hairaṇyagarbha yoga śāstra are from memory and need checking.
alt_summary: Named in the Nārāyaṇīya as the knower (vettā) of Yoga, 'none more ancient' (12.337.60).
alt_notes: U05's contribution; Hiraṇyagarbha as the tradition's founder of Yoga is also treated by U10.

name: Hiraṇyagarbha Prājāpatya
summary: The seer to whom the Anukramaṇī ascribes the Hiraṇyagarbha hymn (RV 10.121); the deity is Ka, i.e. Prajāpati.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Hiraṇyakeśin (Satyāṣāḍha)
summary: Sūtrakāra of the Hiraṇyakeśin branch of the Taittirīya school.

name: Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya
summary: A prince of Kosala who asked Sukeśā about the person of sixteen parts; Sukeśā, not knowing, refused to answer falsely, since one who speaks untruth withers to the root (PrU 6.1).

name: Hiraṇyastūpa Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 1.31–35, including the Indra–Vṛtra hymn 1.32 ('I will proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra…').
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Hṛdayaśiva
summary: Compiler of a Prāyaścittasamuccaya of Śaiva expiatory rites.

name: Hṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Palimaru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa. He is remembered as the copyist of the manuscript collection of Madhva's works (the Sarvamūla) and as author of the short Sampradāyapaddhati.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Icaiñāṉiyār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Cuntarar's mother.

realization_account.text: Cuntarar's mother.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Iṭaikkāṭar
summary: Shepherd-Siddhar (iṭaiyar) whose songs address the herdsman, cattle and flute. The tradition tells that, foreseeing a twelve-year drought, he fed his flock on erukku leaves and stored grain in mud, and when the nine planets came to him he so charmed them that they shifted their places and the rains returned.
places: Tiruvaṇṇāmalai — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Distinct from the Caṅkam poet Iṭaikkāṭaṉār. The planets legend and his discipleship to Bogar are recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Ikṣvāku
summary: First king of the solar dynasty, who received the yoga from Manu; thus the royal sages knew it until it was lost (BhG 4.1–2).

name: Iḷaiyāṉkuṭi Māṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A farmer who fed devotees until he was destitute; on a night of heavy rain he gathered the newly sown paddy from his field and pulled up his roof-beams for firewood to feed a guest, who was Śiva.

realization_account.text: A farmer who fed devotees until he was destitute; on a night of heavy rain he gathered the newly sown paddy from his field and pulled up his roof-beams for firewood to feed a guest, who was Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Indra (as student and teacher)
summary: Lord of the gods: lives 101 years as Prajāpati's student and alone goes beyond the body-self (ChU 8.7-12); in the Kena he meets Umā Haimavatī and first knows the yakṣa as brahman (Kena 3.11-4.3); teaches Pratardana 'I am breath, the intelligent self' (KauU 3).

name: Indradyumna Bhāllaveya
summary: One of the five great householders and great Vedic scholars who asked 'what is our self, what is brahman?' and, with Uddālaka Āruṇi, went to Aśvapati Kaikeya; each had venerated only one part of the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11-17).

name: Indrāṇī
summary: Speaker in the Vṛṣākapi hymn (RV 10.86) and ṛṣikā of RV 10.145, a charm against a co-wife.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Īśāna (Pāśupata tīrthakara)
summary: Number 6 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Īśānaśiva Gurudeva
summary: Author of the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati, a vast Śaiva ritual compendium (Tantrasāra and Siddhāntasāra) that is a principal authority of Kerala temple tantra.

name: Īśvara Purī
summary: Disciple of Mādhavendra Purī who initiated Caitanya at Gayā (c. 1508).

name: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhya Kārikā, who, 'having thoroughly understood the established doctrine handed down by a succession of pupils, summarized it in āryā verses' (SK 71). The Yuktidīpikā says he condensed the Ṣaṣṭitantra out of compassion for pupils of short life. An identification with Vindhyavāsin was proposed by some scholars and is not generally accepted.

name: Iṭaṅkaḻi Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain who pardoned a devotee caught stealing paddy from the royal granary to feed devotees, and threw the granary open to all.

realization_account.text: A chieftain who pardoned a devotee caught stealing paddy from the royal granary to feed devotees, and threw the granary open to all.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Iyaṟpakai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who never refused a devotee; when Śiva came as a brahmin and asked for his wife, he gave her, fought off his kinsmen who tried to stop them, and escorted the pair out of town — whereupon Śiva revealed himself.

realization_account.text: A merchant who never refused a devotee; when Śiva came as a brahmin and asked for his wife, he gave her, fought off his kinsmen who tried to stop them, and escorted the pair out of town — whereupon Śiva revealed himself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Jabālā (mother of Satyakāma)
summary: Satyakāma's mother, who tells him she does not know his lineage because in her youth she went about much as a serving woman (paricāriṇī), and bids him call himself Satyakāma Jābāla (ChU 4.4.1-2).

name: Jābāli
summary: A brāhmaṇa counsellor who urges Rāma, with arguments that deny the other world, to return and rule; Rāma rejects this, and Vasiṣṭha says Jābāli spoke only to bring Rāma back (Rāmāyaṇa 2.108–110).
notes: Distinct from Satyakāma Jābāla (tch:satyakama-jabala).
alt_summary: Teacher of the Jābāli Upaniṣad, who received the Paśupati teaching through Īśāna and Ṣaḍānana and teaches Paippalādi the meaning of paśu and Paśupati.

name: Jaḍa Bharata

realization_account.text: The king after whom Bhāratavarṣa is named retired to the forest, became attached to an orphaned fawn, died thinking of it and was reborn as a deer; then reborn as a brahmin who, remembering, lived as if dull and dumb, and taught the king of Sindhu-Sauvīra (Rahūgaṇa) the distinction of self and body (BhP 5.7-14; VP 2.13-16).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The exemplar of the power of the last thought (anta-smṛti) and of the avadhūta who hides his realization; teacher of Rahūgaṇa.

name: Jaḍabharata
summary: The 'dull' Bharata who hid his knowledge; named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Bhikṣuka) and among rudrākṣa-wearers.

name: Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Kashmiri poet, author of the Stutikusumāñjali, hymns to Śiva in 38 chapters.

name: Jagadīśa Tarkālaṅkāra
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Jāgadīśī on the Dīdhiti, the Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā and the Tarkāmṛta.

name: Jāhnavā Devī (Jāhnavā Mātā)
summary: Wife of Nityānanda and a leader of the second generation, who presided at the Kheturi festival and guided the Nityānanda branch.

name: Jaigīṣavya

realization_account.text: Through direct perception of his saṃskāras he saw the sequence of his births through ten great creation-cycles, and knowledge born of discrimination arose in him (YBh 3.18).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Ancient yoga master cited in the Yoga-bhāṣya: on mastery of the senses he holds that it is non-apprehension arising from the mind's one-pointedness (YBh 2.55); questioned by Āvaṭya (YBh 3.18), he declares everything he experienced in all births to be suffering, and the unsurpassed happiness of contentment to be suffering compared with the happiness of kaivalya.
notes: The Mahābhārata also tells of Jaigīṣavya (with Asita Devala) — from memory.
alt_summary: A yogin mendicant who, unmoved by praise or blame, teaches Asita Devala equanimity (12.222) and, at a tīrtha on the Sarasvatī, shows Devala his yogic powers, moving unseen between the worlds (9.49).

Sage of Sāṃkhya-Yoga lore. The Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 3.18) records his dialogue with Āvaṭya about the suffering even in the highest births, and cites his view (on YS 2.55) that the highest sense-control is non-apprehension (of objects) through one-pointedness of mind. The Mahābhārata places him in stories with Asita Devala.
alt_notes: The Yoga-bhāṣya's mention of Jaigīṣavya is covered by U10.
Mahābhārata passages not checked.

name: Jaimini

tradition.text: pupil of Vyāsa, to whom Vyāsa entrusted the Sāmaveda (Purāṇic account)

scholarly.text: the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra c. 3rd c. BCE – 1st c. CE

notes: The Purāṇic Jaimini (Sāmaveda transmitter, narrator of the Jaimini Aśvamedha) and the sūtrakāra are identified by tradition; the identity is not established historically. The astrological Jaimini Sūtras (src:jaimini-upadesa-sutra) are a separate attribution.
summary: Author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra. In the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra he is cited by name for positions (e.g. that actions too are subsidiaries, MS 3.1.4); the Brahma Sūtra reports his views on the fruit of action, on knowledge as subsidiary to rites and on the released self (BS 3.2.40, 3.4.2, 3.4.18, 4.3.12, 4.4.5).
alt_summary: Author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra; cited by name in the Brahma Sūtras for views Bādarāyaṇa records and often corrects: that knowledge is subsidiary to ritual (BS 3.4.2), that the gods are not eligible for the honey-meditation (1.3.31), that the path of the gods leads to the supreme Brahman (4.3.12), that the liberated has Brahman's qualities (4.4.5) and a body (4.4.11). Tradition makes him a disciple of Vyāsa.

Vyāsa's pupil who received the Sāmaveda (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.21); eponym of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda. The tradition identifies him with the author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (the identification is disputed by scholars).

In the Purāṇas Vyāsa's disciple for the Sāmaveda (VP 3.4), and the questioner of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, who asks about the Mahābhārata's puzzles and then about birth, death and liberation. (His identity with the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra author is the traditional view.)
U02 contribution: eponym of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school whose Brāhmaṇa bears his name; tradition makes him the pupil of Vyāsa and the author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (U12).
alt_notes: U01 contribution: the Sāmaveda transmitter.

name: Jājali
summary: A proud ascetic, on whose head birds nested while he stood motionless, sent to learn dharma from the merchant Tulādhāra (12.253–256).

name: Jālandharanātha
summary: A siddha counted among the nine Nāths; in the Bengali Gopīcandra cycle he is Hāḍipā, the siddha living as a sweeper (hāḍi) who initiates King Gopīcandra at Mayanāmatī's request; his disciple is Kāṇha (Kānipā). Also in the Buddhist siddha lists as Jālandhari(pā).

realization_account.text: A great siddha whose power humbles kings; Gopīcandra's guru.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Jamadagni
summary: Jamadagni Bhārgava, seer of hymns in books 8–10 (e.g. 8.101) and of 'the waters are healing' in the seven-seer hymn (10.137.6); in the Purāṇas the father of Paraśurāma.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Jana Śārkarākṣya
summary: One of the five great householders and great Vedic scholars who asked 'what is our self, what is brahman?' and, with Uddālaka Āruṇi, went to Aśvapati Kaikeya; each had venerated only one part of the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11-17).

name: Janadeva Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā, occupied with the question of what survives death, instructed by Pañcaśikha (12.211–212).

name: Janaka of Videha
summary: King of Videha whose sacrifice is the setting of the debate at BAU 3; he reports six teachers' definitions of brahman (BAU 4.1) and is taught by Yājñavalkya on the self as light, dream, deep sleep and death (BAU 4.3-4); told 'you have reached fearlessness' (BAU 4.2.4).
notes: 'Janaka' is a dynastic name; other units record other Janakas (e.g., tch:daivarati-janaka).
alt_summary: In U06's texts: King of Videha who receives Aṣṭāvakra's teaching and voices his awakening (Aṣṭāvakra Gītā ch. 2 and later chapters); overhears the Siddhas' songs and awakens (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha 5.8-10); his verse 'my wealth is endless, for nothing is mine; if Mithilā burns, nothing of mine burns' is quoted in Mahābhārata 12.171.56.
U02 contribution: questions Yājñavalkya and others on the Agnihotra (ŚB 11.3.1; 11.6.2) and is declared a 'brahman' from then on.
U04 contribution: asks Yājñavalkya about renunciation (Jābāla 4; Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad); in the Mahā Upaniṣad he teaches Śuka.

realization_account.text: On hearing Aṣṭāvakra he exclaims that he is stainless, peaceful consciousness beyond nature, long deceived by delusion (Aṣṭāvakra Gītā 2.1); in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha he awakens through the Siddha Gītā and rules as one liberated while living.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Janamejaya
summary: Kuru king, great-grandson of Arjuna, at whose snake sacrifice Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata; his questions open sections such as the discussion of whether puruṣas are many or one (12.338.1).

name: Janārdana Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Krishnapura maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa
summary: A great-grandson of Janaśruta, a generous giver who kept open houses for food; overhearing geese compare him unfavourably to Raikva, he seeks Raikva and receives the saṃvarga teaching (ChU 4.1-2).

name: Jātavēdamuni
summary: The teacher under whom, in the hagiographies, Basava studied at Kūḍalasaṅgama.

name: Jayāditya
summary: Co-author of the Kāśikāvṛtti.

name: Jayamiśra
summary: Author of the Śarkarikā commentary on the Ślokavārttika.

name: Jayānanda
summary: Author of a Bengali Caitanya Maṅgala.

name: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa
summary: Kashmiri Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyamañjarī, the Nyāyakalikā and the drama Āgamaḍambara, set in the reign of King Śaṅkaravarman (r. 883–902). He defends the Veda and the Lord and examines the validity of the Āgamas.
notes: His son is usually identified as the poet Abhinanda (moderate confidence).

name: Jayaratha
summary: 13th-century Kashmiri scholar, son of Śṛṅgāraratha, author of the Viveka commentary on the whole Tantrāloka - the main source for many lost tantras and for the Mata and Krama - as well as a commentary on the Vāmakeśvarīmata (Śrīvidyā) and a work on poetics.

scholarly.text: 13th c. CE (under King Rājadeva, early 13th c.)

notes: Contribution from U08 (catalogue role); U19 owns his exegesis.
alt_summary: Kashmirian commentator on the Tantrāloka whose Viveka preserves, from the lost Śrīkaṇṭhīya Saṃhitā, the catalogues of the 28 Siddhānta tantras and of the 64 Bhairava tantras.

name: Jayatīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1365–1388 in maṭha lists

realization_account.text: The tradition identifies Jayatīrtha with the bull that carried Madhva's manuscripts, who listened to Madhva's teaching and was blessed to become its commentator; seeing the young horseman drink from a river without dismounting, like an animal, Akṣobhya Tīrtha asked what he had been in his past body, and the memory awakened him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great commentator (Ṭīkācārya) of the tradition: author of the Nyāyasudhā on the Anuvyākhyāna and the Tattvaprakāśikā on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, commentaries on the Gītā works, the Ṛgbhāṣya and all ten prakaraṇas, and the independent Pramāṇapaddhati and Vādāvalī. His commentaries fixed the scholastic form of Dvaita. In the tradition's account he had been a young cavalryman (Dhoṇḍo Raghunātha of Maṅgaḷavēḍhe) whom Akṣobhya Tīrtha awakened to his past birth.
notes: The location of his brindāvana (Malkheḍ, per the Uttarādi Maṭha; Nava Brindāvana, per another view) is disputed within the tradition — recorded at low confidence. The realization account is oral and hagiographic tradition; no textual source was checked for it.
alt_summary: Author of the Prameyadīpikā and Nyāyadīpikā on Madhva's Gītā works.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Jīmūtavāhana
summary: Bengali jurist, author of the Dāyabhāga.

name: Jinendrabuddhi
summary: Author of the Nyāsa on the Kāśikāvṛtti (a Buddhist, by most accounts).

name: Jitvan Śailini
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is speech (BAU 4.1.2); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

name: Jīva Gosvāmī
summary: Nephew and disciple of Rūpa and Sanātana; the systematic theologian of the school (Ṣaṭ Sandarbha, Sarvasaṃvādinī, Kramasandarbha), grammarian (Harināmāmṛtavyākaraṇa), poet (Gopālacampū) and commentator; leader of the Vṛndāvana community after the elder Gosvāmīs.

name: Jñānanetra (Śivānanda)
summary: Regarded as the founder of the Krama in Kashmir, who received the teaching from the goddess (in Oḍḍiyāna, in the tradition's account) and passed it to three female disciples.
notes: Names of the female disciples (Keyūravatī, Madanikā, Kalyāṇikā) recalled from secondary literature - gap.

name: Jñānaprakāśa
summary: Saiddhāntika author (described as resident of Śālivāṭipura) of a Pauṣkara commentary and of a collection on the greatness and authority of the Śaiva Āgamas.

name: Jñānaśiva
summary: Author of the Jñānaratnāvalī, a compendium of Siddhānta ritual.

name: Jñāneśvar
summary: U21 contribution: in the Nāth line through Nivṛttināth; the Jñāneśvarī names the Nāth sequence of teachers at its close and calls the swallowing of the body by the body the secret of the Nāth signal (6.291).
alt_summary: Author of the Jñāneśvarī, the Marathi verse commentary on the Gītā (1290).
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Jñānottama
summary: Advaitin, teacher of Citsukha, author of a commentary (Candrikā) on the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi.

name: Juhū Brahmajāyā
summary: ṛṣikā (with Ūrdhvanābhā Brāhma as alternative) of RV 10.109 on the restoration of the brahmin's wife.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Kabandhī Kātyāyana
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks whence creatures are born (PrU 1).

name: Kaṭuveḷic cittar
summary: Siddhar poet of the 'Joy-song' (Āṉantak kaḷippu), whose refrain 'do no sin, O mind' and whose image of the mendicant breaking his hard-won pot are among the best-known Siddhar lines.

name: Kahola Kauṣītakeya
summary: Asks Yājñavalkya the same question as Uṣasta and is told of the self beyond hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age and death, knowing which brahmins renounce the three desires (BAU 3.5.1).

name: Kairāta
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Kaiyaṭa
summary: Kashmiri author of the Pradīpa on the Mahābhāṣya.

name: Kākapucuṇṭar (Kākabhuśuṇḍa)
summary: The crow-sage, counted among the Siddhars in some Tamil lists; in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha the long-lived crow Bhuśuṇḍa teaches breath-contemplation.
notes: Siddhar-list membership recalled at low confidence.

name: Kakṣīvant
summary: Kakṣīvant Dairghatamasa Auśija, seer of RV 1.116–126 (hymns to the Aśvins and gift-praises); father of the ṛṣikā Ghoṣā.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Kālāgnirudra
summary: Rudra as 'fire of time': teaches Sanatkumāra the tripuṇḍra (Kālāgnirudra) and Bhusuṇḍa the sacred ash (Bṛhajjābāla); rudrākṣa beads arise from his tears (Rudrākṣajābāla).

name: Kālāṅki nātar
summary: Siddhar named in TM 69 among Tirumūlar's disciples in the mantra-lineage; later tradition makes him the guru of Bogar.
notes: TM 69 (checked locally) names 'Kālāṅki'; the guru-of-Bogar link is the later tradition's.

name: Kaḻaṟciṅka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Pallava king whose queen smelled a flower fallen from the temple's flower-hall at Tiruvārūr; after Ceruttuṇaiyār had cut her nose, the king cut off the hand that had picked up the flower.

name: Kalikkampa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who washed devotees' feet; when his wife hesitated to pour water for one who had once been their servant, he cut off her hand.

name: Kaliya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. An oil-presser who kept the temple lamps burning; ruined, he tried to fill the lamps with his own blood, and Śiva stopped him.

name: Kālūrām
summary: Aghora ascetic of Varanasi, guru of Kīnārām, regarded in the tradition as Dattātreya himself; the Krīm Kuṇḍ seat is associated with him.

name: Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Nirṇayasindhu, of the Bhaṭṭa family of Vārāṇasī.

name: Kamalamuṉi
summary: Siddhar of the popular list, with a samādhi place at Tiruvārūr; no works or teachings are recalled here.

name: Kaṇāda

summary: The sage to whom the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra is attributed, founder of Vaiśeṣika; Praśastapāda salutes him after Īśvara. His names Kaṇabhuj / Kaṇabhakṣa ('grain-eater') are traditionally explained by his living on gleaned grains; Buddhist and Jain sources call the school Aulūkya after his name Ulūka.

name: Kaṇampulla Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A poor man who sold kaṇampul grass to buy oil for temple lamps; when he could not sell it he burned the grass itself, and when that ran out he set fire to his own hair.

summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin of Cīkāḻi who served in the temple and trained others in its service; devoted to Campantar.

name: Kāṇha (Kānipā / Kānifnāth)
summary: U21 contribution: in Nāth tradition Kānipā/Kānupā is Jālandhara's disciple (Bengali saga) and, as Kānifnāth, one of the Marathi nine Nāths, with a samādhi shrine at Madhi (Ahilyanagar/Ahmednagar district). Whether this Nāth figure is the same as the Buddhist siddha Kāṇha / Kṛṣṇācārya is not settled.
notes: Registry id for the Buddhist mahāsiddha Kāṇha (U44). Identification with the Nāth Kānipā is the tradition's (shared siddha lists) and is disputed; HYP 1.7 'Kānerī' may or may not be the same figure.

name: Kañcamalaiyaṉ
summary: Named in TM 69 among Tirumūlar's disciples in the mantra-lineage.
notes: Checked in the local TM e-text (69); nothing further recalled.

name: Kaṇṇappa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A hunter who worshipped the liṅga of Kāḷahasti with meat he had tasted, water carried in his mouth and flowers from his hair, to the dismay of the temple priest Civakōcariyār; when blood flowed from the liṅga's eye he plucked out his own eye and set it there; when the other eye bled he placed his foot on it to mark the spot and began to cut out his second eye — Śiva stopped his hand crying 'Stay, Kaṇṇappa!' and took him to his side.

name: Kaṇṭarātittar
summary: Cōḻa king (Gaṇḍarāditya, r. c. 950–957) and poet of a Tiruvicaippā hymn to Naṭarāja at Chidambaram.

name: Kaṇva
summary: Kaṇva Ghaura, seer of RV 1.36–43 (incl. 1.43 to Rudra 'lord of songs, lord of sacrifice, with the healing jalāṣa'); eponym of the Kāṇva family whose hymns fill most of book 8.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Kapardin
summary: Ancient Vedāntin named by Rāmānuja among the earlier teachers.

name: Kapila

tradition.text: born at the beginning of creation endowed with virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power (Gauḍapāda on SK 1, 43); in the Purāṇic account an avatāra, son of Kardama and Devahūti (Māṭhara on SK 1; Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 3)

realization_account.text: Born with innate (sāṃsiddhika) virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power; seeing the world sunk in blind darkness, out of compassion he taught the knowledge of the twenty-five principles to Āsuri. A saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya calls him the first knower who, assuming a created mind (nirmāṇacitta), out of compassion taught the doctrine to the inquiring Āsuri.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Sāṃkhya in the tradition's account: the 'supreme sage' (SK 69) who gave the teaching to Āsuri out of compassion (SK 70). Gauḍapāda counts him among Brahmā's seven mind-born sons; the Māṭhara Vṛtti and the Purāṇas make him an avatāra, son of Kardama and Devahūti. The Sāṃkhya Sūtra and the Tattvasamāsa are ascribed to him; the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Kapila Gītā) preserve further teachings in his name.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: the avatāra Kapila, son of Kardama and Devahūti, who teaches his mother a devotional Sāṃkhya (Kapila Gītā, Bhāgavata 3.25-33). The Bhāgavata identifies him with the founder of Sāṃkhya ('tattva-saṅkhyātā', 3.24-25); some later authors distinguish the two Kapilas.

The Mokṣadharma names Kapila, the supreme seer, as the proclaimer of Sāṃkhya (12.337.60); Nārāyaṇa says the Sāṃkhya teachers call him Kapila (12.326.64); 'among the perfected I am the sage Kapila' (BhG 10.26); in a dialogue Kapila tells Syūmaraśmi that he does not censure the Vedas but that the āśramas' duties have one aim (12.260–262).
In the Bhāgavata the avatāra-teacher of Sāṃkhya, eight-limbed yoga directed to the Lord's form (BhP 3.28) and devotion; a mahājana (6.3.20).

Lineage contribution of lin:upanisadic: SU 5.2 speaks of 'the seer Kapila (or: the tawny seer) born in the beginning, whom he filled with knowledge'. Later tradition reads this as the Sāṃkhya founder, others as Hiraṇyagarbha; the Upaniṣad does not say which.
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Kapilāṇḍa
summary: Number 8 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant's wife who gave one of two mangoes to a hungry devotee; when her husband asked for the second, she prayed and a mango appeared; frightened, he left her and remarried. She asked Śiva to take her beauty and give her the form of a ghoul (pēy), climbed Kailāsa on her hands, and was greeted by Śiva as 'Mother' (Ammai); she asked for no rebirth — or, if born again, never to forget him — and to sing at his feet as he dances, which she does at Tiruvālaṅkāṭu.

realization_account.text: A merchant's wife who gave one of two mangoes to a hungry devotee; when her husband asked for the second, she prayed and a mango appeared; frightened, he left her and remarried. name: Karāla Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā who questions Vasiṣṭha on the perishable and imperishable and on the knowledge of plurality and unity (12.291–296).

name: Kāri Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A poet who used the rewards for his verses to build and serve temples.

realization_account.text: A poet who used the rewards for his verses to build and serve temples.

name: Kārṣṇājini
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (MS 4.3.17, 6.7.35), e.g. holding that fruit-statements within a sacrifice are praise like those for subsidiaries.
alt_summary: Early teacher cited in BS 3.1.9 on the meaning of 'conduct' (caraṇa) in the Chāndogya's account of rebirth (as indicating residual karma).

name: Karuvūrār
summary: Siddhar of Karūr; in the tradition a disciple of Bogar who helped Rājarāja Cōḻa set the great liṅga of the Tañcāvūr temple, where he has a shrine; identified with the Tiruvicaippā poet Karuvūrttēvar.
places: Karūr — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: U22 contribution. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.
alt_summary: Poet of Tiruvicaippā hymns (Tirumuṟai 9), including one on the Rājarājeśvaram at Tañcāvūr; identified by tradition with the Siddhar Karuvūrār.

name: Kāśakṛtsna
notes: A Kāśakṛtsna is also remembered in the grammatical tradition; identity uncertain.
summary: Early Vedāntin named in BS 1.4.22: the supreme self itself abides as the individual self. Śaṅkara declares Kāśakṛtsna's view to be the one in accord with scripture.

name: Kaśyapa
summary: Kaśyapa Mārīca, seer of RV 1.99 and of the closing Soma hymns 9.113–114 (the prayer to be made immortal in the world of unfading light and bliss); one of the seven seers of RV 10.137; in the Atharvaveda 'self-born Kaśyapa' arises from Time (AVŚ 19.53.10).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
alt_summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Jñānakāṇḍa.

name: Kaṭha
summary: Pupil of Vaiśampāyana and eponym of the Kaṭha (Kāṭhaka) branch of the Black Yajurveda.

name: Kātyāyana
summary: Author of the vārttikas on Pāṇini. Tradition credits a Kātyāyana with the White Yajurveda Prātiśākhya, Śrautasūtra and Śulbasūtra and the Ṛgveda index, and identifies him with Vararuci; whether these are one person is doubted by scholars.
alt_summary: The ancient ritualist and phonetician to whom the Sarvānukramaṇī of the Ṛgveda, the Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya and the Śrauta Sūtra of the White Yajurveda are ascribed; the tradition often identifies him with Kātyāyana the critic of Pāṇini (disputed).

name: Kātyāyanī
summary: Yājñavalkya's other wife, whose understanding was that of ordinary women (strīprajñā, BAU 4.5.1); the property is to be divided between her and Maitreyī (BAU 2.4.1, 4.5.2).

name: Kauṇḍinya
summary: Author of the Pañcārthabhāṣya, the only surviving commentary on the Pāśupata Sūtra, which frames the teaching as five categories and five stages. Sometimes identified with the tīrthakara Rāśīkara (uncertain).

name: Kauṇḍinya (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Distinct from the Pāśupata commentator Kauṇḍinya (tch:kaundinya).

name: Kauruṣya
summary: The fourth of Lakulīśa's four disciples (Liṅga P. 1.24.131; Jain lists 'Kauruṣa').

name: Kausalya Āśvalāyana
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks whence prāṇa is born and how it enters and divides itself (PrU 3).

name: Kauśika (the brāhmaṇa of the Vyādha Gītā)
summary: A brāhmaṇa ascetic who burns a crane by his angry glance, is rebuked by a devoted housewife and learns dharma from the meat-seller of Mithilā, then returns to serve his parents (3.196–206).

name: Kauṣītaki
summary: Taught 'breath is brahman' (KauU 2.1); as Sarvajit Kauṣītaki he had three worships of the sun (KauU 2.7).
alt_summary: Eponymous teacher of the Kauṣītaki Ṛgveda school.

name: Kauṭilya
summary: Author by tradition of the Arthaśāstra.

tradition.text: minister of Candragupta Maurya (late 4th c. BCE)

scholarly.text: author-figure of an Arthaśāstra redacted in the early centuries CE

name: Kautsa
summary: The teacher whose view that 'the mantras are meaningless' (anarthakā hi mantrāḥ) Yāska states and refutes (Nirukta 1.15–16).
alt_summary: Teacher whose view that Vedic mantras are meaningless is stated and refuted in Nirukta 1.15–16 (known only as reported there).

name: Kavaṣa Ailūṣa
summary: Seer of RV 10.30–34 (with Akṣa Maujavant as alternative for the gambler's hymn 10.34). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa tells that the seers drove him from a sacrificial session as 'son of a slave woman', until the waters followed him and they accepted him as one known to the gods.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa episode (2.19) is recalled with moderate confidence.

name: Kavikarṇapūra (Paramānanda Sena)
summary: Poet-theologian, son of Śivānanda Sena; author of the Caitanyacandrodaya, the Gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā and the Alaṅkārakaustubha.

name: Kavirāja Yati
summary: Renunciant author of the Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpa; its colophon calls him a paramahaṃsa, pupil of Vaikuṇṭha.

name: Kedāraśakti
summary: A Kālāmukha pontiff of the Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāve (Śakti-pariṣad) named in inscriptions (details to be checked).

name: Keḷadi Basavarāja
summary: Vīraśaiva ruler of Keḷadi (Basavappa Nāyaka) and author of the Sanskrit Śivatattvaratnākara.

name: Keśava Bhāratī
summary: Renouncer who gave Caitanya sannyāsa at Kāṭoyā (c. 1510), naming him Kṛṣṇa Caitanya.

name: Keśava Kāśmīrī Bhaṭṭa
summary: Nimbārka-school teacher credited with a Gītā commentary (Tattvaprakāśikā).

name: Keśava Kāśmīrin Bhaṭṭa
summary: Nimbārka ācārya of Mathurā; author of the Kaustubhaprabhā, the Gītā commentary Tattvaprakāśikā and (attributed) the Kramadīpikā; tradition credits him with defeating rival (tantric) opponents at Mathurā.

name: Keśava Miśra
summary: Author of the Tarkabhāṣā, a primer of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika.

name: Keśava (Sāṃkhya author)
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpikā, a short exposition following Vijñānabhikṣu.

name: Keśidhvaja
summary: A Janaka king devoted to knowledge (ātma-vidyā) who, though acting through karma to exhaust it, taught his rival kinsman Khāṇḍikya the nature of ignorance and the eightfold yoga with Viṣṇu as support (VP 6.6-7); he attained liberation by acting without attachment (VP 6.7.105-106).

name: Kētaladēvi
summary: A woman vacanakāra, wife of the potter-devotee Guṇḍayya.

name: Khaṇḍadeva Miśra
summary: Seventeenth-century Vārāṇasī Bhāṭṭa master: author of the Bhāṭṭadīpikā, Mīmāṃsākaustubha and Bhāṭṭarahasya, known for sharp Bhāṭṭa semantics in a Navya-Nyāya idiom.

name: Khāṇḍikya Janaka
summary: A Janaka king devoted to ritual action (karma), expelled by Keśidhvaja; asked by him for the expiation for a killed cow, he chose instead to ask for the teaching of yoga, then renounced and dissolved into the Brahman called Viṣṇu (VP 6.6-7.104).

name: Kiḍāmbi Āccāṉ
summary: Disciple of Rāmānuja who, the tradition says, cooked for him when attempts were made to poison his food; ancestor of the Kiḍāmbi family of teachers in Deśika's line.

name: Kīnārām
summary: Founder of the present Aghora lineage at Krīm Kuṇḍ (Kīnārām Sthal), Varanasi. Tradition: born at Rāmgaṛh (Chandauli), he was first initiated by the Vaiṣṇava Śivarām, then received Aghora from Bābā Kālūrām, whom he recognised as Dattātreya (after a vision at Girnar); he wandered to Hiṅglāj and elsewhere, founded monasteries and wrote Hindi works — Vivekasār, Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl, Gītāvalī.

tradition.text: 1601–1771 (Vikrama 1658 birth; lived about 170 years)

realization_account.text: Received Aghora-dīkṣā from Kālūrām (Dattātreya); famed for miracles and for compassion to the poor; lived about 170 years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Registry id. The dates are the tradition's; no independent confirmation checked.

name: Kinnari Bommayya
summary: A śaraṇa remembered as a player of the kinnari lute.

name: Kōcceṅkaṭ Cōḻa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. In a former birth a spider that wove a canopy over the liṅga at Tiruvāṉaikkā and fought an elephant that also worshipped there, both dying; reborn as a Cōḻa king, he built many 'elevated temples' (māṭakkōyil) that elephants cannot climb.

realization_account.text: In a former birth a spider that wove a canopy over the liṅga at Tiruvāṉaikkā and fought an elephant that also worshipped there, both dying; reborn as a Cōḻa king, he built many 'elevated temples' (māṭakkōyil) that elephants cannot climb.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Koṅkaṇar
summary: Siddhar and alchemist, in the tradition a disciple of Bogar. A popular story tells that he burnt a crane with his glance and was then rebuked by a devoted housewife who had kept him waiting: 'Did you take me for the crane, Koṅkaṇa?' — sending him to learn from her and from Tiruvaḷḷuvar.
places: Tirupati — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The crane story (kokkeṉṟu niṉaittāyō koṅkaṇavā) is recalled with moderate confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kōrakkar
summary: Siddhar of the popular list whom the tradition identifies with Gorakṣanātha: born from the sacred ash that Maccamuṉi gave a childless woman, who threw it away, until a boy came forth from where it fell. Herbal and alchemical works are ascribed to him; his samādhi is placed at Poyyūr (Vaṭakku Poykainallūr) near Nākappaṭṭiṉam.
places: Vaṭakku Poykainallūr (Poyyūr) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Identification with tch:goraksanatha is the tradition's (see brw:natha-tamil-siddha). Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kōṭpuli Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Cōḻa general who stored paddy for the temple before going to war; returning to find that his kinsmen had eaten it in a famine, he put them to death; Śiva appeared and took them all to his world.

realization_account.text: A Cōḻa general who stored paddy for the temple before going to war; returning to find that his kinsmen had eaten it in a famine, he put them to death; Śiva appeared and took them all to his world.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kriyāśakti
summary: Kālāmukha teacher remembered as preceptor (rājaguru) at the early Vijayanagara court and of the minister Mādhava; among the last prominent Kālāmukhas (identification of his order moderate-low).

name: Kṛṣṇa (Vāsudeva)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga; his departure from the world is taken to begin the Kali yuga (traditionally 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: The tradition regards him as the Lord (Bhagavān) himself born as Vasudeva's son; in the Gītā he speaks as unborn and imperishable, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6), and the Nārāyaṇīya presents him as a manifestation of Nārāyaṇa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Son of Vasudeva and Devakī, prince of the Vṛṣṇis, Arjuna's charioteer and teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā and the Anugītā. In the Gītā he speaks as the Lord who descends age after age (4.6–8), is the source of all (10.8) and shows Arjuna his universal form (ch. 11); the Nārāyaṇīya names his birth at Mathurā among Nārāyaṇa's manifestations (12.326.82). In the Anuśāsana he learns the thousand names of Śiva from Upamanyu (13.14–17).
notes: Historicity recorded as 'legendary' in the scholarly sense only; the tradition holds him to be the Lord incarnate.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: speaker of the Uddhava Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.7-29), in which he gives Uddhava his final teaching before leaving the world, and of the Uttara Gītā; he quotes the Kāma Gītā (Mahābhārata 14.13).

name: Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra
summary: 'Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī', pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa, who on hearing the teaching became free from thirst (ChU 3.17.6).
notes: Later tradition, and some scholars, identify him with Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva of the Gītā (tch:krsna); the Upaniṣad says only 'Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī'. Kept as a separate id; identification not asserted.

name: Kṛṣṇa Mitra
summary: Ācārya named in the colophon of the Sāṃkhya treatise Tattvamīmāṃsā (with his father's and grandfather's names; the e-text reading of the father's name is garbled).

name: Kṛṣṇa Yajvan
summary: Author of the Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā, an elementary manual.

name: Kṛṣṇadās Adhikārī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and manager (adhikārī) of Śrīnāthjī's temple.

name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
summary: Author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta, the Govindalīlāmṛta and the Sāraṅgaraṅgadā commentary on the Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta; wrote in Vṛndāvana in old age from the accounts of Raghunātha Dāsa and Svarūpa's notes.

name: Kṣemarāja
summary: Abhinavagupta's foremost disciple; author of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya and of commentaries that fused Spanda and Pratyabhijñā and read the Bhairava tantras non-dually: Śivasūtravimarśinī, Spandanirṇaya, Spandasandoha, Svacchandoddyota, Netroddyota, Vijñānabhairavoddyota (incomplete), Stavacintāmaṇivṛtti, Śivastotrāvalīvivṛti, Parāprāveśikā.

name: Kuṭampai (Kutampaic cittar)
summary: Siddhar named from the refrain of his thirty-two couplets, addressed to a girl wearing kuṭampai ear-ornaments; for the realized, he asks, what need of mantra, seals, yoga, rejuvenation or hymns?
places: Māyavaram (Mayiladuthurai) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kulacciṟai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Minister of the Pāṇṭiya king Neṭumāṟaṉ who, with the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār, invited Campantar to Madurai and served devotees of every birth.

realization_account.text: Minister of the Pāṇṭiya king Neṭumāṟaṉ who, with the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār, invited Campantar to Madurai and served devotees of every birth.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kullūka Bhaṭṭa
summary: Bengali commentator on Manu whose text and numbering became the vulgate.

name: Kumāra Varadācārya
summary: Son and disciple of Vedānta Deśika (Nayinārācārya), author of the Adhikaraṇacintāmaṇi and continuer of his father's line.

name: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa

tradition.text: older contemporary of Śaṅkara, whom he met at Prayāga at the end of his life (Śaṅkaradigvijaya)

realization_account.text: Hagiographies of Śaṅkara (e.g. the Śaṅkaradigvijaya ascribed to Mādhava-Vidyāraṇya) present Kumārila as an incarnation of Skanda sent to restore the Vedic path; they tell that he studied among Buddhists, survived a fall from a height by the truth of the Veda, and later entered a husk-fire at Prayāga as expiation, where Śaṅkara met him and was sent on to Maṇḍana Miśra.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Hagiographic details are from memory and are not in Kumārila's works (low confidence). The teacher–pupil link with Prabhākara is a Bhāṭṭa legend; its historicity is doubted.
summary: Founder of the Bhāṭṭa school: author of the Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā on Śabara, and a lost Bṛhaṭṭīkā. He defended the authorless Veda and intrinsic validity against Buddhists, rejected omniscience in matters of dharma, a creator and a total dissolution, and set out a path to release through avoidance of desire-prompted and prohibited acts.

name: Kumbhandās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a farmer of Jamunāvato near Govardhana; the tradition remembers his refusal of the imperial court ('what have saints to do with Sīkrī?').

name: Kuṅkiliyakkalaya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He burned kuṅkiliyam incense before Śiva, sold all he had for it, and spent even his wife's marriage badge on incense; at Tiruppaṉantāḷ he straightened the leaning liṅga by pulling with a rope tied to his own neck.

realization_account.text: He burned kuṅkiliyam incense before Śiva, sold all he had for it, and spent even his wife's marriage badge on incense; at Tiruppaṉantāḷ he straightened the leaning liṅga by pulling with a rope tied to his own neck.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kūrakulottama Dāsar
summary: Disciple of Piḷḷai Lokācārya who, the tradition says, preserved and passed on his teacher's doctrine to Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai.

name: Kūreśa
summary: Rāmānuja's foremost disciple and scribe, the father of Parāśara Bhaṭṭar and author of the Pañcastava. The tradition says he memorized the Bodhāyana Vṛtti in Kashmir for Rāmānuja and was blinded by a Cōḻa king for refusing to affirm Śiva's supremacy.

name: Kūṟṟuva Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain who conquered many lands and wished to be crowned at Chidambaram; refused by the Tillai priests, who crown only Cōḻas, he prayed, and Śiva placed his feet on his head as his crown.

realization_account.text: A chieftain who conquered many lands and wished to be crowned at Chidambaram; refused by the Tillai priests, who crown only Cōḻas, he prayed, and Śiva placed his feet on his head as his crown.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kurukai Kāvalappaṉ
summary: Disciple of Nāthamuni to whom, the tradition says, the teaching of yoga (yogarahasya) was entrusted; Yāmuna was directed to him but arrived after his death.

name: Kuśika

tradition.text: first disciple of the incarnate Lord

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. CE (ten generations before Uditācārya, 380 CE)

summary: The first of Lakulīśa's four disciples (Liṅga P. 1.24.131; Kūrma P. 1.51.26). Kauṇḍinya tells that Kuśika, prompted by Rudra, approached the Lord at Ujjayinī, declared his birth, lineage, learning and freedom from debts, and asked whether there is a final and absolute removal of all suffering - the question the Pāśupata Sūtra answers. The Mathurā inscription of 380 CE counts its donor as tenth in succession from Kuśika.

name: Kutsa Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 1.94–98 and 1.101–115, including the Rudra hymn 1.114 and 1.115.1 ('Sūrya is the self of what moves and what stands'); the Atharvaveda hymn to the highest Brahman (AVŚ 10.8) is also ascribed to Kutsa.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Laba Aindra
summary: Seer of RV 10.119, the soma-exalted self-praise with the refrain 'have I not drunk of the soma?'; the Anukramaṇī gives its deity as ātman (Indra).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Lābukāyana
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (MS 6.7.37; spelled Lāvukāyana in one edition).

name: Lagadha
summary: The 'great-souled' teacher whose knowledge of time the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa sets out (v. 2); known only from that text.

name: Lakkaṇṇa Daṇḍēśa
summary: Minister of Dēvarāya II and author of the Kannada Śivatattvacintāmaṇi.

name: Lakṣmaṇa
summary: Rāma's brother: recipient of Rāma's teaching on māyā, knowledge and devotion (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa 3.4) and of the Rāma Gītā (7.5); in the Rāmcaritmānas he himself teaches Guha (the Lakṣmaṇa Gītā).

name: Lakṣmaṇa Deśika
notes: His identification with Abhinavagupta's teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta is sometimes proposed; not accepted here.
summary: Author of the Śāradātilaka, a manual of mantra-śāstra widely used as an authority, including in Kerala.

name: Lakṣmaṇagupta
summary: Disciple of Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta's teacher in the Pratyabhijñā; no works survive.

name: Lakṣmīdhara
notes: Contribution from U08 (catalogue role); U23 owns Śrī Vidyā.
summary: Commentator on the Saundaryalaharī from the Samaya standpoint, who rejects the 64 tantras as Kaula and non-Vedic and upholds the five 'auspicious āgamas'.
alt_summary: Author of the Kṛtyakalpataru, the digest that systematised Purāṇic teaching on vows, gifts, tīrthas and śrāddha.
Minister of the Gāhaḍavāla king Govindacandra, author of the Kṛtyakalpataru.

name: Lakṣmīdhara Kavi
summary: Author of the Advaitamakaranda.

name: Lakulīśa

tradition.text: the 28th and last of Śiva's yoga-teacher incarnations of the Vaivasvata manvantara, in the age when Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva and Vyāsa Dvaipāyana are born (Liṅga P. 1.24.125-131; Kūrma P. 1.51.9-10)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. CE (reckoned back ten teacher-generations from the Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 CE); some scholars say 1st–2nd c.

places: Kāyāvarohaṇa / Kāyāvataraṇa / Kāyārohaṇa (Karvan, near Vadodara, Gujarat)

realization_account.text: Not a human who became realized but the Lord himself: seeing an abandoned corpse in a cremation ground, Śiva entered it by yogic power and became the brahmacārin Lakulī at the siddha-field called Kāyāvatāra (Liṅga P. 1.24.127-130); Kauṇḍinya says the Lord, in human form, took a brahmin's body, descended at Kāyāvataraṇa and walked to Ujjayinī, where he taught Kuśika; the Kāravaṇa-māhātmya says Śiva was born to Viśvarūpa and Sudarśanā, and after the infant died Śiva entered the body and later merged into the Brahmeśvara liṅga at Kāyāvarohaṇa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Lakulīśa, 'Lord with the club', is regarded as the incarnation of Śiva who founded the Pāśupata observance and taught the Pāśupata Sūtra, and the first of the Pāśupata tīrthakaras. His images show him seated, holding a club and a citron, often ithyphallic; the Liṅga Purāṇa (1.76.38-39) prescribes his image surrounded by disciples, hand raised in exposition. Kauṇḍinya does not use the name Lakulīśa; he speaks of 'the Lord' who descended at Kāyāvataraṇa.

name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī, Lallā)
summary: 14th-century Kashmiri yoginī whose vākhs, in the idiom of non-dual Śaivism and yoga, speak of seeking Śiva far and finding him at home in her own body, of breath-practice lighting the lamp of knowledge, and of the indifference of the realized to sectarian names.

realization_account.text: Tradition holds that she left an unhappy married life to wander as an ascetic, dancing unclothed after her teacher's single instruction to turn from the outer to the inner; she is also revered by Kashmiri Muslims (as Lallā Ārifa).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Her teacher is named in tradition as Siddha Śrīkaṇṭha (Sed Bayu) - low confidence, not given as an id.

name: Lāṭyāyana
summary: Author by tradition of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda Śrautasūtra.

name: Laugākṣi Bhāskara
summary: Author of the Arthasaṅgraha, a beginner's primer of Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā closely following Āpadeva, and of the Tarkakaumudī (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika).
alt_summary: Author of the Tarkakaumudī (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika) and of the Arthasaṅgraha, a Mīmāṃsā primer.

name: Līlā
summary: Queen who, grieving for her husband Padma, is taught by the goddess Sarasvatī (Jñapti) and shown in consciousness-body the worlds of her husband's past and future lives (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha 3.15-60).

name: Locana Dāsa
summary: Author of the Bengali Caitanya Maṅgala.

name: Lokanātha Gosvāmī
summary: Early associate of Caitanya in Vṛndāvana and Narottama's initiating guru.

name: Lopāmudrā
summary: Wife of Agastya and seer of RV 1.179.1–2: after many autumns of toil she laments that age wears away the beauty of bodies and asks that husbands come to their wives; the ancient seers too, who spoke truths with the gods, did not reach the end (of tapas).
notes: Named among the brahmavādinīs of the Bṛhaddevatā. The Śākta (Śrīvidyā) tradition names a Lopāmudrā as seer of one form of the Śrīvidyā mantra (reference only, low confidence).
alt_summary: Agastya's wife and companion in pilgrimage in the Kāśī Khaṇḍa, questioner on tīrthas; in the Śrīvidyā tradition a seer of a form of the Goddess's mantra (U23).

name: Maccamuṉi (Macchamuni)
summary: Siddhar of the popular list whom the tradition identifies with Matsyendranātha: born as a fish (maccam) that overheard Śiva teaching Pārvatī, and guru of Kōrakkar.
places: Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Identification with tch:matsyendranatha is the tradition's (see brw:natha-tamil-siddha). Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Madālasā

realization_account.text: The queen who, under pretext of lulling her crying infants, taught her first sons that the self is pure, that its name is a recent imagination, and that the body of five elements is not theirs (MkP 25.10-18), so that they renounced; she taught Alarka rājadharma and gave him a ring containing a teaching for the time of distress (MkP 26-35).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: A woman teacher of self-knowledge in the Mārkaṇḍeya. Her lullaby opens 'śuddho 'si re tāta, na te 'sti nāma' in the checked e-text (MkP 25.11); the popular verse 'śuddho 'si buddho 'si nirañjano 'si ...' recited under her name was not found there.

name: Mādāra Cennayya
summary: A cobbler (mādāra) devotee of the pre-Basava past whom Basava names as his own household's father ('I am the son in the house of Mādāra Cennayya').
notes: Placement before Basava follows the hagiographies; low confidence.

name: Mādhava Mukunda
summary: Later Nimbārka polemicist to whom the Parapakṣagirivajra is attributed.

name: Mādhava Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and pontiff after Narahari Tīrtha in the Uttarādi line.

name: Mādhavendra Purī
summary: Renouncer revered by the Gauḍīyas as the 'seed' of the love-devotion that Caitanya spread; installer of the Gopāla deity at Govardhana; teacher of Īśvara Purī and (tradition) of Advaita Ācārya and Nityānanda. Tradition places him in Madhva's line.
notes: His lament 'ayi dīna-dayārdra nātha …' is quoted in CC 2.4 (verse number to verify).

name: Madhucchandas
summary: Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra, son of Viśvāmitra, seer of the opening hymns of the Ṛgveda (1.1–10: 'I praise Agni, the household priest…') and of the opening of the Soma book (9.1).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī
summary: Bengal-born Advaitin of Vārāṇasī, author of the Advaitasiddhi (against Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta), the Gūḍhārthadīpikā, the Siddhāntabindu, the Bhaktirasāyana, the Vedāntakalpalatikā, the Advaitaratnarakṣaṇa and the Prasthānabheda; joined rigorous Advaita dialectic with ardent devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
alt_summary: Author of the Gūḍhārthadīpikā on the Gītā, dividing it into three six-chapter sections on action, devotion and knowledge.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Madhuvarasa
summary: A brāhmaṇa śaraṇa (Madhuvayya) who gave his daughter in marriage to Haraḷayya's son and was put to death with him in the tradition's account.

name: Madhva

tradition.text: the tradition's own reckoning: born when 4,300 years of the Kali age had passed (Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya 32.120 = c. 1199 CE) and lived 79 years (to c. 1278); a second traditional reckoning, widely used by the maṭhas, gives 1238–1317

scholarly.text: c. 1238–1317 CE (B. N. K. Sharma, from the epigraphic dates of his disciple Narahari Tīrtha, 1264–1293); some earlier scholars followed 1197/1199–1276/1278

realization_account.text: Madhva is the third avatāra of Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), after Hanumān and Bhīma — he says so himself at the end of the Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya (32.162, 32.166) and of the Anuvyākhyāna (4.4.15), reading the Balitthā hymn (Ṛgveda 1.141) as naming Vāyu's three forms; Bhīma was reborn as a brāhmaṇa when 4,300 years of Kali had passed to proclaim the truth about Hari hidden by the daityas (MBTN 32.120). The Sumadhvavijaya tells of boyhood feats, renunciation and naming (4.33, 5.1–2), journeys to Badarī where he met Vyāsa and received his teaching, and closes with the gods hailing him as Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva and showering him with flowers (16.57–58). The tradition holds that he passed from human sight at Uḍupi while expounding the Aitareya Upaniṣad and dwells with Vyāsa at Badarī; the day is kept as Madhva-navamī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Dvaita Vedānta (Tattvavāda). Born at Pājaka near Uḍupi to Madhyageha Bhaṭṭa, he took renunciation as a boy from Acyutaprekṣa, receiving the name Pūrṇaprajña (Pūrṇabodha), and was installed as master of Vedānta with the name Ānandatīrtha; he signs his works 'Madhva'. He toured India debating, twice went to Badarī, installed the image of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi and founded the eight Uḍupi maṭhas, and wrote thirty-seven works (the Sarvamūla) on the Brahmasūtras, the Gītā, ten Upaniṣads, the Ṛgveda, the epics and Purāṇas, ten polemical and doctrinal treatises, hymns and ritual manuals. He taught that Viṣṇu alone is independent, that the five differences are real and eternal, that souls are graded by nature, and that liberation comes by Viṣṇu's grace through knowledge and devotion.
notes: Scholarly and traditional dates are given in 'dating'. The Uḍupi Kṛṣṇa image is said in the tradition to have come ashore in a block of gopīcandana clay from a ship — not verified in this pass. His mother's name (Vedavatī in later tradition) was not found in the Sumadhvavijaya e-text by a simple search.
alt_summary: Author of a Gītā commentary and the Gītātātparyanirṇaya, and of the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya, reading the epic as proclaiming Viṣṇu's supremacy.
U01 contribution: author of the Ṛgbhāṣya on RV 1.1–40, reading the hymns as ultimately praising Viṣṇu, the one denoted by all names.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Maḍivāḷa Mācayya
summary: The washerman śaraṇa of Kalyāṇa, remembered as the fierce defender of the devotees (gaṇācāra) who protected the śaraṇas and their vacana bundles in the flight after the upheaval.

name: Māhācamasya
summary: Knew the fourth vyāhṛti, mahaḥ, as brahman, the self, of which bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ and suvaḥ are the limbs (TU 1.5.1).

name: Mahādeva Vedāntin
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyasūtravṛttisāra, a commentary on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra largely abridging Aniruddha.

name: Mahādevabhaṭṭa
summary: Disciple of Prajñārjuna in Bhāskara's lineage (Vārttika 1.7).

name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
summary: Leader who called the Gītā his 'mother' and read it as teaching action without attachment to fruits (anāsakti) and non-violence; author of Anāsakti Yoga.
notes: Recent (post-1800); no initiatory lineage — lineage field records the text-tradition he interpreted.

name: Maheśacandra Nyāyaratna
summary: Calcutta Sanskrit scholar (principal of the Sanskrit College), author of the Navyanyāyabhāṣāpradīpa, a guide to the technical terms of Navya-Nyāya.

name: Maheśvarānanda
summary: South Indian (Cola country) teacher of the Krama (Mahārtha) around 1300, disciple of Mahāprakāśa; author of the Prakrit Mahārthamañjarī with the Sanskrit Parimala, synthesizing Krama, Pratyabhijñā and Śrīvidyā.
notes: Teacher's name Mahāprakāśa and alias Gorakṣa from memory (low).

name: Mahidāsa Aitareya
summary: The seer to whom the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka are ascribed.

realization_account.text: Son of Itarā, slighted by his father, he was favoured by the Earth goddess and received the Brāhmaṇa (Sāyaṇa's introduction); the Chāndogya says he lived 116 years by his knowledge (ChU 3.16.7).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Knowing the person as sacrifice, he said to sickness 'why do you afflict me? I shall not die of this' and lived 116 years (ChU 3.16.7); the tradition regards him as the seer of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka.

name: Mahīdhara
summary: Vārāṇasī scholar who wrote the Vedadīpa on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā; the same Mahīdhara compiled the tantric manual Mantramahodadhi.

name: Maitreya
summary: Sage who goes to Kailāsa and is taught by Mahādeva that the body is a temple and the jīva is Śiva (Maitreya Upaniṣad 2). Distinct from Yājñavalkya's wife Maitreyī.

name: Maitreya (sage)
summary: The sage who questions Parāśara in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (VP 1.1.1-11) and who, in the Bhāgavata's third and fourth books, instructs Vidura on creation and the Lord's deeds. Not the Buddhist Maitreya.

name: Maitreyī
summary: One of Yājñavalkya's two wives, described as a discusser of brahman (brahmavādinī, BAU 4.5.1); when he is about to leave the household she refuses wealth that cannot make her immortal and receives the teaching on the self (BAU 2.4, 4.5).

name: Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya
summary: Andhra Śaiva teacher contemporary with Basava, founder figure of the Ārādhya Śaivas and subject of Pālkuriki Sōmanātha's Paṇḍitārādhya Caritra.

name: Maṇakkāl Nambi
summary: Disciple of Uyyakkoṇḍār who, the tradition says, drew Yāmuna back from kingship to the teaching, by bringing him greens daily until admitted, and then leading him to Raṅganātha.

name: Māṉakkañcāṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A general who, when Śiva came as a Māvratī ascetic on his daughter's wedding day and asked for her hair, cut it off at once and gave it.

realization_account.text: A general who, when Śiva came as a Māvratī ascetic on his daughter's wedding day and asked for her hair, cut it off at once and gave it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Maṇakkuṭavar
summary: Author of the oldest surviving Kuṟaḷ commentary; his own affiliation (some say Jain) is uncertain.

name: Maṉavācakaṅkaṭantār
summary: Disciple of Meykaṇṭār from Tiruvatikai, author of the Uṇmai Viḷakkam.

name: Maṇavāḷa Māmuni
