summary: The last of the great Teṅkalai teachers: disciple of Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai, commentator on Piḷḷai Lokācārya's works and the Ācārya Hṛdayam, author of the Upadēśa Ratnamālai and Yatirājaviṃśati, and founder of the eight 'elephants' (aṣṭadiggaja) among his disciples; the Teṅkalai regard him as Rāmānuja returned.

realization_account.text: After he expounded the Īṭu for a year before Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam (1432 in the tradition's reckoning), the Lord appeared as a child and recited the verse 'śrīśaileśa-dayāpātram', taking him as his own teacher.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Maṇḍana Miśra

realization_account.text: In Śaṅkara's hagiographies Maṇḍana, a ritualist householder, debates Śaṅkara with his wife Ubhaya-Bhāratī as judge, is defeated, takes sannyāsa and becomes Sureśvara.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The identification with Sureśvara is traditional and disputed by modern scholarship.
summary: Mīmāṃsaka of the Bhāṭṭa line (by tradition Kumārila's pupil): author of the Vidhiviveka (injunction means 'being a means to the desired'), Bhāvanāviveka, Vibhramaviveka, Mīmāṃsānukramaṇī, the Sphoṭasiddhi (defending sphoṭa) and the Advaita Brahmasiddhi.
alt_summary: Mīmāṃsaka and Advaitin, author of the Brahmasiddhi (and of the Mīmāṃsā works Vidhiviveka and Bhāvanāviveka, the Vibhramaviveka and the grammatical Sphoṭasiddhi); held avidyā to reside in the jīvas, the need for prasaṅkhyāna after verbal knowledge, and a helpful role for works; in the tradition's account defeated by Śaṅkara at Māhiṣmatī and became Sureśvara.

name: Maṇikaṇṭha Miśra
summary: Pre-Gaṅgeśa Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyaratna.

name: Māṇikkavācakar
summary: Author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumuṟai 8); the fourth samayācārya, exemplar of the true path (san-mārga, jñāna). Not among the sixty-three.

tradition.text: placed before the Tēvāram poets by much of the tradition

realization_account.text: Chief minister of the Pāṇṭiya king (named Arimarttaṉa in later accounts), sent with treasure to buy horses, he met Śiva as a guru under a kuruntha tree at Tirupperunturai, received initiation and spent the treasure on a temple. Imprisoned, he was saved when Śiva turned foxes into horses (which became foxes again), and when Śiva, hired as a labourer by the old woman Vanti to repair the Vaikai embankment, received the king's blow that struck every creature. At Chidambaram he defeated Buddhists from Laṅkā in debate; Śiva, as a brahmin, wrote down the Tiruvācakam and signed it; asked its meaning, he pointed to Naṭarāja and merged in him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: His absence from Cuntarar's list is used by scholars to date him after Cuntarar.

name: Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. The Cōḻa princess who became queen of Neṭumāṟaṉ and, with the minister Kulacciṟaiyār, brought Campantar to Madurai to restore Śaivism.

realization_account.text: The Cōḻa princess who became queen of Neṭumāṟaṉ and, with the minister Kulacciṟaiyār, brought Campantar to Madurai to restore Śaivism.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Maṅki
summary: A man who, after losing his young bulls, renounces desire and speaks the Maṅki Gītā (12.171).
alt_summary: Singer of the Maṅki Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.171), who renounced desire after his efforts at wealth failed. A Maṅki is also taught by Vasiṣṭha in the Mokṣopāya's Nirvāṇa book (MU 6.180-183; identity of the two not asserted).

name: Manu Svāyambhuva
summary: The first Manu, son of the self-existent, who received dharma from Svayambhū and taught it; his teaching is recited in the Manusmṛti by Bhṛgu. Parāśara assigns Manu's dharma to the Kṛta age.

tradition.text: the first Manu, at the beginning of creation

name: Manu Vaivasvata
summary: Son of Vivasvat, who received the yoga from him and passed it to Ikṣvāku (BhG 4.1).
notes: Distinguished from Svāyambhuva Manu, to whom the Manusmṛti is ascribed.
alt_summary: Son of Vivasvant, ancestor of humankind, seer of RV 8.27–31. (Distinct in the tradition from Manu Svāyambhuva of the Manusmṛti.)
Lineage contribution of lin:upanisadic: link in the teacher-lines Brahmā -> Prajāpati -> Manu -> creatures (ChU 3.11.4, 8.15.1); Vāmadeva says 'I was Manu' (BAU 1.4.10).
The present (seventh) Manu, son of Vivasvat; in ŚB 1.8.1 he saves a fish that later tows his ship over the flood, and his offering gives rise to Iḍā.
alt_notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Manuṣyaka
summary: Number 9 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Maṟaimalai Aṭikaḷ
summary: Tamil scholar and Śaiva Siddhānta advocate, leader of the 'pure Tamil' movement; argued for an early date of Māṇikkavācakar and led the 1921 fixing of the Tiruvaḷḷuvar era.

name: Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar
summary: Disciple of Aruṇanti and guru of Umāpati Civācāriyār; third of the four teachers of the outer lineage. No Meykaṇṭa treatise is his.

realization_account.text: Seeing the Chidambaram priest Umāpati carried in a palanquin with a torch in daylight, he called out 'a day-blind man riding a dead log'; stung, Umāpati followed him and became his disciple, eating food from his hand, for which the Tillai priests excluded him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Details of his caste and the palanquin story are given at low confidence (they come from later hagiography).

name: Marīci
notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Vimānārcanakalpa.

name: Maritoṇṭadārya
summary: Author of the Tattvapradīpikā commentary on the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi and of the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā.

name: Mārkaṇḍeya
summary: The long-lived sage who instructs the Pāṇḍavas in the forest (3.180–221): on karma, the ages and the dissolution — in which he saw the worlds within the body of a divine child on a banyan branch (3.186.81–91) — the devoted wife and the righteous meat-seller.

realization_account.text: The long-lived sage who, by Nara-Nārāyaṇa's boon, witnessed an illusory deluge and saw the Lord as an infant lying on a banyan leaf, entering and leaving the child's body (BhP 12.8-10).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: The ever-young sage in whose name the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa is told; he directs Jaimini to the wise birds and narrates the Devī Māhātmya as the story of the eighth Manu.
Long-lived sage whom Śaunaka and others ask, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Upaniṣad, how he lives in bliss; he answers with the knowledge of Śiva as Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

name: Maruḷārādhya (Maruḷasiddha)
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Ujjayinī pīṭha (Ujjaini, Kūḍligi taluk, Karnataka).

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Seat name Saddharma-siṃhāsana (low confidence).

name: Maskarin
summary: Commentator on the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

name: Mastnāth
summary: 18th-century Nāth yogī regarded as founder of the monastery at Asthal Bohar near Rohtak (Haryana).

name: Māṭhara
summary: Commentator on the SK named in the colophon of the Māṭhara Vṛtti; his date is disputed.

name: Mathurānātha Tarkavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Rahasya commentaries (Māthurī) on the Tattvacintāmaṇi, the Dīdhiti and Udayana's works.

name: Matsyendranātha
summary: The first human Nāth after Ādinātha and guru of Gorakṣa; the Kaulajñānanirṇaya calls itself 'brought down' by Macchaghnapāda/Mīnapāda from Candradvīpa and tells how Bhairava as a fisherman recovered the scripture from a fish's belly (KJN 16). Nāth sagas tell how he forgot himself among the women of the Kadalī (or Strī) kingdom and was awakened by Gorakṣa. In the Kathmandu valley he is worshipped as Karuṇāmaya (Buṅga-dyaḥ, Rāto Macchindranāth), brought to end a drought caused by Gorakṣa; Tibetan tradition relates the name to the siddha Lūipa. Abhinavagupta praises 'Macchanda' as a Kaula master (Tantrāloka 1.7).

tradition.text: present in the four ages; Nāth hagiography

realization_account.text: Received the Kaula teaching from Bhairava/Ādinātha (in some Nāth tellings while in the form of a fish, overhearing Śiva teaching Pārvatī); fell into forgetfulness in the Kadalī kingdom and was re-awakened by his disciple Gorakṣa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: HYP 1.5 lists both 'Matsyendra' and 'Mīna', and some traditions distinguish Mīnanātha from Matsyendra (e.g. as father/son); this shard keeps one entry and records the question in dsp:identity-of-matsyendra.

name: Mauṉa kuru (the silent guru of Tāyumāṉavar)
summary: The silent teacher of Tāyumāṉavar at Tiruchirappalli, praised in his songs as coming in Tirumūlar's line (mūlaṉ marapu), who taught by the instruction 'be still'.

name: Maunappa Paṇḍita
summary: Author of the Vīraśaivācārakaustubha.

name: Mayanāmatī
summary: Queen-mother in the Bengali Nāth cycle, a disciple of Gorakṣa who received the 'great knowledge' (mahājñāna) and with it power over death; she compels her son Gopīcandra to renounce. One of the few women siddhas of the Nāth tradition.

name: Māyidēva
summary: Author ascribed the Sanskrit Anubhavasūtra on the ṣaṭsthala path.

name: Medhas
summary: The brahmin sage (dvijavarya, MkP 81.9) in whose forest hermitage the Devī Māhātmya is taught to the deposed king Suratha and the merchant Samādhi.

name: Medhātithi
summary: Author of the oldest surviving commentary on Manu, reasoning in the manner of Mīmāṃsā.

name: Medhātithi Kāṇva
summary: Seer of RV 1.12–23, including 1.22.20: 'the wise ever see that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched out in heaven'.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Medhāvin
summary: The son in the father–son dialogue of the Mokṣadharma (12.169), who urges his father to seek the self now because death is always near.

name: Medhya Kāṇva
summary: Seer of the Vālakhilya hymn RV 8.58: 'one Agni kindled in many ways … one has become all this'.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Meghanādāri Sūri
summary: Viśiṣṭādvaita logician before Deśika, author of the Nayadyumaṇi.

name: Meykaṇṭār
summary: Founder of the Tamil Siddhānta school; author of the Civañāṉa Pōtam; head of the lineage of 'outer' teachers (puṟaccantāṉam).

realization_account.text: Born to a childless Vēḷāḷa couple after they bathed at Tiruveṇkāṭu as Campantar's hymn instructed, and named after its Lord; as a child he was taught by the sage Parañcōti from Kailāsa, who named him Meykaṇṭār, 'he who saw the truth'. He gathered 49 disciples; the learned family priest Aruṇanti, who came to test the child, became his foremost disciple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Meypporuḷ Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain stabbed by his enemy Muttanātaṉ, who had come disguised as a Śaiva ascetic; dying, he ordered his guard Tattaṉ to escort the assassin safely out, because he wore Śiva's garb.

realization_account.text: A chieftain stabbed by his enemy Muttanātaṉ, who had come disguised as a Śaiva ascetic; dying, he ordered his guard Tattaṉ to escort the assassin safely out, because he wore Śiva's garb.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mitra Miśra
summary: Author of the Vīramitrodaya.

name: Mitra (Pāśupata)
summary: The third of Lakulīśa's four disciples (Liṅga P. 1.24.131 'Mitra'; Kūrma P. 1.51.26 'Mitraka'; Jain lists 'Maitrya').

name: Mōḷige Mahādēvi
summary: Wife of Mōḷige Mārayya and a vacanakāra.

name: Mōḷige Mārayya
summary: A king (Kashmir in the tradition's account) who renounced his kingdom and lived in Kalyāṇa by selling bundles of firewood (mōḷige).

name: Mudaliyāṇḍāṉ
summary: Nephew of Rāmānuja, called his 'triple staff' (tridaṇḍa), entrusted with the administration of the Śrīraṅgam temple.

name: Muddadeva
summary: An ācārya of the Śivayogin lineage from which the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi's author descends; named Muddadeva because he gave joy (mud) to all beings (SSM 1.15–16).

name: Muḍumba Narasiṃhasvāmin
summary: Author to whom the Sāṃkhyataruvasanta, a late commentary on the SK, is ascribed.

name: Mūka (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Muktananda
summary: In U06's context (recent reception): made the Guru Gītā the daily morning chant of his ashrams (Ganeshpuri recension).

name: Muktāyakka
summary: The woman śaraṇa who, grieving her brother Ajagaṇṇa, was met by Allama; their exchange on grief, speech and silence is a chapter of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Muṉaiyaṭuvā Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A warrior who fought for the losing side in others' battles for hire and spent the fees on feeding devotees.

realization_account.text: A warrior who fought for the losing side in others' battles for hire and spent the fees on feeding devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Murāri Gupta
summary: Physician of Navadvīpa and companion of Caitanya; author of the earliest Sanskrit biography (kaḍacā).

name: Murāri Miśra
notes: Modern literature numbers several Murāris inconsistently (II/III); low confidence on dating and on the second work.
summary: Mīmāṃsaka whose distinct account of how validity is known (through the after-cognition, anuvyavasāya) made him proverbially the founder of a 'third path'; fragments of his Tripādīnītinayana and (attributed) Aṅgatvanirukti survive.

name: Mūrkka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A gambler who fed devotees with his winnings and dealt harshly with those who would not pay — hence 'the rough one'.

realization_account.text: A gambler who fed devotees with his winnings and dealt harshly with those who would not pay — hence 'the rough one'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mūrtti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who supplied sandal paste to the Madurai temple; when a Jain-favouring usurper stopped the supply he ground his own elbow on the stone; made king by Śiva's will, he ruled with the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa and matted hair as his crown and insignia.

realization_account.text: A merchant who supplied sandal paste to the Madurai temple; when a Jain-favouring usurper stopped the supply he ground his own elbow on the stone; made king by Śiva's will, he ruled with the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa and matted hair as his crown and insignia.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Muruka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who wove flower garlands for Śiva; friend of Campantar, he attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who wove flower garlands for Śiva; friend of Campantar, he attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Naciketas

realization_account.text: KU 2.3.18: having received this knowledge from Death and the whole rule of yoga, Naciketas attained brahman and became free of stain and death.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Boy who, given to Death by his father, waits three nights in Yama's house and chooses as his third boon the knowledge of what happens after death; refusing all worldly gifts, he receives the teaching of the self and the whole method of yoga and attains brahman (KU 1.1-2.3.18).
alt_summary: U02 contribution: in TB 3.11.8 he is given to Death by his father Vājaśravasa, receives three boons and learns the Nāciketa fire by which he conquers re-death — the Brāhmaṇa root of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.
In U06's texts: the addressee of the Agni Purāṇa's Yama Gītā, which retells the Kaṭha Upaniṣad teaching.

name: Naḍādūr Ammāḷ
summary: Vātsya Varadaguru, celebrated expounder of the Śrībhāṣya at Kāñcī, whose lectures Sudarśana Sūri recorded in the Śrutaprakāśikā; disciple of Engaḷāḻvāṉ and teacher of Ātreya Rāmānuja.

name: Nāganātha
summary: One of the Marathi nine Nāths (Nāgnāth / Nāgeśnāth), held to be an incarnation of the Nārāyaṇa Āvirhotra.

name: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Last great Pāṇinian of the classical period; his philosophical works belong to lin:vyakarana (U31).
alt_summary: Pāṇinian grammarian (Laghuśabdenduśekhara, Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā) who also wrote a vṛtti on the Yoga Sūtra.
U09 contribution: the grammarian Nāgeśa of Vārāṇasī, to whom a short vṛtti on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra is ascribed (low confidence).

name: Nahuṣa
summary: Ancient king cursed to be a python; he seizes Bhīma and is freed when Yudhiṣṭhira answers his questions on who is a brāhmaṇa (3.173–178).

name: Nāka Maudgalya
summary: Holds that Vedic study and teaching alone matter, for that is austerity (TU 1.9).

name: Nakkīrar
summary: Poet of the Madurai academy in tradition; author of the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (Tirumuṟai 11). The Tiruviḷaiyāṭal story tells of his dispute with Śiva over a poem.

name: Naminanti Aṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who, refused oil by Jains for the temple lamps at Tiruvārūr, lit them with water at Śiva's word, and they burned.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who, refused oil by Jains for the temple lamps at Tiruvārūr, lit them with water at Śiva's word, and they burned.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nammāḻvār
summary: (U25 owns.) For Viśiṣṭādvaita: the 'first head of the clan' (kulapati) of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, from whom Nāthamuni received the Prabandham; his Tiruvāymoḻi is the 'Tamil Upaniṣad' (Dramiḍopaniṣad) expounded by the ācāryas, and Deśika's Pādukāsahasra identifies him with the Lord's sandals.

name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
summary: Priest of Tirunāraiyūr who, by the tradition's account, recovered the Tēvāram at Chidambaram and arranged the first eleven Tirumuṟai; author of ten works in the eleventh, including the Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti.

realization_account.text: As a boy he fed the Gaṇeśa (Poḷḷāppiḷḷaiyār) of Tirunāraiyūr, who ate and taught him; guided by that Gaṇeśa he found the hymns in a sealed chamber at Chidambaram, half eaten by termites — what remained was what the Lord wished preserved.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nampiḷḷai
summary: Nampūr Varadarājar, disciple of Nañjīyar, whose lectures on the Tiruvāymoḻi at Śrīraṅgam drew great crowds and were recorded as the Īṭu; called Lokācārya, a title passed to Piḷḷai Lokācārya.

name: Nandapaṇḍita
summary: Commentator on the Viṣṇusmṛti.

name: Nanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, author of the Rāspañcādhyāyī and a Bhramargīt.

name: Nandi (Nantīcar)
summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition Nandi (Nantīcar, Nantitēvar) is the first of the eighteen Siddhars and the channel through whom Śiva's knowledge — including medicine — reached Tirumūlar and the others (TM 67–68).
places: Kāśī — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the entry. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.
alt_summary: Śiva's chief attendant and doorkeeper at Kailāsa; in Tamil Siddhānta the first human-facing teacher of the inner lineage, and the guru of Tirumūlar.

name: Nandikeśvara
summary: Śiva's attendant Nandin, to whom tradition ascribes a verse commentary on the Māheśvara sūtras (and, separately, works on dance); historical authorship uncertain.

name: Nandikeśvara (author of the Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā)
summary: Vīraśaiva author of the Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā defending the wearing of the liṅga.
notes: Distinct from the mythic Nandikeśvara and from the authors on grammar and dance of that name.

name: Nandīśvara
summary: Prābhākara author of the Prābhākaravijaya.

name: Nañjīyar
summary: Formerly the Advaitin Vedānti Mādhava, converted by Parāśara Bhaṭṭar; renouncer and author of the Oṉpatiṉāyirappaṭi ('Nine Thousand') on the Tiruvāymoḻi; teacher of Nampiḷḷai.

name: Nantaṉār (Tirunāḷaippōvār)
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Pulaiya (outcaste) labourer who supplied leather and strings for temple drums; at Tiruppuṅkūr Śiva moved the bull Nandi aside so he could see; long saying 'I will go to Tillai tomorrow', he at last reached Chidambaram where, at Śiva's command conveyed to the priests, he passed through fire, rose as a brahmin sage and entered the sanctum, never to be seen again.

realization_account.text: A Pulaiya (outcaste) labourer who supplied leather and strings for temple drums; at Tiruppuṅkūr Śiva moved the bull Nandi aside so he could see; long saying 'I will go to Tillai tomorrow', he at last reached Chidambaram where, at Śiva's command conveyed to the priests, he passed through fire, rose as a brahmin sage and entered the sanctum, never to be seen again.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Naracinka Muṉaiyaraiya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. The chieftain who adopted the boy Cuntarar; he honoured every wearer of the ash, giving double gifts even to one whose conduct was unworthy.

realization_account.text: The chieftain who adopted the boy Cuntarar; he honoured every wearer of the ash, giving double gifts even to one whose conduct was unworthy.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nārada

realization_account.text: In a former life the son of a maidservant who served Vedāntin sages, heard Hari's glories, had a vision of the Lord and was told he would see him again only in a later body (BhP 1.5.23-1.6.38); reborn as the celestial sage who wanders singing Hari's names with his vīṇā. BhP 1.3.8 counts him the third avatāra, who 'expounded the Sātvata tantra'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The divine sage and wandering devotee: teacher of Vyāsa (urging him to write the Bhāgavata), initiator of Dhruva with the twelve-syllable mantra, teacher of Prahlāda while still in his mother's womb, pupil of the Kumāras in the Nārada Purāṇa; one of the twelve mahājanas (BhP 6.3.20).
alt_summary: Divine seer; in the Nārāyaṇīya he visits Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Badarī and the White Island, where Nārāyaṇa shows himself and teaches him (12.321–339); he asks Asita Devala about the origin of beings (12.267) and relates the origin of Death (12.248–250); he tells Vālmīki the story of Rāma (Rāmāyaṇa 1.1). 'Among divine seers I am Nārada' (BhG 10.26).
The divine seer (devarṣi) who comes to Sanatkumāra learned in all the sciences yet 'a knower of mantras, not of the self', and in sorrow; he is taught the ladder to bhūman (ChU 7).

In the Saṃhitās, Nārada Kāṇva is seer of RV 8.13 and, with Parvata, of the Soma hymns 9.104–105; the Sāmaveda phonetic manual (Nāradīya Śikṣā) is ascribed to Nārada (the Vedic contributions only are recorded here).

The divine sage; in the Nimbārka line he receives the teaching from the four Kumāras (Sanaka and brothers), who received it from Haṃsa (Viṣṇu as swan), and gives it to Nimbārka (Daśaślokī 6). Gauḍīyas hold Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura to be his incarnation.
U02 contribution: the divine sage to whom the Nāradasmṛti and the Nāradīya Śikṣā are ascribed.

U04 contribution: asks the Lord about the paramahaṃsa (Paramahaṃsa), Brahmā about crossing Kali (Kalisantaraṇa), Vāsudeva about the ūrdhvapuṇḍra (Vāsudeva) and Brahmā about Hayagrīva; teaches the sages at Naimiṣa the renouncer's life (Nāradaparivrājaka).
notes: U05's contribution; the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is covered by U25.
alt_notes: Later traditions attach the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra and other works to a Nārada; this entry records only the Upaniṣadic figure.
Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).
Contribution from U08 (Pāñcarātra role); other units record his other roles.

name: Narahari Cakravartī
summary: 18th-c. author of the Bhaktiratnākara.

name: Narahari Tīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1324–1333 in maṭha lists

scholarly.text: his inscriptions at Śrīkūrmam are dated c. 1264–1293 CE

summary: Disciple of Madhva and his successor after Padmanābha Tīrtha in the Uttarādi line. The tradition says he had served as regent of the Kaliṅga kingdom and brought from its treasury the images of Rāma and Sītā (Mūla Rāma) that Madhva had asked for; inscriptions of his at Śrīkūrmam are used by scholars to date Madhva.
notes: The tradition also credits him with fostering Yakṣagāna — low confidence, not verified.

name: Narasiṃha Tīrtha (Adamaru)
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Adamaru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Narasiṃhagupta (Cukhulaka)
summary: Abhinavagupta's father and his first teacher (in grammar), named by Abhinavagupta in the Tantrāloka's closing chapter.

name: Nārāyaṇa
summary: In the Nārāyaṇīya the supreme Lord, also present as the ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa who with Nara performs austerity at Badarī (both born in Dharma's house, 12.332.19); he shows himself to Nārada in the White Island and teaches the fourfold form, his manifestations and the ekāntin dharma (12.321–339).
alt_summary: Viṣṇu as speaker: the Person in the solar orb who teaches Yājñavalkya (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa), Ādi-Nārāyaṇa who answers Brahmā on the paramahaṃsa and the avadhūta (Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka, Turīyātīta), Mahāviṣṇu of the Tripādvibhūti, and Hṛṣīkeśa who teaches Brahmā the Yogatattva.

name: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa (Mānameyodaya)
notes: Identification with the author of the Nārāyaṇīyam is traditional; low confidence.
summary: Kerala scholar credited with the first (means-of-knowledge) part of the Mānameyodaya; traditionally identified with Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri of Melpattūr.

name: Nārāyaṇa (author of Dīpikās)
summary: Commentator who glossed many Atharvan and minor Upaniṣads (e.g. the Nīlarudra); dates uncertain.

name: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya
summary: Son of Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya and author of the Sumadhvavijaya, the principal life of Madhva, of the Maṇimañjarī and of the Yogadīpikā, a manual of worship and meditation.
notes: Authorship of all three works as named in their colophons in the raw_etexts corpus.

name: Nārāyaṇa (seer of the Puruṣa Sūkta)
summary: The seer of the Puruṣa Sūkta (RV 10.90) and of the Atharvaveda hymn on the making of man (AVŚ 10.2); Vaiṣṇava tradition identifies him with Nārāyaṇa, the Lord.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha
summary: U09 contribution: author to whom the Sāṃkhyacandrikā on the SK is ascribed; several authors share the name, and identifications are uncertain.
notes: Whether he is the same as the devotional composer Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha is uncertain.
alt_summary: Author of the Bhāṭṭabhāṣāprakāśa.

name: Nārāyaṇācārya (author of the Sadācāradīpikā)
summary: Author named in the colophon of the Mādhva conduct manual Sadācāradīpikā; date and identity not established.

name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika, author of the Vṛtti on the Mṛgendra, which explains the Āgama's doctrine of Lord, souls and bonds and defends the Siddhānta's realism; father of Rāmakaṇṭha II.
alt_summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika who wrote the Vṛtti on the Mṛgendra, defending a dualist reading of the scripture; father of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha.

name: Nārāyaṇatīrtha
summary: Author of two commentaries on the Yoga Sūtra, the Yogasiddhāntacandrikā and the Sūtrārthabodhinī; a devotee of Kṛṣṇa who interprets Yoga within Vedānta and subsumes many named yogas under the eight-limbed yoga.
notes: Identity with Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha, composer of the Kṛṣṇalīlātaraṅgiṇī, is sometimes asserted — not verified.

name: Narottama Dāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Second-generation leader from Kheturi whose Bengali songs (Prema-bhakti-candrikā, Prārthanā) shaped Gauḍīya practice; organiser of the Kheturi festival that unified the Bengal community.

name: Nāthamuni
summary: First ācārya of the Śrīvaiṣṇava lineage (after Nammāḻvār), of Vīranārāyaṇapuram (Kāṭṭumannārkōyil). The tradition says he recovered and arranged the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, set its hymns to music for temple recitation, and taught yoga; his works on logic and yoga are lost.

tradition.text: 824–924 CE in one commonly cited traditional reckoning; hagiographies give an extremely long life

realization_account.text: Hearing ten verses of the Tiruvāymoḻi ending 'these ten out of a thousand', he sought the rest at Kurukūr, recited Madhurakavi's Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu twelve thousand times in yogic absorption, and received from Nammāḻvār in vision the whole four thousand hymns and their meaning.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nēca Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A weaver who made loincloths and sacred threads for devotees.

realization_account.text: A weaver who made loincloths and sacred threads for devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Niṉṟacīr Neṭumāṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. The Pāṇṭiya king, a patron of the Jains, whose burning fever Campantar cured with sacred ash; his hunched back was straightened and he turned Śaiva; he won the battle of Nelvēli.

realization_account.text: The Pāṇṭiya king, a patron of the Jains, whose burning fever Campantar cured with sacred ash; his hunched back was straightened and he turned Śaiva; he won the battle of Nelvēli.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nema Bhārgava
summary: Seer of RV 8.100.1–3, 6–12, in which 'Nema says Indra does not exist — who has seen him? whom shall we praise?', whereupon Indra answers 'here I am, singer, see me' (8.100.3–4).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Nidāgha
summary: Disciple of Ṛbhu in the Varāha, Tejobindu, Mahā and Annapūrṇā Upaniṣads; asks about the seven stages (bhūmikā) and about yoga; named among the paramahaṃsas and among rudrākṣa-wearing sages.
alt_summary: Son of Pulastya and disciple of Ṛbhu, who lived at Vīranagara on the Devikā; Ṛbhu returns twice in disguise to test and teach him (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15-16); the recipient of the Ṛbhu Gītā.
Pulastya's son and Ṛbhu's disciple, visited by his teacher twice in disguise and brought to see that there is no difference between 'king' and 'elephant', 'I' and 'you' (VP 2.15-16).

name: Nijaguṇa Śivayōgi
summary: Vīraśaiva yogin and author of the Kannada encyclopaedia Vivekacintāmaṇi and of the songs of the Kaivalya Paddhati.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Bhagavantabhāskara (the Mayūkhas).

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara
summary: Seventeenth-century Mahārāṣṭrian scholar in Vārāṇasī, famous for his Mahābhārata commentary; in U06 the commentator on the Gaṇeśa Gītā.
alt_summary: Maharashtrian scholar at Vārāṇasī, author of the Bhāratabhāvadīpa, the commentary on the whole Mahābhārata that fixed the vulgate text.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya
summary: Vīraśaiva author of the Kriyāsāra, which presents Śrīkaṇṭha's commentary as Vīraśaiva doctrine.
alt_summary: Author of the Sanskrit Vīraśaiva Kriyāsāra.

name: Nīlāmbike
summary: Basava's wife and a vacanakāra in whose vacanas Basava appears as her spiritual guide.

name: Nimbārka (Nimbāditya, Niyamānanda)
summary: Founder of the Dvaitādvaita school; author of the Vedāntapārijātasaurabha and the Daśaślokī; taught natural difference-and-non-difference, Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā as Brahman, and the five means culminating in surrender.

realization_account.text: An incarnation of the Sudarśana discus, born to Aruṇa and Jayantī in the Telugu country; named Nimbārka ('sun on the nimba tree') because he held the sun on a neem tree so that a visiting ascetic could eat before sunset; taught by Nārada on Govardhana.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

tradition.text: a former age (tradition gives very early dates)

scholarly.text: variously 7th–13th c. CE; many place him c. 12th–13th c.

name: Niṣkriyānandanātha
summary: Krama master named in Anantaśaktipāda's commentary on the Vātūlanāthasūtra as having received instruction from the siddhas of Gandhamādana; the Chummāsaṅketaprakāśa is ascribed to him.

name: Nityānanda (Nitāi, Avadhūta)
summary: Wandering avadhūta from Ekacakrā who joined Caitanya at Navadvīpa and led the mission in Bengal; held to be Balarāma; his wives Vasudhā and Jāhnavā and son Vīrabhadra continued his line (Khaḍadaha).

realization_account.text: Balarāma (Kṛṣṇa's brother) appearing as Caitanya's first expansion; famed for delivering the sinners Jagāi and Mādhāi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nityanātha
summary: Siddha named in the Haṭhapradīpikā's list (1.7); a Nityanātha is credited with alchemical and magical works (Rasaratnākara, Kāmaratna) and, in some manuscripts, with the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati.
notes: Whether these are one person is uncertain.

name: Nivṛttināth
summary: Elder brother and guru of Jñāneśvar, initiated in the Nāth line by Gahinīnāth; Jñāneśvar calls himself 'Nivṛtti's servant' (nivṛttidāsu) throughout the Jñāneśvarī. Abhaṅgas are ascribed to him.

tradition.text: 1273–1297 (tradition)

notes: Works field notes only that the Jñāneśvarī is dedicated to him; he is not its author.

name: Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī (author of the Subodhinī)
summary: Commentator on the Vedāntasāra (Subodhinī). Distinct from Narasiṃha Sarasvatī of the Datta tradition.

name: Nṛsiṃhāśrama
summary: 16th-c. Advaitin of the Vivaraṇa line, author of the Vedāntatattvaviveka, the Advaitadīpikā and the Bhedadhikkāra.

name: Nuliya Candayya
summary: The rope-maker śaraṇa remembered for insisting that kāyaka is not to be interrupted even for worship.

name: Padmanābha Tīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1317–1324 in maṭha lists

summary: Disciple of Madhva and first pontiff after him in the line that became the Uttarādi Maṭha; author of the Sattarkadīpāvalī (on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya) and Nyāyaratnāvalī (on the Anuvyākhyāna). In the tradition's account he had been a learned opponent (named Śobhana Bhaṭṭa) before becoming Madhva's disciple.
notes: Former name, pontificate dates and brindāvana location recalled at low confidence.

name: Padmapāda
summary: Senior disciple of Śaṅkara, author of the Pañcapādikā, root of the Vivaraṇa school; in the tradition's account named 'lotus-foot' because lotuses sprang up under his feet when he crossed the Gaṅgā at his guru's call, and first head of the Govardhana maṭha at Purī.

name: Paila
summary: Vyāsa's pupil who received the Ṛgveda (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.21; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4) and divided it among his own pupils, from whom the Ṛgveda śākhās descend.

name: Paiṅgala
summary: Disciple who serves Yājñavalkya for twelve years and then asks about kaivalya (Paiṅgala Upaniṣad).

name: Paiṅgya
summary: Taught 'breath is brahman' with the ordering of the senses (KauU 2.2).

name: Paippalādi
summary: Questioner of Jābāli in the Jābāli Upaniṣad (a descendant or pupil of Pippalāda by name).

name: Pakṣadhara Miśra
summary: Mithilā Naiyāyika, also called Jayadeva, author of the Āloka commentary on the Tattvacintāmaṇi.
notes: Tradition makes him the Mithilā master whom Raghunātha Śiromaṇi challenged (low confidence).

name: Pālkuriki Sōmanātha
summary: Telugu and Kannada Vīraśaiva poet-scholar, author of the Basava Purāṇamu, the Paṇḍitārādhya Caritra and the Vṛṣādhipa Śatakamu.

name: Pālyakīrti (Śākaṭāyana)
summary: Yāpanīya Jain grammarian who wrote under the name Śākaṭāyana.

name: Pāmbāṭṭi (Pāmpāṭṭic cittar)
summary: The 'snake-charmer Siddhar', whose songs with the refrain 'dance, O snake!' teach the inner ascent and scorn caste, learning and ritual. The tradition says he was a snake-catcher seeking a jewelled serpent in the hills when a Siddhar (usually Caṭṭaimuṉi) showed him that the true serpent lies coiled within.
places: Caṅkaraṉkōyil — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The meeting with Caṭṭaimuṉi is recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Pañcādhikaraṇa
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher known from the Yuktidīpikā: the organs are elemental (bhautika); the instrument is by nature empty, like a deserted village or dry river bed, its knowledges coming from pradhāna; all transformation of the organs is 'from another'; a permanent conveying (ātivāhika) subtle body enters the embryo; knowledge is natural (at the same time as the principles, innate, or flowing) or acquired. Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Pañcaśikha
summary: Pupil of Āsuri by whom 'the doctrine was expanded' (SK 70). In the Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma he teaches King Janaka (Janadeva) of Mithilā. Sayings ascribed to him are quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 1.4, 1.25, 1.36, 2.13, as identified by Vācaspati Miśra) and in the Tattvakaumudī on SK 2; the Sāṃkhya Sūtra cites his views by name (5.32, 6.68).
notes: Mahābhārata chapter (Śāntiparvan, c. 12.211–212 in the critical edition) recalled, not checked.
alt_summary: In the Mokṣadharma, Pañcaśikha 'Kāpileya' (so called because the brāhmaṇī Kapilā nursed him), 'Āsuri's first disciple', comes to Mithilā and so impresses king Janadeva Janaka that he leaves a hundred teachers to follow him (12.211.6–18); he teaches the Sāṃkhya discrimination (12.211–212); Sulabhā refers to Janaka's having learned from him (12.308).
alt_notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Paṇḍitārādhya (of the five ācāryas)
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Śrīśaila pīṭha.

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Emergence from the Mallikārjuna liṅga at Śrīśaila and seat name Sūrya-siṃhāsana: low confidence. Distinct entry from the historical Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya (tch:mallikarjuna-panditaradhya); some accounts connect them.

name: Pāṇini
summary: Author of the Aṣṭādhyāyī, the grammar that fixed classical Sanskrit and described the Vedic language; Patañjali calls him 'Dākṣīputra', son of Dākṣī. He names ten predecessors (Āpiśali, Kāśyapa, Gārgya, Gālava, Cākravarmaṇa, Bhāradvāja, Śākaṭāyana, Śākalya, Senaka, Sphoṭāyana).

tradition.text: a sage of old who received the phoneme list from Śiva

realization_account.text: After austerities he received the fourteen phoneme-sūtras from Maheśvara (Śiva), who sounded them on his drum; from them he proclaimed the whole of grammar (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 56–57; Nandikeśvara-kāśikā). A later story (Kathāsaritsāgara) makes him a dull pupil of Varṣa who won Śiva's grace by tapas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Pāragārgya
summary: Number 7 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Paramānanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet of Kṛṣṇa's childhood and the gopīs' longing (Paramānandsāgar).

name: Paramārtha
summary: Indian Buddhist monk-translator who reached China in 546. Besides Yogācāra works he translated the Sāṃkhya Kārikā with a commentary (Jin qishi lun) and wrote a Life of Vasubandhu that tells of the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa's debate with Buddhamitra.

name: Parañcōti Muṉivar (guru of Meykaṇṭār)
summary: The sage from Kailāsa who, in the tradition's account, taught the child Meykaṇṭār; last of the 'inner' lineage (akaccantāṉam) of Nandi, Sanatkumāra and Satyajñānadarśin.
notes: Distinct from Parañcōti Muṉivar, author of the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam (tch:parancoti-tiruvilaiyatal).

name: Parañcōti Muṉivar (author of the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam)
summary: Author of the Tamil Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam on Śiva's sixty-four sports at Madurai.

name: Parāśara
summary: Grandson of Vasiṣṭha and father of Vyāsa; the speaker of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa to Maitreya, which he received from Vasiṣṭha and Pulastya after renouncing his rite to burn the rākṣasas (VP 1.1.12-26).
alt_summary: Parāśara Śāktya, seer of RV 1.65–73 (hymns to Agni). The tradition makes him the son of Śakti and grandson of Vasiṣṭha, father of Vyāsa, and the narrator of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (the Vedic contribution is recorded here).
Seer, father of Vyāsa; he instructs king Janaka in the Parāśara Gītā (12.279–287).
U02 contribution: the sage, father of Vyāsa, to whom the Parāśarasmṛti — the code for the Kali age — is ascribed.
In U06's texts: the sage who instructs King Janaka in the Parāśara Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.279-287).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).
alt_notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Parāśara Bhaṭṭar
summary: Son of Kūreśa, named by Rāmānuja in fulfilment of Yāmuna's wish; successor at Śrīraṅgam after Embār; author of the Śrīraṅgarājastava, Śrīguṇaratnakośa, Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa and Aṣṭaślokī; the tradition says he won over the Advaitin Mādhava (Nañjīyar).
alt_summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher, son of Kūrattāḻvāṉ, author of the Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa on the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma.

name: Pāraskara
summary: Author by tradition of the White Yajurveda Gṛhyasūtra.

name: Paraśurāma Devācārya
summary: Disciple of Harivyāsadeva associated with the Nimbārka seat at Salemabad (Rajasthan).

name: Parīkṣit
summary: Grandson of Arjuna, protected in the womb by Kṛṣṇa; cursed to die in seven days, he renounced his kingdom and sat in prāyopaveśa on the Gaṅgā (BhP 1.19), where he heard the Bhāgavata from Śuka; the model hearer (śravaṇa) of the Purāṇa. He also subdued Kali and assigned him five places (BhP 1.17).

name: Parimēlaḻakar
summary: Author of the most celebrated commentary on the Tirukkuṟaḷ (and on the Paripāṭal); a Vaiṣṇava brahmin of Kāñcīpuram by tradition.
notes: Vaiṣṇava affiliation is traditional; the lineage ids are approximate.

name: Paritoṣa Miśra
summary: Author of the Ajitā commentary on the Tantravārttika.

name: Pārthasārathi Miśra
summary: Leading Bhāṭṭa author: the Śāstradīpikā (independent commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra), Nyāyaratnākara (on the Ślokavārttika), Nyāyaratnamālā and Tantraratna. He defined a means of knowledge as a cognition apprehending what was not apprehended, free from defects of cause and from contradicting cognition, and held release to be the end of the threefold bond, without bliss.

name: Pārvatī
summary: Śiva's consort, the questioner in the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (her doubt why the supreme Rāma grieved for Sītā, 1.1.13-15) and in the Guru Gītā; in Śākta texts identified with the Goddess who herself teaches (Devī Gītā, Bhagavatī Gītā).

name: Patañcala Kāpya
summary: Man of Madra in whose house Uddālaka studied the sacrifice; through a gandharva possessing his wife they learned of the thread and the inner controller (BAU 3.7.1).

name: Patañjali
alt_names: Śeṣa / Ananta (as whose incarnation he is regarded)

tradition.text: not dated by the tradition (incarnation of Śeṣa); identified with the grammarian

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE if author of the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra (Maas); the grammarian Patañjali is dated c. 2nd c. BCE

realization_account.text: Regarded as an incarnation of Śeṣa (Ananta), the serpent of Viṣṇu, who took a human form out of compassion to teach; the bhāṣya's maṅgala verse praises the 'lord of serpents, giver of yoga'. Later tradition credits him with removing the impurities of speech (grammar), mind (yoga) and body (medicine) — Bhoja's introductory verses praise Bhoja for doing the same 'like the lord of serpents'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Author (re-teacher) of the Yoga Sūtra. The tradition regards him as Śeṣa incarnate and as the same Patañjali who wrote the grammatical Mahābhāṣya; modern scholarship mostly distinguishes the two and debates whether he also wrote the bhāṣya (the 'Pātañjala Yogaśāstra' hypothesis).
alt_summary: The Tamil tradition counts Patañjali among the eighteen Siddhars and, with Vyāghrapāda, among Nandi's disciples who worshipped at the hall (maṉṟu) of Chidambaram (TM 67); it identifies him with the author of the Yoga Sūtras.
places: Rāmēśvaram — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution. The identification of the Chidambaram sage, the grammarian and the Yoga Sūtra author is the tradition's; scholars keep them apart. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Patañjali (the grammarian)
summary: Author of the Vyākaraṇa-Mahābhāṣya. The tradition identifies him with Patañjali of the Yoga Sūtra (tch:patanjali); most scholars distinguish the two. Kept as a separate id so that both accounts stay visible.

tradition.text: an incarnation of the serpent Śeṣa, identical with the author of the Yoga Sūtra

scholarly.text: mid-2nd c. BCE (the Mahābhāṣya refers to sacrificing for Puṣyamitra)

realization_account.text: Tradition regards him as Śeṣa (Ananta) incarnate and as the one who purified speech by grammar, the mind by yoga and the body by medicine (a widely quoted invocatory verse).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Patañjali (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: A Sāṃkhya teacher cited by the Yuktidīpikā: mahat arises directly from pradhāna; all transformation of the organs is 'from itself'; subtle bodies arise and cease repeatedly (one leads the organs to the womb, another arises at death). Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Whether he is the author of the Yoga Sūtra (tch:patanjali) is disputed.

name: Paṭṭiṉattār (Tiruveṇkāṭar)
summary: Renouncer-poet: a rich merchant of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam who renounced after his adopted son left him an eyeless needle; his songs on impermanence, the body, women and renunciation are among the most loved in Tamil. Guru of Pattirakiriyār; his samādhi is at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr (Chennai). The tradition treats him as one person with Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of the eleventh Tirumuṟai; scholars usually distinguish two or more poets.

tradition.text: Cōḻa period

scholarly.text: the Siddhar songs c. 14th–17th c.; Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār c. 10th c.

realization_account.text: Childless, Tiruveṇkāṭar received a boy (Śiva's gift, Marutavāṇaṉ) who went trading and returned with cakes of dung; the angry father broke them and found gems. The boy vanished, leaving a box with an eyeless needle and a palm-leaf: 'even an eyeless needle will not come with you on the final road'. He renounced at once; survived his sister's poisoned cake ('one's own deed burns oneself; the baked cake burns the house'); returned to cremate his mother, singing ten songs; at Ujjain was condemned to the stake, which burst into flame, and the king Bhadragiri became his disciple; at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr, playing with boys who covered him with a basket, he vanished and a liṅga was found in his place.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The story is recalled at moderate confidence from the popular hagiography; details vary between tellings.

name: Paurika
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher who held, according to the Yuktidīpikā (on SK 56), that each puruṣa has its own pradhāna producing its body and the rest; when the pradhāna of the great-bodied one (māhātmyaśarīra) operates, the others operate, and when it ceases, they cease. The Yuktidīpikā rejects this for want of proof. Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Pavitra Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 9.83: the filter of the lord of sacred speech is spread out; the raw one whose body is unheated does not attain it.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Periya Nambi
summary: Disciple of Yāmuna who gave Rāmānuja the five sacraments (pañcasaṃskāra) at Madhurāntakam; the tradition says he was blinded and died under the Cōḻa persecution.

name: Periya Tirumalai Nambi
summary: Disciple of Yāmuna and maternal uncle of Rāmānuja, who taught him the Rāmāyaṇa at Tirupati and brought Govinda (Embār) back to Vaiṣṇavism.

name: Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai
summary: Disciple of Nampiḷḷai, called the 'emperor of commentators' (vyākhyāna-cakravarti), who wrote Maṇipravāḷa commentaries on nearly the whole Divya Prabandham, including the Irupattunālāyirappaṭi on the Tiruvāymoḻi.

name: Perumiḻalaikkuṟumpa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain devoted to Cuntarar; knowing by yoga that Cuntarar would leave for Kailāsa, he left his body through the crown of the head a day before, to reach Kailāsa first.

realization_account.text: A chieftain devoted to Cuntarar; knowing by yoga that Cuntarar would leave for Kailāsa, he left his body through the crown of the head a day before, to reach Kailāsa first.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Piḷḷai Lokācārya
summary: Eldest son of Vaṭakku Tiruvīti Piḷḷai, named after Nampiḷḷai (Lokācārya); a lifelong celibate who wrote the eighteen rahasya works in Maṇipravāḷa, above all the Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam, Mumukṣuppaṭi, Tattvatrayam and Arthapañcakam; the Teṅkalai regard him as their doctrinal source.

tradition.text: 1205–1311 CE in commonly given Teṅkalai dates; the tradition places his death at Jyotiṣkuḍi while escorting Raṅganātha's processional image away from the sack of Śrīraṅgam (an event usually dated 1323 — not reconciled here)

realization_account.text: The Teṅkalai tradition holds that Raṅganātha himself, in the form of a teacher, instructed him, and that he taught the secret doctrine openly out of compassion.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Piḷḷai Lōkam Jīyar
summary: Teṅkalai author of the Yatīndrapravaṇa Prabhāvam, the life of Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, and of commentaries on the rahasya works.

name: Piṅgalā
summary: A courtesan of Videha whose sudden disenchantment while waiting for clients makes her one of the avadhūta's teachers (Bhāgavata 11.8.22-44) and the singer of the Piṅgalā Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.168.46-52): 'hope is the greatest misery, hopelessness the greatest happiness'.

realization_account.text: Waiting through the night for a rich lover, she felt deep disgust, turned to the Self as her true beloved and slept happily, free of expectation.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: A courtesan who, waiting in vain for a lover, gave up hope and slept happily; her saying 'freedom from hope is the highest happiness' is quoted in the Mokṣadharma (12.168.52).
Author of the Chandaḥśāstra, the root text of prosody. The kinship with Pāṇini is a late report (low confidence).

tradition.text: a sage sometimes called a nāga; a late tradition makes him Pāṇini's younger brother

name: Piṅgala (Pāśupata tīrthakara)
summary: Number 12 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Piṉpaḻagiya Perumāḷ Jīyar
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher to whom the Ārāyirappaṭi Guruparamparāprabhāvam, the chief hagiography of the Āḻvārs and ācāryas, is attributed.

name: Pippalāda
summary: Sage of the Praśna Upaniṣad who answers the six questions of six seekers after making them live a year with austerity, celibacy and faith (PrU 1.2).
notes: Tradition connects him with the Paippalāda śākhā of the Atharvaveda (moderate).
alt_summary: Eponym of the Paippalāda Atharvaveda; the teacher of the Praśna Upaniṣad (U03 contributes that role).
U04 contribution: answers Śaunaka in the Brahma and Parabrahma Upaniṣads (prāṇa as self; inner topknot and thread); as Paippalāda asks the Lord in the Pañcabrahma and Brahmā in the Śarabha.

name: Poṉṉaḍikkāl Jīyar
summary: Foremost disciple of Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, first head of the Vānamāmalai (Nāṅguneri) maṭha.

name: Prabhākara Miśra

tradition.text: a pupil of Kumārila who earned the title 'Guru' when he construed a passage his teacher could not (Bhāṭṭa story)

scholarly.text: c. 7th c. CE; relation to Kumārila uncertain

notes: 'teachers' records the tradition's claim only; the story of the title is from memory (low). Śālikanātha as a direct pupil is the tradition's view.
summary: Founder of the Prābhākara school ('Guru'): author of the Bṛhatī and the lost Laghvī on Śabara. Taught five means of knowledge, self-luminous cognition, error as non-apprehension and the kārya-centred meaning of Vedic sentences.

name: Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava
summary: One of the five great householders and great Vedic scholars who asked 'what is our self, what is brahman?' and, with Uddālaka Āruṇi, went to Aśvapati Kaikeya; each had venerated only one part of the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11-17).

name: Pradyumnabhaṭṭa
summary: Kallaṭa's maternal cousin (mātuleya), to whom he transmitted the secret teaching of the Śiva Sūtra (Bhāskara, Vārttika 1.6).

name: Pragātha Ghaura Kāṇva
summary: Seer of RV 8.1.1–2 and 8.48, 'we have drunk the soma, we have become immortal'.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Prahlāda

realization_account.text: Son of the demon-king Hiraṇyakaśipu, devoted to Viṣṇu from the womb; unharmed by his father's attempts to kill him; saved by Narasiṃha; refuses boons and liberation for himself alone (BhP 7.4-10; VP 1.16-20).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The child-devotee who taught his demon schoolfellows the nine forms of devotion (BhP 7.5.23-24) and that devotion should be practised from childhood (7.6.1); a mahājana (6.3.20) and king of the daityas in Sutala.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: the asura king who realizes the Self through his own inquiry and Viṣṇu's grace and remains in long samādhi until awakened by Viṣṇu to rule (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha 5.30-43); he questions the python-vow sage (Mahābhārata 12.172).

Daitya king; in the Mokṣadharma he explains to Indra that all states arise and cease by their own nature (svabhāva), so pride and grief are baseless (12.215), and questions a sage living like a python (12.172).

name: Prajāpati (as teacher)
summary: Lord of creatures, teacher of gods, humans and asuras: teaches 'da' (BAU 5.2); teaches Indra and Virocana the self free from evil over 101 years (ChU 8.7-12); link in teacher-lines (ChU 3.11.4, 8.15.1); in MaiU 2 he teaches the Vālakhilyas.
alt_summary: U04 contribution: teaches Āruṇi renunciation (Āruṇi), the gods on Sītā (Sītā) and renunciation (Kaṭharudra), and sees the Narasiṃha mantra-king (Nṛsiṃhatāpanī).

name: Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin
summary: The seer to whom the Anukramaṇī ascribes the creation hymn (RV 10.129).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Prajñārjuna
summary: Son and disciple of Pradyumnabhaṭṭa in Bhāskara's lineage (Vārttika 1.6-7).

name: Prakāśānanda
notes: Gauḍīya hagiography (Caitanya Caritāmṛta) tells of a Prakāśānanda Sarasvatī of Vārāṇasī won over by Caitanya; identity with this author is uncertain.
summary: Author of the Vedāntasiddhāntamuktāvalī, the chief exponent of dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi-vāda and eka-jīva-vāda.

name: Prakāśānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Leader of the Advaita renouncers at Vārāṇasī whom, the Caitanya Caritāmṛta says, Caitanya won over to devotion (CC 1.7; 2.25).
notes: Known for this episode only from Gauḍīya sources; identification with an Advaita author of the same name is disputed.

name: Prakāśātman
summary: Author of the Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa, founder of the Vivaraṇa school.

name: Praśastapāda
summary: Author of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, which gave Vaiśeṣika its classical form: six categories, twenty-four qualities, creation and dissolution by Maheśvara's will, and a systematic theory of cognition and dharma.

name: Praskaṇva Kāṇva
summary: Seer of RV 1.44–50, ending with the Sūrya hymn 1.50 ('from the darkness we have come up … to the highest light').
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Pratardana Daivodāsi
summary: Son of Divodāsa, who reached Indra's abode by fighting and valour and asked Indra for the boon most beneficial to humans; taught that Indra is breath, the intelligent self (KauU 3.1-2); the 'inner agnihotra of Pratardana' is named after him (KauU 2.5).

name: Prativādi Bhayaṅkaram Aṇṇaṉ
summary: Disciple of Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, one of his eight chief disciples, to whom the Veṅkaṭeśa Suprabhātam is attributed.

name: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali
summary: King of the Pañcālas; asks Śvetaketu the five questions and teaches Gautama Āruṇi the doctrine of the five fires and the two paths, saying this knowledge had never before dwelt with brahmins (BAU 6.2; ChU 5.3-10); in ChU 1.8-9 he teaches that space (ākāśa) is the final support of the sāman.

name: Pūcalā Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A poor brahmin who built a temple in his mind stone by stone and fixed a day for its consecration; the Pallava king, who had fixed the same day for his great stone temple at Kāñcī, was told by Śiva in a dream that he would first attend Pūcalār's consecration, and went to see that temple.

realization_account.text: A poor brahmin who built a temple in his mind stone by stone and fixed a day for its consecration; the Pallava king, who had fixed the same day for his great stone temple at Kāñcī, was told by Śiva in a dream that he would first attend Pūcalār's consecration, and went to see that temple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Pūjyapāda Devanandin
summary: Digambara teacher; U02 adds only his grammar, the Jainendra-vyākaraṇa.

name: Pukaḻccōḻa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Cōḻa king whose elephant was cut down by Eṟipattar; later, finding among the heads of slain enemies one with matted hair — a devotee's — he entered the fire in remorse.

realization_account.text: A Cōḻa king whose elephant was cut down by Eṟipattar; later, finding among the heads of slain enemies one with matted hair — a devotee's — he entered the fire in remorse.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Pukaḻttuṇai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A temple priest who kept up worship through a famine; fainting, he let the water-pot fall on the liṅga; Śiva left a gold coin for him on the pedestal each day until the famine ended.

realization_account.text: A temple priest who kept up worship through a famine; fainting, he let the water-pot fall on the liṅga; Śiva left a gold coin for him on the pedestal each day until the famine ended.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Pulastiyar
summary: Sage named in Siddha lore as a disciple of Agastya and an authority on medicine.
notes: Recalled at low confidence.

name: Pulippāṇi
summary: Disciple of Bogar who, the tradition says, rode a tiger (puli) and carried water for his guru; associated with Palani, where a line of Pulippāṇi priests traced itself to him; medical works bear his name.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Palani priestly line is recalled at low confidence.

name: Purūravas (Aila)
summary: King, son of Iḍā, infatuated with the apsaras Urvaśī; his song of disenchantment is the Aila Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.26).

name: Puruṣottama (Puruṣottamajī, of the Vallabha line)
summary: The most prolific later Śuddhādvaita scholar: Bhāṣyaprakāśa on the Aṇubhāṣya, Suvarṇasūtra on the Vidvanmaṇḍana, Prasthānaratnākara and many commentaries.

name: Puruṣottamācārya (of the Nimbārka school)
summary: Nimbārka scholar, author of the Vedāntaratnamañjūṣā on the Daśaślokī and the Śrutyantasuradruma on the Kṛṣṇastavarāja.

name: Puṣpaka
summary: Number 13 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Rāghavabhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Padārthādarśa (1493/94), a learned commentary on the Śāradātilaka.

name: Rāghavānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Pātañjalarahasya, a gloss on Vācaspati's Tattvavaiśāradī.

name: Rāghavāṅka
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet, nephew and disciple of Harihara, author of the Hariścandra Kāvya, the Siddharāma Cāritra and the Sōmanātha Cāritra.

name: Rāghavendra Tīrtha

tradition.text: entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that Rāghavendra was Prahlāda reborn (through Bāhlīka and Vyāsatīrtha), that he entered his brindāvana alive in 1671, and that he remains present there, answering devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Born Veṅkaṭanātha at Bhuvanagiri, disciple of Sudhīndra Tīrtha, and author of the Parimala on the Nyāyasudhā (hence 'Parimalācārya'), the Bhāvadīpa on the Tattvaprakāśikā, the Tantradīpikā, the Nyāyamuktāvalī, the Candrikāprakāśa, the Bhāṭṭasaṅgraha on Mīmāṃsā, Upaniṣad khaṇḍārthas and the Gītāvivṛti. His brindāvana at Mantrālaya is the tradition's greatest pilgrimage centre.
notes: The claim that he will remain in the brindāvana for 700 years is recalled at low confidence.

name: Raghudeva Nyāyālaṅkāra
summary: Navya-Naiyāyika to whom a set of vāda treatises (Muktivāda, Īśvaravāda, Prāgabhāvavāda, Ākāṅkṣāvāda, Sāmagrīvāda and others) is attributed in their modern edition.

name: Raghunandana
summary: Bengali author of the Smṛtitattva.

name: Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of Tapana Miśra of Vārāṇasī; lived in Vṛndāvana as a sweet-voiced reciter of the Bhāgavata; wrote no treatise (tradition).

name: Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of a wealthy landholder of Saptagrāma who renounced home, served Caitanya at Purī under Svarūpa Dāmodara and later lived at Rādhākuṇḍa; poet of the Stavāvalī (Manaḥśikṣā, Vilāpakusumāñjali) and exemplar of renunciation and mañjarī-bhāva.

name: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi
summary: Founder of the Navadvīpa school of Navya-Nyāya; his Dīdhiti on the Tattvacintāmaṇi became the base of later study, and his Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa re-examined the list of categories.
notes: The tradition tells of his defeating Pakṣadhara in debate in Mithilā (low confidence).

name: Raghūttama Tīrtha
summary: Uttarādi Maṭha pontiff called Bhāvabodhācārya after his Bhāvabodha commentaries (e.g. on Madhva's Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya); his brindāvana is at Tirukoilur.

name: Rahūgaṇa
summary: The king who forced Jaḍa Bharata to carry his palanquin and received from him instruction on the self beyond the body (BhP 5.10-13; the VP 2.13-16 version names the king of Sauvīra).

name: Raikva 'with the cart' (sayugvan)
summary: A sage found scratching his sores under a cart, whom King Jānaśruti seeks out; he rebuffs the king's gifts, calling him śūdra, and teaches the saṃvarga ('gatherer') doctrine: wind among the deities and breath among the vital powers absorb all others (ChU 4.1-3).
alt_summary: U04 contribution: asks the questions answered in the Subāla Upaniṣad (in some sections).

name: Raivataka
summary: Named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).

name: Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma
summary: Later Kashmiri commentator on the Parātrīśikā.

name: Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha (author of the Spandavivṛti)
summary: Kashmiri commentator, a disciple of Utpaladeva, author of the Spandavivṛti (ascribing the kārikās to Kallaṭa) and of the Sarvatobhadra commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā.
notes: Distinct from tch:ramakantha (Rāmakaṇṭha II of the Śaiva Siddhānta).

name: Rājeśvar Rām
summary: 20th-century head (pīṭhādhīśvar) of Kīnārām Sthal, Krīm Kuṇḍ, Varanasi.

name: Rāma (Dāśarathi)

tradition.text: Tretā yuga

summary: Prince of Ayodhyā, hero of the Rāmāyaṇa, called 'dharma embodied' (3.37.13); he goes into exile to keep his father's word, teaches Bharata on impermanence (2.105) and kingship (2.100), answers Jābāli that truth is the root of all (2.109), and vows protection to whoever seeks refuge (6.18.33); the Nārāyaṇīya names him among Nārāyaṇa's manifestations (12.326.78).
alt_summary: In U06's texts: the student of Vasiṣṭha in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (whose first book records his dispassion at sixteen); the teacher of Hanumān (Rāma-hṛdaya), Lakṣmaṇa (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa 3.4 and the Rāma Gītā), Śabarī (the nine means of devotion) and Vibhīṣaṇa (Rāmcaritmānas); in the Śiva Gītā the recipient of Śiva's teaching. The Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa presents him as the supreme Brahman.

Rāma, regarded as the supreme Brahman, teaches Hanumān the canon of 108 Upaniṣads and the path to liberation in the Muktikā; the Rāma-Upaniṣads and Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's maṅgala verses make him the goal of every Upaniṣad.

realization_account.text: In the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Rāma, after Vasiṣṭha's teaching, rests in the supreme state (Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, opening chapters, e.g. MU 6.5 'rāghava-viśrānti'); the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa instead treats him as the Lord who never lost knowledge.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Rāma Tīrtha (Kaniyooru)
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Kaniyooru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Rāmatēvar (Irāmatēvar)
summary: Siddhar whose Pūjāviti teaches the worship of the goddess Maṉōṉmaṇi/Vālai at the root; the tradition says he went to Mecca, lived there as 'Yākōpu' and returned, and medical works under that name are ascribed to him.
places: Aḻakar malai (Alagar Kovil) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Mecca/Yākōpu account is the tradition's, recalled at moderate confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (Rāmakaṇṭha II)
summary: The foremost Kashmirian exegete of the Siddhānta: commentaries on the Mataṅgapārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Sārdhatriśatikālottara, and Sadyojyoti's Nareśvaraparīkṣā, Mokṣakārikā and Paramokṣanirāsakārikā. He argued that mala is a substance removable only by Śiva's power in initiation, that the liberated soul becomes equal to Śiva, and answered the non-dualist Śaivas.
notes: Correction to the unit brief: 'Rāmakaṇṭha II' and 'Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha' are the same person (the Saiddhāntika son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha). He is distinct from Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha, author of the Spandakārikāvivṛti and a Gītā commentary (non-dualist milieu). Some scholars suggest the Śrīkaṇṭha of the Ratnatraya was his teacher (low confidence).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08.
alt_summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika exegete, son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, who commented on the Kiraṇa, the Mataṅgapārameśvara and the Sārdhatriśatikālottara, and on works of Sadyojyoti, maintaining that liberation is the soul's becoming equal to Śiva, not identity with him.

name: Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmiri author credited with the Sarvatobhadra commentary on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā.
notes: Not identified here with the Saiddhāntika Rāmakaṇṭha (tch:ramakantha).

name: Rāmakṛṣṇa Adhvarin
summary: Son of Dharmarāja, author of the Śikhāmaṇi on the Vedāntaparibhāṣā.

name: Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Yuktisnehaprapūraṇī on the tarkapāda of the Śāstradīpikā.

name: Ramana Maharshi
summary: In U06's context (recent reception): recommended the Ṛbhu Gītā, which was read aloud in his presence, and quoted the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā.

name: Rāmānanda Rāya
summary: Governor at Vidyānagara (Godāvarī) and author of the drama Jagannāthavallabha, whose dialogue with Caitanya on the goal and means (CC 2.8) rises from varṇāśrama to Rādhā's love.

name: Rāmānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Yogamaṇiprabhā, a vṛtti that follows the bhāṣya; its colophon names him a paramahaṃsa pupil of Govindānanda.

name: Rāmānuja
summary: The principal systematizer of Viśiṣṭādvaita: born at Śrīperumbūdūr, he renounced at Kāñcī, led the Śrīraṅgam temple and community, spent years at Melkote during the Cōḻa persecution, and wrote nine works — the Śrībhāṣya, Vedārthasaṅgraha, Vedāntasāra, Vedāntadīpa, Gītābhāṣya, the three Gadyas and the Nityagrantha.

scholarly.text: 11th–12th c. CE; some scholars doubt the 120-year span and propose c. 1077–1157

realization_account.text: Varadarāja answered his doubts through Tirukkacci Nambi; Tirukkōṭṭiyūr Nambi gave him the secret mantra after eighteen visits, and he proclaimed its meaning to all from the temple tower, accepting hell for himself if others could be saved; he surrendered to Śrī and Raṅganātha on Paṅguni Uttiram, and the Lord's reply is recorded in the Śaraṇāgati Gadya. The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition regards him as an incarnation of Ādiśeṣa (and Lakṣmaṇa).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Author of a Gītā commentary reading it as teaching bhakti-yoga to Nārāyaṇa, supported by karma- and jñāna-yoga.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Rāmānujācārya (Prābhākara author)
summary: Late Prābhākara author of the Tantrarahasya; distinct from the Vedāntin Rāmānuja.

name: Rāmarudra Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Rāmarudrī, a gloss on the Muktāvalī continuing the Dinakarī.

name: Rāmatīrtha
summary: Commentator on the Vedāntasāra (Vidvanmanorañjanī) and on the Upadeśasāhasrī. Distinct from the recent Swami Rama Tirtha.

name: Raṅgarāmānuja Muni
summary: Viśiṣṭādvaita commentator on the principal Upaniṣads (the Prakāśikās) and on the Śrībhāṣya.

name: Rāśīkara
summary: The seventeenth of the eighteen Pāśupata tīrthakaras in the Jain lists (Guṇaratna; Rājaśekhara); the Ratnaṭīkā has the ascetic salute 'the tīrthakaras from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara', and the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha cites a 'Rāśīkara-bhāṣya'. His identification with Kauṇḍinya is a scholarly suggestion.

name: Ratannāth (Hājī Ratan)
summary: Nāth yogī remembered in Punjab and among Muslims of the north-west as Hājī Ratan; a centre of his cult was at Peshawar.

name: Rātri Bhāradvājī
summary: Named (beside Kuśika Saubhara) as ṛṣikā of the hymn to Night, RV 10.127.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Ṛbhu
summary: Sage of the Advaita dialogues: taught by Varāha after long austerity (Varāha 1–3), he teaches his disciple Nidāgha (Varāha 4–5, Tejobindu 5, Mahā, Annapūrṇā); named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6, Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).
alt_summary: A mind-born son of Brahmā, knower of reality from birth, teacher of Nidāgha (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15-16, verified); in the Śivarahasya he teaches Nidāgha the Ṛbhu Gītā received from Śiva.

Mind-born son of Brahmā (KūP 1.10.13 lists him with the Kumāras) who teaches his disciple Nidāgha the non-difference of all selves (VP 2.15-16) - told within Jaḍa Bharata's teaching; the Ṛbhu Gītā (U06) is a separate text.

name: Reṇukācārya (Revaṇasiddha)
summary: The first of the five ācāryas: the gaṇa Reṇuka who, cursed for leaping over his fellow gaṇa Dāruka in Śiva's assembly, emerged from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki, taught Agastya the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, and in the tradition founded the Rambhāpurī pīṭha at Bāḷehonnūr.

tradition.text: appears in every yuga; in the Kali age as Revaṇa/Reṇuka

realization_account.text: A pramatha created by Śiva (SSM 2.25–27), sent to earth for overstepping Dāruka (3.66–77), he appeared from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki without human birth (3.83–84; 4.1), taught Agastya, visited Vibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā, and returned into the liṅga (ch. 21).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Seat: Vīra-siṃhāsana at Rambhāpurī (low confidence on the siṃhāsana name).

name: Revaṇanātha
summary: One of the Marathi nine Nāths (Revaṇnāth), held to be an incarnation of the Nārāyaṇa Camasa. In Karnataka the name Revaṇasiddha also belongs to a Vīraśaiva founder-figure; the relation between the two is unclear.

name: Romaharṣaṇa

realization_account.text: The sūta disciple to whom Vyāsa gave the Purāṇa-saṃhitā; his own saṃhitā is the root (mūla) of the three made by his disciples (VP 3.6.16-18). BhP 12.7.5-7 names six paurāṇikas who learned from him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The first paurāṇika: Vyāsa's disciple for the Purāṇa, reciter at Naimiṣa in several Purāṇas, father of Ugraśravas; the four root saṃhitās of the Purāṇa descend from him and his pupils.

name: Urōmarisi (Romarishi)
summary: Sage counted among the Siddhars in some Tamil lists; works on medicine and wisdom circulate under his name.
notes: Recalled at low confidence.

name: Romaśā
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 1.126.7.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Ṛṣabha

realization_account.text: Son of Nābhi and Merudevī, the eighth avatāra 'who showed the path honoured by all āśramas' (BhP 1.3.13); after teaching his sons that the human body is not for dog-like pleasures but for austerity (BhP 5.5.1-27), he lived as a naked avadhūta and gave up his body in a forest fire in Kuṭaka (BhP 5.5.28-5.6.8).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: In the Bhāgavata an avatāra of Viṣṇu and avadhūta-teacher; the same figure the Jains honour as the first Tīrthaṅkara. BhP 5.6.9 adds that a king named Arhat of Koṅka, Veṅka and Kuṭaka, imitating him, will spread a heterodox path in Kali (a polemical report).

name: Ṛṣabheśvara
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Not to be confused with the Jain Ṛṣabha.

name: Rūpa Bhavānī
summary: 17th-century Kashmiri Śaiva yoginī and poet in the line of Lal Ded, revered as a saint; her vākhs teach inner realization of Śiva.

tradition.text: 1621-1721 CE (traditional dates)

name: Rūpa Gosvāmī
summary: Formerly Dabir Khās, minister of Sultan Husain Shah of Gauḍa; taught by Caitanya at Prayāga (CC 2.19); settled in Vṛndāvana; the chief theorist of Gauḍīya devotion: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, Ujjvalanīlamaṇi, Laghubhāgavatāmṛta, Upadeśāmṛta, dramas and hymns.

name: Śabarasvāmin

realization_account.text: A late popular verse makes Śabarasvāmin, a brāhmaṇa, the father by wives of the four varṇas of Varāhamihira, King Vikramāditya, Bhartṛhari and others; another story says he lived disguised as a śabara (forest-dweller). These are legends, not Mīmāṃsā doctrine.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Legend details are from memory (low confidence).
summary: Author of the Śābarabhāṣya, the earliest surviving commentary on the whole Mīmāṃsā Sūtra and the base text of both later schools.

name: Śabarī
summary: A forest woman of low birth, disciple of the sage Mataṅga, who waited for Rāma; he teaches her that gender, caste and stage of life are no cause of devotion and gives her the nine means of devotion (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa 3.10).

realization_account.text: After guiding Rāma to Sugrīva she entered the fire before him and, freed of all bonds made by ignorance, attained liberation by Rāma's grace (AR 3.10.39-42).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: An aged female ascetic (śramaṇī) of the Śabara people who served the sages of Mataṅga's hermitage, receives Rāma and ascends to the heavenly worlds (Rāmāyaṇa 3.73–74).

name: Śacī Paulomī
summary: Indra's consort, ṛṣikā of RV 10.159, in which she praises herself as victorious.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Ṣaḍakṣaradēva
summary: Seventeenth-century Kannada Vīraśaiva poet of campū works including the Rājaśēkharavilāsa and the Vṛṣabhēndravijaya.

name: Sadānanda (Yogīndra)
summary: Author of the Vedāntasāra.

name: Sadāśiva Brahmendra
places: Tamil country, Kāveri region (samādhi shrine at Nerur by tradition)
summary: Advaita avadhūta and composer of Sanskrit songs remembered in South Indian tradition; author of the Yogasudhākara on the Yoga Sūtra.
notes: Tradition makes him a pupil of Paramaśivendra Sarasvatī and credits him with further works (Brahma Sūtra vṛtti, Ātmavidyāvilāsa) — not verified here.
alt_summary: Avadhūta and poet of the Kāverī region (c. 17th–18th c.), author of the Ātmavidyāvilāsa, a Brahmasūtra commentary (Brahmatattvaprakāśikā), a Yoga Sūtra commentary and Sanskrit songs; remembered as a jīvanmukta who wandered naked and silent.

name: Ṣaḍguruśiṣya
summary: Commentator on the Sarvānukramaṇī (Vedārthadīpikā) and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (Sukhapradā).

name: Sadyojyoti
summary: The earliest Siddhānta author whose works survive: philosophical treatises proving the soul and the Lord against Buddhists and others, and defining liberation as the soul's equality with Śiva; commentaries on the Svāyambhuva and (reportedly) the Raurava.
notes: Names his teacher as Ugrajyoti (moderate confidence). A commentary on the Raurava(sūtrasaṅgraha) is reported but not treated here (gap).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08 (catalogue: commentaries). Doctrine is U18's.
alt_summary: Kashmirian theologian of the Śaiva Siddhānta, the earliest datable exegete of its scriptures; he commented on the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha and wrote short doctrinal treatises (the Nareśvaraparīkṣā, Mokṣakārikā, Bhogakārikā and others).

name: Sāhib Kaul
summary: 17th-century Kashmiri Śaiva scholar-poet: a commentary on the Śiva Sūtra, the Devīnāmavilāsa, and works of Śrīvidyā ritual (Śrīvidyānityapaddhati).

name: Śaibya Satyakāma
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks what world the one who meditates on Om until death wins (PrU 5); distinct from Satyakāma Jābāla.

name: Sakalēśa Mādarasa
summary: A chieftain-poet among the śaraṇas.

name: Śākalya
summary: The teacher credited with the Padapāṭha of the Ṛgveda and eponym of the Śākala recension; cited by Yāska and Pāṇini. Tradition sometimes identifies him with Vidagdha Śākalya, Yājñavalkya's questioner on the number of the gods in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.9) — an identification scholars dispute.
