alt_summary: Author of the word-by-word text (padapāṭha) of the Ṛgveda, cited by Pāṇini (e.g. 1.1.16) and the Aitareya Āraṇyaka. Some Purāṇic accounts identify him with Vidagdha Śākalya, Yājñavalkya's opponent (tch:vidagdha-sakalya).

name: Śākaṭāyana (the ancient grammarian)
summary: Pre-Pāṇinian grammarian cited by Yāska and Pāṇini (e.g. 3.4.111); author of the thesis that all nouns derive from verbs (Nirukta 1.12). Distinct from the Jain grammarian Pālyakīrti who took his name.

name: Śākāyanya
summary: Sage who teaches King Bṛhadratha the knowledge of the self in the Maitrī Upaniṣad, relaying what Prajāpati taught the Vālakhilyas.
alt_summary: U04 contribution: his teaching to Bṛhadratha is recapitulated in Maitreya Upaniṣad 1.

name: Śālikanātha Miśra
notes: Direct discipleship of Prabhākara is traditional.
summary: Principal systematizer of the Prābhākara school: author of the Prakaraṇapañcikā and of the Ṛjuvimalā and Dīpaśikhā on Prabhākara's works.

name: Samādhi (the merchant)
summary: A merchant cast out by his greedy family who still could not stop worrying about them; with Suratha he heard the Devī Māhātmya, and asked the Goddess not for wealth but for the knowledge that frees from attachment, which she granted (DM 13).

name: Samagāra Haraḷayya
summary: The cobbler śaraṇa whose son's marriage to the daughter of the brāhmaṇa Madhuvarasa precipitated the orthodox reaction and the upheaval at Kalyāṇa; both fathers were put to death by the king's order in the tradition's account.

name: Sāmaśravas
summary: Yājñavalkya's pupil, told to drive home Janaka's thousand cows (BAU 3.1.2).

name: Śambhu Bhaṭṭa
summary: Pupil of Khaṇḍadeva; author of the Prabhāvalī on the Bhāṭṭadīpikā.

name: Śambhunātha
summary: Abhinavagupta's teacher in the Kaula form of the Trika, from Jālandhara; the Tantrāloka credits him with the teaching of the seven ānandas of the breath (TĀ 5.52) and with the Kula ritual of ch. 29.
notes: Teacher-name Sumati(nātha) from TĀ ch. 1 as quoted in Jayaratha (low confidence on the relationship).

name: Śāṃśapāyana
summary: Disciple of Romaharṣaṇa and maker of one of the root Purāṇa-saṃhitās (VP 3.6.17-18); absent from the Bhāgavata's list of six paurāṇikas, which names Trayyāruṇi, Kaśyapa, Sāvarṇi, Akṛtavraṇa, Vaiśampāyana and Hārīta instead (BhP 12.7.5).

name: Saṃvanana Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 10.191, the closing hymn of concord.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Saṃvartaka
summary: Named first among the paramahaṃsas who live with unmanifest marks and conduct (Jābāla 6; Bhikṣuka; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).

name: Sanaka
summary: Eldest of the four mind-born sons of Brahmā (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra), whose question on separating mind from the guṇas occasions the Haṃsa Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.13).

name: Sanandana
summary: Named by the Sāṃkhya Sūtra (6.69): 'the (owner–owned relation of puruṣa and prakṛti) is caused by the subtle body, says the teacher Sanandana'. Gauḍapāda (on SK 1, 43) names Sanaka, Sanandana (Sananda), Sanātana and Sanatkumāra among Brahmā's sons, in whom the dispositions arose naturally at sixteen.
notes: Whether the SS's teacher is the Kumāra of Purāṇic lore is not stated in the text.

name: Sanātana Gosvāmī
summary: Rūpa's elder brother, formerly Sākar Mallik, minister at Gauḍa; taught by Caitanya at Vārāṇasī for two months (CC 2.20–24); author of the Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta and the Vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī; associated with the Haribhaktivilāsa.

name: Sanatkumāra
summary: Teacher of Nārada in ChU 7: leads him from name to plenitude (bhūman) and shows him 'the far shore beyond darkness'; 'they call him Skanda' (ChU 7.26.2).
alt_summary: Eldest of the four Kumāras (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra), mind-born sons of Brahmā who refused to procreate and remained celibate knowers (VP 1.7; KūP 1.10.13-14); the first avatāra in BhP 1.3.6; with his brothers he instructs Nārada in the Nārada Purāṇa; the first Upapurāṇa bears his name (KūP 1.1.17).
Mind-born sage who, in the Vṛtra Gītā, teaches the greatness of Viṣṇu and the six colours of living beings (12.271).
U04 contribution: asks Kālāgnirudra about the tripuṇḍra (Kālāgnirudra) and, with Pippalāda and Aṅgiras, asks Atharvan about the first meditation (Atharvaśikhā).
notes: U05's contribution; his teaching in Chāndogya 7 is covered by U03.

name: Sanatsujāta
summary: An ever-youthful sage (kumāra) summoned by Vidura's thought, who teaches Dhṛtarāṣṭra that heedlessness is death and heedfulness immortality, and describes the brāhmaṇa, silence, the virtues and the shining Brahman seen by yogins (5.41–45).
notes: The tradition counts him among Brahmā's mind-born sons (not checked here).
alt_summary: One of Brahmā's mind-born sons; in this recension of the Haṃsa Upaniṣad he teaches Gautama the haṃsa-vidyā that Śiva told Pārvatī.

name: Śāṇḍilya
summary: Named author of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā: all this is brahman; the self within the heart, smaller than a grain and greater than the worlds, is brahman, which 'I shall attain on departing' (ChU 3.14.1-4).
notes: The same teaching appears in Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.3 (moderate). Later works (Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra, Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad) are attributed to a Śāṇḍilya; identity not asserted here.
alt_summary: U04 contribution: disciple of Atharvan in the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad, who, not finding brahmavidyā in the four Vedas, asks for it.

The authority of the fire-altar books of the Śatapatha (6–10), whose meditation on the self 'made of mind, with breath for body, of the form of light', smaller than a grain yet greater than the worlds, is the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā (ŚB 10.6.3; ChU 3.14). The Bhakti Sūtra ascribed to a Śāṇḍilya (U25) is a separate, much later attribution.
Sage who relates the Jayākhya's teaching to other sages; a Pāñcarātra account quoted by Śaṅkara (BSBh 2.2.45) says he took up this teaching after not finding the highest good in the four Vedas.
alt_notes: Contribution from U08.

name: Saṅgamāditya
summary: Descendant of the Tryambaka siddhas (son of the fifteenth, who married a brāhmaṇa woman) who came wandering to Kashmir; great-great-grandfather of Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.115-119).

name: Sañjaya

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra's charioteer and counsellor, given divine sight by Vyāsa to see and report the battle (6.2); he narrates the Gītā to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and says he heard it 'by the grace of Vyāsa' directly from Kṛṣṇa (18.75).

name: Śaṅkara (Ādi Śaṅkarācārya)

tradition.text: 788–820 CE in the commonest traditional reckoning; 509–477 BCE in the Kāñcī and Dvārakā maṭha reckonings

scholarly.text: c. 700–750 CE (Hacker, Nakamura); other scholars up to c. 800

places: Kedāranātha or Kāñcī (death, by differing accounts)

realization_account.text: The Śaṅkaradigvijaya tells that Śaṅkara, an only son of Śivaguru and Āryāmbā, obtained his mother's consent to renounce when a crocodile seized him in the river; that Govinda initiated him; that Vyāsa appeared to him at Kāśī and extended his life from sixteen to thirty-two years; and that he ascended the Sarvajña-pīṭha in Kashmir.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Scholarly consensus (Hacker, Mayeda, Ingalls) accepts the BSBh, the principal Upaniṣad commentaries, the Gītā commentary and the Upadeśasāhasrī; most prakaraṇas and stotras are doubted.
summary: The systematizer of Advaita Vedānta: commentator on the Brahma Sūtras, the principal Upaniṣads and the Gītā, author of the Upadeśasāhasrī; in the tradition's account a child renunciant from Kālaṭi who studied under Govinda, debated Maṇḍana Miśra, founded the four āmnāya maṭhas and the Daśanāmī order, revived Vedic dharma and died at thirty-two.
alt_summary: Author of the oldest extant Gītā commentary, which reads the Gītā as teaching liberation by knowledge of the self with renunciation, action serving to purify the mind; also credited with commentaries on the Sanatsujātīya and the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma.

U04 contribution: cites the Jābāla (4) for renunciation directly from studentship (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 3.4.20); a commentary on the Nṛsiṃhatāpanī is attributed to him (questioned by scholars). The Daśanāmī tradition traces its four maṭhas to him (Maṭhāmnāya).

(Yoga unit contribution) The Pātañjalayogaśāstravivaraṇa, a sub-commentary on the Yoga-bhāṣya, is ascribed in its colophons to Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, pupil of Govinda; whether this is the Advaita teacher is disputed.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only (Gītā and epic works).

name: Śaṅkara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Son of Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa; author of the Mīmāṃsābālaprakāśa and a critique of Appayya's Vidhirasāyana.

name: Śaṅkara Miśra
summary: Mithilā scholar, author of the Upaskāra on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (the standard commentary until Candrānanda's was recovered) and of the Vādivinoda.

name: Śaṅkarānanda
summary: 14th-c. Advaitin saluted as guru in the opening verse of the Pañcadaśī; author of the Ātmapurāṇa and of Upaniṣad and Gītā commentaries.
alt_summary: Advaitin commentator (Dīpikās) on many Upaniṣads including Atharvan ones; tradition makes him a teacher of Vidyāraṇya.

name: Sāṅkṛti
summary: Sage who questions Dattātreya in the Darśana and Avadhūta Upaniṣads and visits the sun's world in the Akṣi Upaniṣad; at the end of the Darśana he abides fearless in the Self.

name: Ṣaṇmukhasvāmi
summary: A later Vīraśaiva ascetic and vacanakāra.

name: Santāna
summary: Number 16 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Sārparājñī
summary: The 'serpent queen', ṛṣikā of RV 10.189 (the dappled bull who has come; deity ātman or the Sun).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Vāsudeva Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Logician and Advaita teacher at Purī who, after a seven-day Vedānta discussion, became Caitanya's devotee (CC 2.6).

name: Sarvajña
summary: Wandering Kannada poet of the tripadi sayings, claimed by the Vīraśaiva tradition.
notes: Affiliation debated.

name: Sarvajñātman

tradition.text: disciple of Sureśvara; claimed by the Kāñcī tradition as an early pontiff

summary: Author of the Saṃkṣepaśārīraka; disciple of 'Deveśvara', traditionally identified with Sureśvara; held pure consciousness to be both the locus and object of ignorance.

name: Śarvavarman
summary: Author by tradition of the Kātantra grammar, composed for a Sātavāhana king.

name: Śaśadhara
summary: Pre-Gaṅgeśa Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyasiddhāntadīpa.

name: Śaśvatī Āṅgirasī
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 8.1.34.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Swami Satchidanandendra Sarasvati
summary: Advaitin of Holenarsipur (1880–1975) who argued that Śaṅkara's avidyā is superimposition itself, not a positive root-ignorance, and that post-Śaṅkara schools (esp. the Vivaraṇa) diverged from him.

name: Caṭṭaimuṉi (Sattaimuni)
summary: Siddhar whose name is taken from the cloak (caṭṭai) he wore; his Ñāṉam contrasts outward worship with the Siddhars' worship of the goddess on the 'Meru' of triangles and with vāci yoga. Some accounts say he wrote openly what other Siddhars veiled.
places: Srirangam — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Origins and the 'open writing' story recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Satyadharma Tīrtha
summary: Uttarādi Maṭha pontiff of the 18th–19th centuries, remembered for glosses (ṭippaṇīs) on the Bhāgavata and on Madhva's commentaries; his brindāvana is at Holehonnur on the Tuṅgā.
notes: Titles of his works and his dates were not verified; no work entries are created (see REPORT gaps).

name: Satyadhyāna Tīrtha
summary: Uttarādi Maṭha pontiff of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, remembered for public debates with Advaita scholars and for promoting Dvaita learning.

name: Satyajñānadarśin
summary: Third teacher of the inner lineage of Tamil Siddhānta (after Nandi and Sanatkumāra), teacher of Parañcōti.

name: Satyakāma Jābāla
summary: Son of Jabālā, who did not know his lineage; accepted as a pupil by Hāridrumata Gautama for telling the truth (ChU 4.4); taught the four quarters of brahman by a bull, fire, a goose and a diver-bird (ChU 4.5-9); teacher of Upakosala (ChU 4.10-15); in BAU 4.1.6 he holds that brahman is the mind.

name: Satyakka
summary: A woman śaraṇa remembered as a sweeper, whose vacanas affirm devotion over outward observance.

name: Satyanātha Tīrtha
summary: Uttarādi Maṭha pontiff and polemicist, author of the Abhinavāmṛta and other works titled 'Abhinava-'.

name: Satyavacas Rāthītara
summary: Holds that truth (satya) is what matters (TU 1.9).

name: Satyavāha Bhāradvāja
summary: Link in the Muṇḍaka's line: from Aṅgir to Aṅgiras, handing on the knowledge 'higher and lower' (MuU 1.1.2).

name: Satyayajña Pauluṣi
summary: One of the five great householders and great Vedic scholars who asked 'what is our self, what is brahman?' and, with Uddālaka Āruṇi, went to Aśvapati Kaikeya; each had venerated only one part of the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11-17).

name: Śaunaka (of Naimiṣa)
summary: Head (kulapati) of the sages of the Naimiṣa forest, at whose twelve-year sacrifice Ugraśravas recites the Mahābhārata.
notes: A brāhmaṇa Śaunaka also instructs Yudhiṣṭhira at the start of the exile (3.2, the eightfold path of dharma at 3.2.71); the identity of the two is not asserted here.
alt_summary: The ancient teacher to whom the tradition ascribes the Śaunaka recension of the Atharvaveda and the Ṛgveda ancillaries — the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, the Anukramaṇīs, the Bṛhaddevatā and the Ṛgvidhāna — and whom it makes the teacher of Āśvalāyana. Whether these are one Śaunaka, and whether he is the Śaunaka of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad or of the Naimiṣa forest in the epics, is not settled.

Ṛgvedic teacher to whom tradition ascribes the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya, the Bṛhaddevatā, the Ṛgvidhāna and several indices, and the fifth book of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka; teacher of Āśvalāyana. The Śaunaka 'great householder' of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad and the Atharvan Śaunaka school's eponym may or may not be the same.

name: Śaunaka Kāpeya
summary: Being served food with Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni when a student begs from them and speaks of the one god who swallowed four great ones (ChU 4.3.5-7).

name: Śaunaka Mahāśāla
summary: 'Śaunaka, the great householder', who approached Aṅgiras in the proper way and asked by knowing what all this becomes known (MuU 1.1.3).
notes: Disambiguated from other Śaunakas (tch:saunaka).
alt_summary: U04 contribution: asks Pippalāda in the Brahma and Parabrahma Upaniṣads; leads the sages who ask Mārkaṇḍeya (Dakṣiṇāmūrti) and hear Nārada at Naimiṣa (Nāradaparivrājaka).

name: Śaunaka (of Naimiṣa)
summary: The kulapati of the thousand-year sacrificial session (sattra) at the Naimiṣa forest who questions the Sūta in the frame of the Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas. Tradition's link to the Vedic Śaunakas is not asserted here.

name: Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks what sleeps and what wakes in a person and who sees dreams (PrU 4).

name: Sāvarṇi (paurāṇika)
summary: Disciple of Romaharṣaṇa and maker of one of the root Purāṇa-saṃhitās (VP 3.6.17-18; BhP 12.7.5-7). Not to be confused with the Manu Sāvarṇi (the eighth Manu).

name: Sāvitrī
summary: Princess who chooses the doomed Satyavat, follows Yama when he takes Satyavat's life and wins it back through her words on dharma and the friendship of the good (3.277–283).

name: Sāyaṇa
summary: Sāyaṇa (Sāyaṇācārya), minister of the early Vijayanagara kings and director of the great series of Vedic commentaries (Vedārthaprakāśa) on the Saṃhitās, Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas, which explain the hymns chiefly by their ritual use; also author of digests (the 'Sudhānidhi' works).
notes: Brother of Mādhava, whom the tradition identifies with Vidyāraṇya (tch:vidyaranya) — identification disputed. Birth year unknown; 'from' is a rough estimate.
alt_summary: Author (with collaborators) of commentaries on the Vedic Saṃhitās, Brāhmaṇas and Āraṇyakas; his introductions define the Veda as the text that makes known the non-worldly means to gain the desired and avoid the undesired. Tradition makes him the brother of Mādhava (Vidyāraṇya).

name: Śekh Phayjullāh
summary: Bengali Muslim poet to whom the Gorakṣavijaya is ascribed.

name: Senajit
summary: A king grieving for his son, consoled by a brāhmaṇa who cites Piṅgalā (12.168).

name: T. G. Siddappārādhya
summary: Twentieth-century author of a Vīraśaiva commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā (1965).

name: Siddha Kṛṣṇadāsa Bābā (of Govardhana)
summary: 18th-c. Braj renunciate associated with manuals (guṭikā/paddhati) of meditative service in the eightfold daily play and the siddha-praṇālī tradition.

name: Siddhanañjeśa Śivācārya
summary: Author of the Sanskrit Śivasiddhāntacandrikā, of the Pūvalli Pañcavarṇa Bṛhanmaṭha.

name: Siddhanātha Śivācārya
summary: Father of Śivayogi Śivācārya, praised as 'crest-jewel of the Vīraśaivas' and a determiner of Śiva-siddhānta (SSM 1.17–20).

name: Siddharāma
summary: Siddharāma (Siddharāmēśvara) of Sonnalige, the builder of tanks and temples for Mallikārjuna who, in the tradition's account, was challenged by Allama, received liṅga-initiation from Cennabasava and joined the śaraṇas; vacanas signed Kapilasiddhamallikārjuna.

realization_account.text: A karmayogin devoted to Mallikārjuna of Śrīśaila, he was met at Sonnalige by Allama, who mocked his works; he went to Kalyāṇa, received liṅga-initiation and later attained union at Sonnalige.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The Tattvapradīpikā's introduction calls the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi's author a member of the lineage of Siddharāma, 'born from the glance of Revaṇasiddha' (e-text M00207).

name: Siddhārth Gautam Rām
summary: Present head (pīṭhādhīśvar) of Kīnārām Sthal, Krīm Kuṇḍ, Varanasi (from 1978, as commonly reported), a disciple of Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām.

name: Śikhidhvaja
summary: King of Mālava who renounced his kingdom for forest austerities but found no peace until his wife Cūḍālā, disguised as Kumbha, taught him that renunciation of everything includes renunciation of the mind that renounces.

realization_account.text: After giving up even his ascetic's belongings and his body-identification he entered a long samādhi, awoke liberated and returned to rule with Cūḍālā.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Śilaka Śālāvatya
summary: One of three experts on the udgītha who discuss the support of the sāman (ChU 1.8).

name: Ṣimānanda Dīkṣita
alt_names: Kṣemānanda (identification suggested by the e-text's editor, uncertain)
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana on the Tattvasamāsa; by his own account son of Raghunandana, a Kānyakubja brahmin living at Iṣṭikāpura.

name: Siṅgirāja
summary: Kannada poet of the Amala Basavarāja Cāritra.

name: Ciṟuttoṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. General of the Pallava king who led the capture of Vātāpi; retiring to serve devotees, he was visited by Śiva as a Bhairava ascetic who asked for a meal cooked from an only son of five; he and his wife Veṇkāṭṭu Naṅkai cooked their son Cīrāḷaṉ; the ascetic bade them call the boy to eat with him, and the boy came running, alive.

realization_account.text: General of the Pallava king who led the capture of Vātāpi; retiring to serve devotees, he was visited by Śiva as a Bhairava ascetic who asked for a meal cooked from an only son of five; he and his wife Veṇkāṭṭu Naṅkai cooked their son Cīrāḷaṉ; the ascetic bade them call the boy to eat with him, and the boy came running, alive.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Sītā
summary: Daughter of Janaka of Mithilā and Rāma's wife; the Rāmāyaṇa's exemplar of the devoted wife, taught by Anasūyā (2.117–119).
alt_summary: In the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa she instructs Hanumān (1.1.31-43): Rāma is the non-dual Brahman and she is primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), the agent of all the deeds superimposed on him.

name: Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭha
summary: Author of the Mahānayaprakāśa on the Krama in Old Kashmiri with a Sanskrit commentary.

name: Śiva
summary: In U06's texts: speaker of the Īśvara Gītā (to the sages), the Śiva Gītā (to Rāma), the Guru Gītā (to Pārvatī) and the Rudra Gītā (to the Pracetās); narrator of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa to Pārvatī; in the Mokṣopāya he teaches Vasiṣṭha the true worship of the divine as consciousness (MU 6.31-46).
alt_summary: In the epic, Śiva teaches Umā dharma (13.126–134), is named as the proclaimer of the Pāśupata knowledge (12.337.62), grants Arjuna the Pāśupata weapon after testing him as a hunter (3.38–41), and is praised with a thousand names (13.14–17); 'among the Rudras I am Śaṃkara' (BhG 10.23); Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).

Śiva/Maheśvara as speaker: teaches Brahmā the Yogaśikhā and Yogakuṇḍalī ch.3, teaches Kumāra in the Tejobindu, Maitreya in the Maitreya, Śuka in the Śukarahasya, and Pārvatī the haṃsa-vidyā reported in the Haṃsa; whispers the tāraka to the dying at Kāśī (Muktikā 1.19–21, Jābāla 1).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Śivāditya
summary: Author of the Saptapadārthī, which expounds the categories as seven (adding absence) and fuses Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika.

name: Śivagaṇaprasādi Mahādēvayya
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Śivāgrayogin
summary: Sixteenth-century bilingual Siddhānta scholar of the Tamil country who wrote in Sanskrit (the Śaivaparibhāṣā; a commentary on the Sanskrit Śivajñānabodha) and in Tamil (a commentary on the Civañāṉa Cittiyār).
alt_summary: Late Saiddhāntika author of the Śaivasiddhāntaparibhāṣā and ritual works.

name: Śivakumāra Svāmi (Siddhagaṅgā)
summary: Head of the Siddhagaṅgā maṭha, known for dāsōha — daily free feeding and schooling of thousands of children of every background.

name: Śivarām (Kīnārām's Vaiṣṇava guru)
summary: Vaiṣṇava ascetic who gave Kīnārām his first initiation (tradition).

name: Sivavākkiyar (Civavākkiyar)
summary: The most iconoclastic Siddhar poet: his Civavākkiyam mocks stone images, temple ritual, pilgrimage, Vedic recitation and caste, locates the Lord within, and in one famous verse denies the rebirth of the dead. His name is explained as 'he whose (first) utterance was Śiva'.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition identifies him with Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār in his Śaiva phase; others reject the identification. Not in the popular list of eighteen, but in other lists and in every Siddhar anthology.

name: Śivayogi Śivācārya
summary: Compiler of the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, son of the Vīraśaiva ācārya Siddhanātha in the line of Muddadeva (SSM 1.13–24), who composed it from the Āgamas 'from Kāmika to Vātula' and the Śaiva Purāṇas without contradicting the Vedic path (1.25–27).

scholarly.text: debated: placed variously between the 12th and 15th c.

notes: The Tattvapradīpikā places him in the lineage of Siddharāma; the SSM colophon also styles the composition Reṇukācārya's.
alt_summary: Author of the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, presenting Reṇukācārya's teaching to Agastya on the 101 sthalas.

name: Śivopādhyāya
summary: 18th-century Kashmiri commentator who completed the commentary on the Vijñāna Bhairava from v. 24, where Kṣemarāja's breaks off.

name: Skanda / Guha
summary: Son of Śiva: teaches Prajāpati the rosary (Akṣamālikā); the Skanda Upaniṣad is his declaration of the identity of jīva and Śiva; in the Jābāli his line (Īśāna → Ṣaḍānana → Jābāli) transmits the Paśupati teaching.

name: Skandasvāmin
summary: Author of an early Ṛgveda commentary (partly surviving) and, with Maheśvara, a commentary on the Nirukta.
notes: Reported as teacher of Harisvāmin, commentator on the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (low confidence).
alt_summary: Commentator on the Ṛgveda and the Nirukta.

name: Somānanda
summary: Founder of the Pratyabhijñā philosophy with the Śivadṛṣṭi; he traced his descent from the mind-born siddhas of Durvāsas' Tryambaka line (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-122). Teacher of Utpaladeva; also wrote a (lost) commentary on the Parātrīśikā cited by Abhinavagupta.

realization_account.text: Heir of a line of siddhas born of the mind of Durvāsas, descended through the fifteenth who married, whose son came to Kashmir.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Somanātha Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Mayūkhamālikā on the Śāstradīpikā.

name: Somaśambhu
summary: Abbot of a Śaiva monastery in central India (the Golagī maṭha tradition is usually named — moderate confidence), author of the most influential Siddhānta ritual manual, the Somaśambhupaddhati (Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī), completed 1095/96.
alt_summary: Author of the Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī (Somaśambhupaddhati, 1095/96), the most influential manual of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual, covering daily worship, initiation, consecration and funeral rites.

name: Someśvara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Nyāyasudhā ('Rāṇaka') on the Tantravārttika.

name: Śraddhā Kāmāyanī
summary: The ṛṣikā of the hymn to Faith (RV 10.151).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Sri Aurobindo
summary: U01 contribution: author of The Secret of the Veda, a symbolic-psychological reading of the Ṛgveda.
alt_summary: Author of the Essays on the Gita (1916–20).
notes: U05's contribution only; his lineage is owned by U52.

name: Śrī Bhaṭṭa
summary: Disciple of Keśava Kāśmīrin; author of the Yugalaśataka, Braj verses on the divine couple.

name: Śrīdhara Svāmin
summary: The most influential commentator on the Bhāgavata and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (and on the Gītā, Subodhinī), a renunciant whose non-dualism is devotional (Narasiṃha-bhakti); later Vaiṣṇava schools build on or argue with his readings.
alt_summary: Commentator on the Bhāgavata (Bhāvārthadīpikā), the Gītā (Subodhinī) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, blending non-dualism with devotion; Caitanya insisted on respect for him (CC 3.7).
Advaita commentator who emphasizes devotion; author of the Subodhinī on the Gītā (and of the Bhāvārthadīpikā on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa).
Advaita renunciant (associated with Purī) whose commentaries on the Bhāgavata (Bhāvārthadīpikā), the Gītā (Subodhinī) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa combine non-dualism with devotion.

name: Śrīdhara
summary: Bengali author of the Nyāyakandalī on the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, dated 991 CE in its colophon. (Distinct from Śrīdhara Svāmin, the Bhāgavata commentator.)

name: Śrīharṣa
summary: Poet and dialectician, author of the Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya and of the mahākāvya Naiṣadhīyacarita; demolished the Nyāya definitions in defence of Advaita.

name: Śrīkaṇṭha Śivācārya
summary: Author of the Śaiva Brahmasūtrabhāṣya: Śiva with his cit-śakti is Brahman; souls and world are his body; Veda and Śivāgama are equal; liberation is equality with Śiva.

tradition.text: Vīraśaiva authors place him before Śaṅkara

name: Śrīkaṇṭha (author of the Ratnatraya)
summary: Saiddhāntika author of the Ratnatraya on Śiva, Śakti and bindu, commented on by Aghoraśiva.
notes: Distinct from tch:srikantha (Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya, Śivādvaita). Possibly the Śrīkaṇṭha named as a teacher of Rāmakaṇṭha (low confidence).

name: Śrīkaṇṭhabhaṭṭa
summary: Son of Mahādevabhaṭṭa, from whom Bhāskara received the Śiva Sūtra teaching (Vārttika 1.8).
notes: Distinct from tch:srikantha (Śaiva Vedānta) and tch:srikanthanatha (mythic).

name: Śrīkaṇṭha(nātha)
summary: The form of Śiva who, wandering on Mount Kailāsa when the Śaiva secrets had been lost at the start of the Kali age, descended for grace and commanded the sage Durvāsas to keep the scripture from being cut off (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-110).

realization_account.text: A form of Śiva himself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Distinct from tch:srikantha (the Śaiva Vedāntin) and tch:srikanthabhatta (Bhāskara's teacher).

name: Śrīkumāra
summary: Commentator (Tātparyadīpikā) on Bhoja's Tattvaprakāśa.

name: Śrīnivāsa Ācārya
summary: Second-generation leader who, with Narottama and Śyāmānanda, carried the Gosvāmīs' books from Vṛndāvana to Bengal; the tradition says they were stolen at Viṣṇupur and recovered when King Vīra Hāmvīra became his disciple.

name: Śrīnivāsa Dīkṣita
notes: Self-description checked in sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/4_rellit/vaisn/srinivasamakhi_vedantadesika_dasavidhahetunirupana.md (GRETIL, input by U. Hüsken) (DHN 1.15–20). Date not established here.
summary: Vaikhānasa scholar ('Śrīnivāsamakhin', titled Vedāntadeśika), of the Kauśika lineage, son of Govindācārya and devotee of Veṅkaṭeśa, author of the Tātparyacintāmaṇi commentary containing the Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa.

name: Śrīnivāsācārya (of the Nimbārka school)
summary: Direct disciple of Nimbārka (tradition) and author of the Vedāntakaustubha, the classical commentary on Nimbārka's Brahma Sūtra commentary.

name: Śrīnivāsa Tīrtha
summary: Mādhva commentator, author of the Ṛgarthoddhāra on the Ṛgveda hymns covered by Madhva's Ṛgbhāṣya.

name: Śrīnivāsadāsa
summary: Author of the Yatīndramatadīpikā, the standard short manual of Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.

name: Śrīpādarāja
summary: Ascetic of Mulbagal (monastic name Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Tīrtha), teacher of Vyāsatīrtha in the śāstras, author of the Vāgvajra on the Nyāyasudhā, and, in the tradition, the 'grandfather' of the Kannada Haridāsa movement, composing songs with the signature Raṅgaviṭhala.

name: Śrīpati Paṇḍita
summary: Author of the Śrīkarabhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtras, the Vīraśaiva Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita: Śiva and soul, both qualified by Śakti, are non-dual; liberation is liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya.
alt_summary: Author of the Śrīkarabhāṣya, the Vīraśaiva commentary on the Brahmasūtra that names the doctrine Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita (philosophy owned by U16; this entry records the Vīraśaiva lineage link).

name: Śrīvallabha
summary: Author of the Nyāyalīlāvatī, an independent Vaiśeṣika treatise. (Distinct from Vallabha of the Puṣṭimārga.)

name: Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Navadvīpa devotee in whose courtyard the nightly kīrtanas were held; identified with Nārada; one of the Pañca-tattva.

name: Sucarita Miśra
summary: Author of the Kāśikā commentary on the Ślokavārttika.

name: Sudarśana Sūri
summary: Author of the Śrutaprakāśikā on the Śrībhāṣya; the tradition says he perished when Śrīraṅgam was sacked and that Vedānta Deśika saved his manuscript and his sons.

tradition.text: died in the sack of Śrīraṅgam (c. 1323)

name: Sudhīndra Tīrtha
summary: Successor of Vijayīndra Tīrtha and the teacher who gave renunciation to Rāghavendra Tīrtha.

name: Śuka

realization_account.text: Born liberated and absorbed in Brahman, he was drawn by the qualities of Hari to learn the Bhāgavata from his father (BhP 1.7.9-11); an avadhūta wandering naked whom women did not notice as a man (BhP 1.4.5); he recited the Bhāgavata to Parīkṣit in seven days and ended with the non-dual instruction 'I am Brahman, the supreme abode' (BhP 12.5.11).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Vyāsa's son, the paramahaṃsa narrator of the Bhāgavata to King Parīkṣit on the bank of the Gaṅgā; one of the twelve 'great ones' (mahājana) who know the dharma of devotion (BhP 6.3.20, 'vaiyāsaki').
alt_summary: Son of Vyāsa, instructed by his father (12.224–247) and by Janaka at Mithilā (12.312–313); he rises by yoga from the peak of Kailāsa into the sky and attains the highest state, while Vyāsa grieves after him (12.318–320).

Son of Vyāsa: receives the great sayings from Śiva at his initiation (Śukarahasya), asks about Rudra (Rudrahṛdaya); model of the 'bird's path' of immediate liberation (Varāha 4.34–37) and named among paramahaṃsas (Bhikṣuka, Yājñavalkya).
Son and disciple of Vyāsa; in the Advaita guru-paramparā the teacher of Gauḍapāda (tradition), and a model of the born-free renunciant.
notes: U05's contribution; his role as reciter of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is covered by U07. The Janaka who teaches Śuka is referenced by the registry id tch:janaka without asserting identity with the Upaniṣadic king.

name: Sukeśā Bhāradvāja
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks about the person of sixteen parts (PrU 6).

name: Sulabhā
summary: A female mendicant (bhikṣukī) practising the dharma of yoga who wanders the earth alone; doubting king Janaka's liberation, she enters his mind by yoga ('sattva by sattva', 12.308.16) and answers his rebuke with a discourse showing that his attachments remain (12.308).

name: Sūle Saṅkavva
summary: A courtesan who became a śaraṇa and vacanakāra.

name: Sumantu
summary: Vyāsa's pupil who received the Atharvaveda ('the fierce sage of the Atharvāṅgirasas', Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.22).

name: Sumati ('Jaḍa')
summary: Son of a Bhārgava brahmin who behaved like a dullard (jaḍa) because he remembered past births; he told his father how beings are born, die, travel to Yama and suffer in hell (MkP 10-15), the account the wise birds relate to Jaimini.

name: Sumati(nātha)
summary: Kaula teacher praised in the Tantrāloka as the one whose wisdom dispelled Śambhunātha's darkness; Abhinavagupta's teacher's teacher.

name: Śunaḥśepa
summary: Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti, later adopted as Devarāta Vaiśvāmitra, seer of RV 1.24–30, including the prayer that Varuṇa loosen the upper, middle and lower fetters so that we may be sinless before Aditi (1.24.15). His rescue from being sacrificed is told in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa narrative (7.13–18) is cited from memory.
alt_summary: The boy sold by his father Ajīgarta to be sacrificed in place of Rohita, freed by praising the gods, and adopted by Viśvāmitra (AB 7.13–18).

name: Cuntarāṉantar (Sundarānandar)
summary: Siddhar associated with Madurai: the Siddhar shrine in the Mīṉākṣī temple is linked by tradition with him and with Śiva's sport as the 'all-powerful Siddhar' (ellām valla cittar) who made the stone elephant eat sugarcane.
places: Madurai — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The link between the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal episode and this Siddhar is recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Sundarapāṇḍya
summary: Early author to whom later commentators attribute the three verses quoted at the end of Śaṅkara's BSBh 1.1.4 (that once 'I am the existent Brahman' is known, there is nothing further to be done, and the knower-status lasts only until the self is known).

name: Suratha
summary: A king of the Caitra line, deposed by enemies and ministers; after hearing the Devī Māhātmya he worshipped the Goddess for three years and received his kingdom back and the boon of becoming Sāvarṇi, the eighth Manu (DM 13; MkP 93.17).

name: Sūrdās
summary: Blind Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of Kṛṣṇa's childhood and the gopīs' love and separation (Sūrsāgar); foremost of the aṣṭachāp.

realization_account.text: The Caurāsī Vārtā says Sūrdās, blind from birth, lived at Gaughāṭ near Agra singing songs of humility (dainya) until Vallabha initiated him and told him to sing Kṛṣṇa's play instead; he then sang at Śrīnāthjī's temple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Puṣṭimārga)

notes: Registry id; primary owner U26/U27. Scholarly account: the sectarian link rests on Vallabhan sources only.

name: Surendra Tīrtha
summary: Pontiff of the Kumbhakonam maṭha who, in the tradition's account, received Vijayīndra Tīrtha from Vyāsatīrtha as his successor.

name: Sureśvara
notes: Identity with Maṇḍana: the tradition's account (Śaṅkaradigvijaya). Most modern scholars (Hiriyanna, Kuppuswami Sastri) hold them distinct because their doctrines differ (e.g. on prasaṅkhyāna and on works).
summary: Disciple of Śaṅkara, author of the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi and of the Vārttikas on Śaṅkara's Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya commentaries; exponent of the semblance theory (ābhāsa-vāda) and of knowledge alone as liberating; in the tradition's account first head of Śṛṅgeri and identical with Maṇḍana Miśra after his defeat in debate.

name: Sūryā Sāvitrī
summary: Daughter of Savitṛ, the ṛṣikā of the wedding hymn RV 10.85, which opens 'by truth the earth is upheld' and distinguishes the pressed soma from the soma the brahmins know.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Svarūpa Dāmodara
summary: Caitanya's intimate secretary at Purī, whose notebook (kaḍacā) is quoted in the Caitanya Caritāmṛta's opening verses.

name: Svātmārāma
summary: U21 contribution: author of the Haṭhapradīpikā, who bows to the Nātha guru and places himself after Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the siddhas (HYP 1.2–9).

name: Śvetaketu Āruṇeya
summary: Son of Uddālaka Āruṇi; returns proud after twelve years of Vedic study and is taught being and tat tvam asi (ChU 6); cannot answer Pravāhaṇa Jaivali's five questions (BAU 6.2; ChU 5.3); sent to Citra (KauU 1.1).
alt_summary: U04 contribution: named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Bhikṣuka; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).

name: Śvetāśvatara

realization_account.text: SU 6.21: by tapas and the grace of God (devaprasāda) he knew brahman.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The sage named at SU 6.21: by the power of austerity and by God's grace he knew brahman and declared it to the renunciants beyond the stages of life (atyāśramin).
notes: The name may be that of a Vedic school; historicity is unknown.

name: Śyāmānanda
summary: Second-generation leader who spread Gauḍīya devotion in Odisha.

name: Śyāvāśva Ātreya
summary: Seer of RV 5.81 to Savitṛ, which opens 'the inspired yoke their mind and yoke their thoughts' (5.81.1).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Syūmaraśmi
summary: A sage who, entering a sacrificial cow, challenges Kapila's exclamation at the Vedas (12.260–262).

name: Tāṇḍavarāya Svāmī
summary: Author of the Tamil Advaita classic Kaivalya Navanītam.

name: Taṇṭiyaṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Born blind, he dug out the silted temple tank at Tiruvārūr guided by ropes and stakes, mocked by Jains; Śiva gave him sight and the Jains lost theirs (the account adds that they left the town).

realization_account.text: Born blind, he dug out the silted temple tank at Tiruvārūr guided by ropes and stakes, mocked by Jains; Śiva gave him sight and the Jains lost theirs (the account adds that they left the town).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi
summary: Holds that austerity (tapas) is what matters (TU 1.9).

name: Tāyumāṉavar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint (early 18th c.) whose songs join Siddhānta and Vedānta in a 'harmony' (camaracam), extol the silent guru and stillness (cummā iruttal), honour the Siddhars, and pray that all beings be happy. Named after Śiva as 'He who became the mother' at the Tiruchirappalli rock temple.

realization_account.text: An accountant-minister at the Nāyak court of Tiruchirappalli, he met the silent guru (Mauṉa kuru) of Tirumūlar's line, who told him 'be still' (cummā iru); he later left the court, married at his guru's bidding, and after his wife's death lived as a renouncer until his samādhi near Rāmanātapuram.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Biographical details recalled at moderate–low confidence. Not post-1800, so not flagged recent.

name: Tēraiyar
summary: Physician-Siddhar, disciple of Agastya, to whom many Siddha medical works are ascribed. The tradition tells that he cured a king by drawing a frog out of his skull with a bowl of water — hence his name ('frog-man').

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Frog story and works recalled at low confidence.

name: Tirukkacci Nambi
summary: Non-brahmin devotee who served Varadarāja at Kāñcī by fanning him; the tradition says the Lord spoke through him the six sayings that settled Rāmānuja's doubts.

realization_account.text: Varadarāja conversed with him directly and answered Rāmānuja's questions through him with six sayings.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirukkōṭṭiyūr Nambi
summary: Disciple of Yāmuna who, after making Rāmānuja come to him eighteen times, taught him the secret meaning of the tirumantra and the carama-śloka.

name: Tirukkuṟipputtoṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A washerman who washed devotees' clothes; Śiva as a poor ascetic left a garment that had to be dry by evening, rain fell, and he began to dash his head against the washing stone — Śiva's hand stopped him.

realization_account.text: A washerman who washed devotees' clothes; Śiva as a poor ascetic left a garment that had to be dry by evening, rain fell, and he began to dash his head against the washing stone — Śiva's hand stopped him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ
summary: Disciple (and adopted son, in tradition) of Rāmānuja who, at his direction, wrote the first commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi, the Ārāyirappaṭi ('Six Thousand'); a link in the teacher-line the Vaṭakalai follow.

name: Tirumālai Āṇḍāṉ
summary: Disciple of Yāmuna who taught Rāmānuja the meaning of the Tiruvāymoḻi.

name: Tirumāḷikaittēvar
summary: First of the nine poets of the Tiruvicaippā (Tirumuṟai 9).

name: Tirumūlar
summary: Author of the Tirumantiram, one of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars.
alt_names: Cuntaraṉātar (his name before entering Mūlaṉ's body, per the Periya Purāṇam)

tradition.text: lived 3,000 years in yoga

places: Chidambaram — samādhi in the popular list

realization_account.text: A yogī-disciple of Nandi from Kailāsa, travelling south to meet Agastya, found the herdsman Mūlaṉ dead at Cāttaṉūr with his cows grieving; he entered Mūlaṉ's body by yogic power to console them, later found his own body gone by Śiva's will, and sat in yoga under a pipal tree at Tiruvāvaṭuturai, singing one verse a year for three thousand years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition Tirumūlar heads many lists of the eighteen Siddhars; his Tirumantiram is their root text for eightfold yoga, the eight great powers and the perfecting of the body ('I nourished the body and so nourished the life', TM 724). Later Siddhar works (Tirumūla nāyaṉār ñāṉam, medical treatises) circulate under his name.
notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the full entry. TM 69 names his seven (or eight) disciples, among them Kālāṅki and Kañcamalaiyaṉ. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Tirunīlakaṇṭa Yāḻppāṇa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A bard (pāṇar) who accompanied Campantar's hymns on the yāḻ (harp) with his wife Mataṅkacūḷāmaṇiyār; he entered Śiva's light at Campantar's wedding.

realization_account.text: A bard (pāṇar) who accompanied Campantar's hymns on the yāḻ (harp) with his wife Mataṅkacūḷāmaṇiyār; he entered Śiva's light at Campantar's wedding.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirunīlakaṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A potter of Tillai who, reproached by his wife for his infidelity, vowed 'by Tirunīlakaṇṭam' never to touch her and kept the vow into old age; when Śiva as a yogī's begging bowl left in his keeping vanished, the couple had to bathe holding hands to prove their word — they held a stick between them, the vow was revealed, and they rose from the water young again.

realization_account.text: A potter of Tillai who, reproached by his wife for his infidelity, vowed 'by Tirunīlakaṇṭam' never to touch her and kept the vow into old age; when Śiva as a yogī's begging bowl left in his keeping vanished, the couple had to bathe holding hands to prove their word — they held a stick between them, the vow was revealed, and they rose from the water young again.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirunīlanakka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin priest whose wife blew away a spider that fell on the liṅga; he rebuked her for defiling it, and Śiva showed him blisters everywhere on his body except where she had blown. He attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.

realization_account.text: A brahmin priest whose wife blew away a spider that fell on the liṅga; he rebuked her for defiling it, and Śiva showed him blisters everywhere on his body except where she had blown. He attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tiruvaḷḷuvar
summary: Author of the Tirukkuṟaḷ. His affiliation is contested (Jain, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, non-sectarian); the Jain tradition identifies him with Elācārya/Kundakunda; Tamil Śaivas honour him as Tiruvaḷḷuva Nāyaṉār.

tradition.text: Sangam age; Tamil Nadu's Tiruvaḷḷuvar era begins 31 BCE

scholarly.text: c. 5th–6th c. CE (range proposed: 300 BCE–6th c. CE)

realization_account.text: Later legends make him a weaver of Mayilāppūr with a devoted wife Vācuki, and a son of the brahmin Pakavaṉ and the Pulaiya woman Āti (from the late Kapilar Akaval — low confidence); his Kuṟaḷ was the only work the academy's plank would bear.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: lineages records the traditions that have claimed him, not an established affiliation.
alt_summary: The Siddha tradition counts Tiruvaḷḷuvar among the Siddhars and ascribes to him works such as the Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam on kāya-siddhi, muppu and vāci; the medicine chapter of the Kuṟaḷ (941–950) is the classical statement of the three humours.
alt_notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the entry and the Kuṟaḷ affiliation dispute.

name: Tiruvaraṅga Perumāḷ Araiyar
summary: Son (or kinsman) of Yāmuna and temple singer (araiyar) of Śrīraṅgam, one of Rāmānuja's five teachers.

name: Tiruvaraṅgattu Amudaṉār
summary: Śrīraṅgam temple functionary who became Rāmānuja's devotee through Kūreśa and composed the Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti.

name: Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai
summary: Teacher of Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, who restored the worship at Āḻvār Tirunagari and handed on the Īṭu and Piḷḷai Lokācārya's works.

name: Tittiri
summary: Eponym of the Taittirīya school. The Purāṇa derives the name from Vaiśampāyana's pupils who became partridges (tittiri) to take up the disgorged Yajus (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.13); the grammatical tradition derives it from a teacher named Tittiri (Pāṇini 4.3.102).
notes: The Pāṇini sūtra number is recalled from memory (moderate).
alt_summary: Eponym of the Taittirīya school; the Purāṇas instead derive the name from partridges (tittiri).

name: Toṇṭada Siddhaliṅga
summary: Fifteenth-century Vīraśaiva ascetic of Yeḍiyūr whose Ṣaṭsthalajñānasārāmṛta renewed the vacana tradition; teacher of a line of renunciant (virakta) masters.

name: Toṇṭadārya
summary: A renunciant Vīraśaiva teacher (parivrājakācārya) to whom the Kaivalyasāra's exposition of the 101 sthalas is ascribed.
notes: Relation to Toṇṭada Siddhaliṅga (tch:tontada-siddhalinga) not settled here.

name: Toṭaka (Toṭakācārya)
notes: Not to be confused with Ānandagiri (Ānandajñāna), the 13th-c. commentator.
summary: Disciple of Śaṅkara, author (tradition) of the Toṭakāṣṭaka in praise of his guru and the Śrutisārasamuddharaṇa; in the tradition's account a devoted servant (called Giri) whose realization came through the guru's grace, first head of Jyotirmaṭh.

name: Trilocana
summary: Naiyāyika named by Vācaspati Miśra as his teacher ('following the path led by my teacher Trilocana', Tātparyaṭīkā on NS 1.1.4); his works are known only from citations.

name: Trilocanaśiva
summary: Twelfth-century South Indian Saiddhāntika, author of the Siddhāntasārāvalī and the Prāyaścittasamuccaya (and reportedly a commentary on the Somaśambhupaddhati — low confidence).
alt_summary: South Indian Saiddhāntika author of the Siddhāntasārāvalī, a verse digest of ritual.

name: Tripurāntaka (Pāśupata)
summary: Pāśupata ascetic eulogised in the Cintra praśasti of 1287 CE for his foundations at Somanātha; the inscription traces his line to one of Lakulīśa's disciples (details to be checked).

name: Triśaṅku
summary: Seer whose declaration after realization, beginning 'I am the mover of the tree', is recorded as 'the Veda-recitation of Triśaṅku' (TU 1.10).

name: Triśikhi
summary: A brāhmaṇa who goes to Āditya's world with questions on body, self and liberation (Triśikhibrāhmaṇa).

name: Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya
summary: An Advaita scholar who, in the tradition's account, debated Madhva for many days at Viṣṇumaṅgala (Kasaragod) and became his disciple. He wrote the Tattvapradīpa, the first commentary on Madhva's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, and the Vāyustuti praising Vāyu's three avatāras; his son Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya wrote the Sumadhvavijaya.

name: Tryambakāditya
summary: Mind-born son of Durvāsas who received the Śaiva secrets, went to a cave named Tryambaka and in turn created a mind-born son; fourteen such siddhas followed (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.111-114). The lineage was known as Tryambaka, 'Terambā' in the local language (7.121).

name: Tulādhāra
summary: A merchant of Vārāṇasī who teaches the ascetic Jājali that the eternal dharma is friendliness and non-injury to all beings (12.253–256).

name: Tulsīdās
summary: In U06's texts: author of the Rāmcaritmānas passages known as the Lakṣmaṇa Gītā and the Vibhīṣaṇa Gītā; he drew on the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (Śiva-Pārvatī frame, Śabarī's nine devotions).

name: Tura Kāvaṣeya
summary: Near the head of the final teacher-line of the BAU, receiving from Prajāpati (BAU 6.5.4).
alt_summary: The first human link in the Agnicayana lineage of ŚB 10.6.5.9, who received it from Prajāpati, who received it from Brahman the self-existent.

name: Turaimaṅkalam Śivaprakāśar
summary: Tamil Vīraśaiva poet who rendered the Prabhuliṅgalīle into Tamil.

name: Turugāhi Rāmaṇṇa
summary: A cowherd śaraṇa and vacanakāra.

name: Ubhaya Bhāratī
summary: Wife of Maṇḍana Miśra who, in the tradition's account, judged the debate between Śaṅkara and her husband by the fading of the garlands they wore, then herself debated Śaṅkara; venerated as Sarasvatī (Śāradā), associated with the Śāradā shrine at Śṛṅgeri.
notes: Known only from hagiography.
alt_summary: Wife of Maṇḍana Miśra in Śaṅkara's hagiographies, learned in the śāstras, who acts as judge of the debate between Maṇḍana and Śaṅkara and is presented as an incarnation of Sarasvatī.

name: Udaṅka Śaulbāyana
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is breath (BAU 4.1.3); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

name: Udayana

tradition.text: Lakṣaṇāvalī dated Śaka 906 = 984 CE by its own closing verse

summary: Called simply 'the Ācārya' by later Naiyāyikas; the great defender of Īśvara (Nyāyakusumāñjali) and of the self against the Buddhists (Ātmatattvaviveka), commentator on Vācaspati (Pariśuddhi) and on Praśastapāda (Kiraṇāvalī), author of the Lakṣaṇāvalī. He joined Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika and is regarded as the bridge between old and new Nyāya.
notes: Hagiographic tradition (low confidence): denied entry to the Jagannātha temple at Puri, he is said to have addressed the Lord: 'Drunk with lordship you disregard me; when the Buddhists come, your existence depends on me.'

name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
summary: Brahmin teacher of the Gautama clan, father of Śvetaketu: teaches the doctrine of being (sat) with the refrain tat tvam asi (ChU 6); questions Yājñavalkya on the thread and the inner controller (BAU 3.7); goes as a pupil to Pravāhaṇa Jaivali (BAU 6.2; ChU 5.3), to Aśvapati Kaikeya (ChU 5.11) and to Citra (KauU 1.1).
notes: ChU 3.11.4 says his father taught him the honey-doctrine as the eldest son.
alt_summary: U02 contribution: in ŚB 11.4.1 he challenges and is defeated by Svaidāyana Śaunaka in a brahmodya; teacher of Yājñavalkya in the vaṃśas.
U04 contribution: tradition identifies him with the Āruṇi who goes to Prajāpati's world to learn renunciation (Āruṇi Upaniṣad); named among paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Bhikṣuka).

name: Uddhava
summary: Kṛṣṇa's cousin, counsellor and devotee; recipient of the Uddhava Gītā. Earlier Kṛṣṇa sent him to Vraja, where he learned from the gopīs' love (Bhāgavata 10.46-47). At the end of the teaching he departs for Badarikāśrama (11.29).

realization_account.text: Having heard the teaching, Uddhava, freed of doubt, went to Badarikāśrama to live it out (Bhāgavata 11.29).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Kṛṣṇa's friend and counsellor, sent to Vraja with Kṛṣṇa's message to the gopīs, whose love in separation he came to revere (BhP 10.46-47); later the recipient of the Uddhava Gītā (BhP 11.7-29, owned by U06).

name: Uddyotakara
summary: Author of the Nyāyavārttika, written to remove the 'ignorance created by bad reasoners' — Dignāga and others, as Vācaspati glosses. The colophon of his work calls him a Pāśupata teacher.
notes: The Pāśupata affiliation rests on the colophon as usually reported (moderate confidence).
alt_summary: Author of the Nyāyavārttika; the colophon of that work calls him 'Pāśupatācārya', a sign of the link between Nyāya and the Pāśupatas (this unit's contribution; the full entry belongs to the Nyāya unit).

name: Uditācārya
summary: Pāśupata teacher of the Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 CE, described as tenth in succession from Kuśika; he installed two liṅgas named after his teachers (Kapileśvara and Upamiteśvara) in a teachers' shrine.

name: Ugrajyoti
summary: Named by Sadyojyoti as his teacher; no work of his survives.

name: Ugraśravas Sauti

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Son of Lomaharṣaṇa, the bard who retells the Mahābhārata, as heard at Janamejaya's sacrifice, to the sages assembled for Śaunaka's twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest (1.1).
alt_summary: Son of Romaharṣaṇa, the Sūta who recites the Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas to Śaunaka and the sages of the Naimiṣa forest (having heard the Bhāgavata from Śuka at Parīkṣit's assembly); he learned all four root saṃhitās (BhP 12.7.6).

name: Ulūka (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others. 'Ulūka' is also a name of the Vaiśeṣika founder Kaṇāda; no identity is implied.

name: Umā (Pārvatī)
summary: Śiva's consort, who questions him on dharma and herself expounds the dharma of women in the Anuśāsana (13.126–134).

name: Umā Haimavatī
summary: The very beautiful woman who appears to Indra in the sky where the yakṣa vanished and tells him it was brahman, in whose victory the gods had been glorifying themselves (Kena 3.12-4.1).
notes: Later Śākta and Śaiva readers identify her with the Goddess Umā/Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat.

name: Umāpati Civācāriyār
summary: Chidambaram priest (Tillai dīkṣitar) turned disciple of Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar; author of eight of the fourteen Meykaṇṭa Śāstras (Civappirakācam, Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ, Viṉāveṇpā, Poṟṟippahṟoṭai, Koṭikkavi, Neñcuviṭu Tūtu, Uṇmai Neṟi Viḷakkam [disputed], Caṅkaṟpa Nirākaraṇam), of the Sanskrit Pauṣkarabhāṣya and Śataratnasaṅgraha, and of Tamil purāṇas of Chidambaram and the saints.

realization_account.text: Excluded by the Tillai priests, he lived at Koṟṟavaṉkuṭi; when the festival flag would not rise he sang the Koṭikkavi and it rose. Naṭarāja is said to have sent him a verse-letter ordering liberation for the outcaste Peṟṟāṉ Cāmpāṉ, and he granted release even to a thorn bush.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Contribution from U08 (Sanskrit Āgama works); Tamil works are U18's.
alt_summary: Cidambaram Saiddhāntika who wrote in Tamil and Sanskrit; in Sanskrit he commented on the Pauṣkarāgama's jñānapāda and compiled the Śataratnasaṅgraha of Āgama verses.

name: Umbeka
notes: Identification with Bhavabhūti is traditional and disputed; being Kumārila's direct pupil is also traditional.
summary: Early commentator on the Ślokavārttika (Tātparyaṭīkā) and on Maṇḍana's Bhāvanāviveka; tradition identifies him with the dramatist Bhavabhūti.

name: Upakosala Kāmalāyana
summary: Pupil of Satyakāma who tended his teacher's fires for twelve years; the fires themselves taught him 'breath is brahman, ka is brahman, kha is brahman' before his teacher taught him the person in the eye (ChU 4.10-15).

name: Upamanyu
summary: The Śaiva sage who, having won Śiva's favour as a child through austerity, gives Kṛṣṇa Pāśupata initiation and teaches him Śaiva doctrine, worship, the pañcākṣara and yoga in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā (ŚiP 7.2) and in LiP 1.107.
alt_summary: A sage devoted to Śiva who teaches Kṛṣṇa the thousand names of Śiva first revealed by Taṇḍi (13.14–17).

name: Upaniṣad Brahmayogin

tradition.text: 18th c.

summary: Advaitin renouncer of Kāñcīpuram who wrote commentaries on all 108 Muktikā Upaniṣads; his maṅgala verses open each text in the South Indian printed collection used here.
alt_summary: 18th-c. Advaitin of Kāñcī who wrote commentaries on all 108 Upaniṣads of the Muktikā canon.

name: Uparicara Vasu
summary: A king devoted to Nārāyaṇa who performed a horse sacrifice without slaughter; when he sided with the gods that 'aja' in the injunction means a goat, he fell, and was restored by his devotion (12.322–324).

name: Upavarṣa
notes: Whether Upavarṣa is the same as the Vṛttikāra quoted by Śabara, or as Bodhāyana (the Vṛttikāra of Rāmānuja's tradition), is disputed.
summary: Called 'the revered (bhagavān) Upavarṣa' by Śabara, who cites his view that the word 'gauḥ' is simply the letters g, au and ḥ; Śaṅkara (BSBh 3.3.53) reports that Upavarṣa in the first treatise deferred the proof of the self to the Śārīraka.
alt_notes: Some later tradition identifies him with Bodhāyana the vṛttikāra; the Kathāsaritsāgara makes him a grammarian of Pāṭaliputra (low confidence).
alt_summary: Ancient commentator on the Mīmāṃsā (and, by Śaṅkara's report, the one who deferred discussion of the self to the Śārīraka); Śaṅkara calls him 'bhagavān Upavarṣa' (BSBh 1.3.28; 3.3.53).

name: Upendra Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Puttige maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Uriliṅgadēva
summary: A śaraṇa teacher whose disciple and successor Uriliṅgapeddi came from the margins of society.

name: Uriliṅgapeddi
summary: A former thief of low-caste birth who became Uriliṅgadēva's disciple, successor and a vacanakāra.

name: Uruttirapacupati Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who stood in a tank day and night reciting the Śrī Rudram until Śiva granted him release.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who stood in a tank day and night reciting the Śrī Rudram until Śiva granted him release.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Urvaśī
summary: The apsaras whose dialogue with King Purūravas forms RV 10.95; ṛṣikā of her verses.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Uśanas (Śukra)
summary: Preceptor of the asuras, who questions Vṛtra (12.270); 'among poets I am Uśanas' (BhG 10.37).

name: Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa
summary: Asks Yājñavalkya to explain the brahman that is immediate and direct, the self within all (BAU 3.4, as Uṣasta); in ChU 1.10-11 he survives a famine among the Kurus by eating an elephant-keeper's leftover beans but refuses the leftover water, and then instructs priests on the deities of the chant.
notes: Identity of the BAU Uṣasta and the ChU Uṣasti is assumed from the shared patronymic (moderate).

name: Utpala Vaiṣṇava
notes: Quotations noted in the introduction to the JS edition (local e-text).
summary: Kashmirian Vaiṣṇava author of the Spandapradīpikā, a commentary on the Spandakārikā that quotes Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (the Jayākhya, the Ahirbudhnya), furnishing an early date-limit for them.
alt_summary: A Kashmiri Vaiṣṇava (Pāñcarātra) scholar who wrote the Spandapradīpikā, a commentary on the Spandakārikā ascribing it to Kallaṭa - an instance of Vaiṣṇava engagement with Spanda.

name: Utpaladeva
summary: Son of Udayākara (ĪPK 4.18) and disciple of Somānanda; systematized the Pratyabhijñā in the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with a short and a long commentary, wrote the Siddhitrayī and the devotional hymns of the Śivastotrāvalī.

realization_account.text: His hymns present devotion as the relish of an identity with Śiva already recognized.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Uttamūr Vīrarāghavācārya
summary: 20th-century Vaṭakalai scholar and editor-commentator of Viśiṣṭādvaita works (post-1800; recorded as recent).

name: Uvaṭa
summary: Son of Vajraṭa of Ānandapura; wrote at Avantī under King Bhoja a commentary (Mantrabhāṣya) on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā and a commentary on the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya.
alt_summary: Commentator on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā and on the Ṛgveda and Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhyas.

name: Uyyakkoṇḍār
summary: Disciple of Nāthamuni and teacher of Maṇakkāl Nambi; the tradition says he preferred the Lord's service to learning yoga.

name: Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tirukkaṭavūr
summary: Author of the Tirukkaḷiṟṟuppaṭiyār (c. 1177), a commentary in verse on the Tiruvuntiyār; in the teaching line of the Tiruviyalūr author (through Āḷuṭaiya Tēvanāyaṉār — low confidence).

name: Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tiruviyalūr
summary: Author of the Tiruvuntiyār (c. 1147), earliest of the Meykaṇṭa Śāstras.

name: Vācaspati Miśra

scholarly.text: 9th or 10th c. CE (Nyāyasūcīnibandha dated 898 of an era read as Vikrama = 841 CE or Śaka = 976 CE)

summary: Polymath of Mithilā who commented on every Vedic school; for Nyāya he wrote the Tātparyaṭīkā — rescuing Uddyotakara's 'aged cows' from the mire of bad commentaries — and the Nyāyasūcīnibandha, which fixed the sūtra text. He reads 'avyapadeśya' and 'vyavasāyātmaka' in NS 1.1.4 as indeterminate and determinate perception, following his teacher Trilocana.
notes: His non-Nyāya works belong to U09, U10, U12 and U13.
alt_summary: (Yoga unit contribution) Author of the Tattvavaiśāradī, the standard sub-commentary on Vyāsa's Yoga-bhāṣya; a polymath who also commented on Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsā and Advaita texts.
U09 contribution: author of the Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī, the standard later commentary on the SK; the Yuktidīpikā's colophon also names him, an ascription scholars reject.
Polymath of Mithilā who commented on the works of six schools; his Bhāmatī on Śaṅkara's BSBh founded the Bhāmatī line of Advaita, and his lost Tattvasamīkṣā commented on Maṇḍana's Brahmasiddhi.
Polymath commentator; for Mīmāṃsā he wrote the Nyāyakaṇikā on Maṇḍana's Vidhiviveka and the Tattvabindu on sentence meaning (defending abhihitānvaya).

name: Vāddhali
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). The reading of the name in the e-text is uncertain.

name: Vādikesari Aḻagiya Maṇavāḷa Jīyar
summary: Teṅkalai commentator credited with the Paṉṉīrāyirappaṭi ('Twelve Thousand') on the Tiruvāymoḻi.

name: Vādirāja Tīrtha

tradition.text: the tradition gives him 120 years, 1480–1600

realization_account.text: The tradition regards Vādirāja as a ṛju soul — one of the class destined for the highest offices — and as a future Vāyu (bhāvi-samīra).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Pontiff of the Sode maṭha (Uḍupi), worshipper of Hayagrīva, poet and polemicist: author of the Yuktimallikā, the Tīrthaprabandha, the Rukmiṇīśavijaya and a commentary on the Mahābhārata, and of Kannada songs signed 'Hayavadana'. The tradition credits him with making the Uḍupi paryāya of Kṛṣṇa worship a two-year turn.
notes: The 1522 start of the two-year paryāya and the 'bhāvi-samīra' belief are recalled at moderate/low confidence.

name: Vaiśampāyana

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Vyāsa's disciple who recites the Mahābhārata to king Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice; the narrator of the Nārāyaṇīya to Janamejaya.
alt_summary: Vyāsa's pupil who received the Yajurveda and made twenty-seven branches of it (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.1); teacher of Yājñavalkya, whose disgorged Yajus the other pupils took up as partridges (tittiri) — hence the Taittirīyas; narrator of the Mahābhārata to Janamejaya.
Teacher of the Black Yajurveda and, in the Purāṇic story, the teacher with whom Yājñavalkya quarrelled.

name: Vaiśravaṇa (Vālakhilya)
summary: Questioner in the Pāśupatabrahma Upaniṣad, called a son of Brahmā and a Vālakhilya; not the Kubera of the Purāṇas as far as the text says.

name: Vājaśravasa (father of Naciketas)
alt_names: Uśan (some read uśan in KU 1.1.1 as a name)
summary: Naciketas's father, who in the Viśvajit sacrifice gives away all his possessions, offering worn-out cows; in anger he gives his son to Death (KU 1.1.1-4). Yama calls him Auddālaki Āruṇi (KU 1.1.11) and Naciketas calls him Gautama (KU 1.1.10).
notes: Whether he is the Uddālaka Āruṇi of ChU/BAU is not settled; KU 1.1.11 calls him Auddālaki ('son of Uddālaka').

name: Vāc Āmbhṛṇī
summary: Vāc, daughter of the seer Ambhṛṇa, the ṛṣikā of RV 10.125, in which Speech proclaims herself the queen and self of all, moving with the gods, the power by which beings eat, see, breathe and hear, who makes whom she loves a brahman and a seer.

realization_account.text: The Anukramaṇī gives the deity of her hymn as 'ātman', the seer praising herself as the self of all; later commentary (Sāyaṇa) presents her as a knower of Brahman who spoke from identity with it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). Sāyaṇa's characterization recalled with moderate confidence.

name: Vallabhācārya (Śrī Vallabha, Mahāprabhujī)
summary: Founder of Śuddhādvaita and the Puṣṭimārga; author of the Aṇubhāṣya, Tattvārthadīpanibandha, Subodhinī and the sixteen short works; established the worship of Śrīnāthjī at Govardhana and taught the brahmasambandha initiation.

realization_account.text: Born at Campāraṇya to the Telugu Brahmin Lakṣmaṇa Bhaṭṭa and Illammā; won a debate at the Vijayanagara court and was honoured as ācārya; travelled India three times (the 84 'seats', baiṭhak, mark where he expounded the Bhāgavata); at midnight on Śrāvaṇa śukla ekādaśī at Gokul, Kṛṣṇa appeared and gave him the brahmasambandha, and the next day he initiated Dāmodaradās Harsānī; at the end he took renunciation and entered the Ganges at Kāśī (1531), leaving the Śikṣāślokī as his last instruction.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Founder of the Puṣṭimārga; counts the Gītā among the four authorities and expounds its meaning in the first section of his Tattvārthadīpanibandha.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Vālmīki

tradition.text: Tretā yuga, contemporary of Rāma

summary: The first poet (ādikavi), author of the Rāmāyaṇa; told Rāma's story by Nārada (1.1), he utters the first śloka in grief at a hunter's killing of a krauñca bird (1.2.15–18) and teaches the poem to Kuśa and Lava.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: the traditional author of the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha / Mokṣopāya, who opens it by telling Bharadvāja that Brahmā sent him to complete a Rāmāyaṇa of liberation (MU 1.1).
Counted among the eighteen Siddhars in the popular Tamil list, with a samādhi place at Eṭṭukkuṭi.
places: Eṭṭukkuṭi — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; whether the list intends the epic poet or a Tamil namesake is not settled. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Vālmīki (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others. No identification with the poet of the Rāmāyaṇa is implied.

name: Vāmadeva

realization_account.text: AU 2.1.5-6: while still in the womb he knew the births of the gods; knowing thus, on the body's breaking he rose up and became immortal.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The Ṛgvedic seer who, seeing that he was brahman, declared 'I was Manu, I was the sun' (BAU 1.4.10) and who, lying in the womb, knew all the births of the gods (AU 2.1.5, quoting RV 4.27.1).
alt_summary: Vāmadeva Gautama, seer of Ṛgveda book 4. His verses 'I was Manu and I the Sun' (4.26.1) and 'while still in the womb I knew all the births of the gods' (4.27.1) are cited in the Upaniṣads as the words of one who realized himself as all (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10; Aitareya 2.5).
U04 contribution: model of the 'ant's path' of gradual liberation through births (Varāha 4.38–42) and named among the paramahaṃsas (Bhikṣuka).
Author of the Janmamaraṇavicāra on birth and death.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The Anukramaṇī allows Indra (or the self, ātman) as speaker/deity of 4.26.1–3.

name: Vāmana (co-author of the Kāśikā)
summary: Co-author of the Kāśikāvṛtti; distinct from Vāmana the theorist of poetics.

name: Vāmana Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Shirur maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Vāmanadatta
summary: Author of the Svabodhodayamañjarī.

name: Vāmaśakti

scholarly.text: 12th c. (inscriptions name more than one Vāmaśakti)

summary: Kālāmukha pontiff of the Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāve, praised in 12th-c. inscriptions for learning and influence (details to be checked).

name: Varadarāja (Kṛṣṇadāsa)
summary: Author of a second Śivasūtravārttika, following Kṣemarāja.

name: Varadarāja (grammarian)
summary: Pupil of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita; author of the Laghu- and Madhya-siddhāntakaumudī.

name: Varadarāja (commentator on the Nayaviveka)
summary: Author of the Nayavivekadīpikā on Bhavanātha's Nayaviveka.

name: Varadarāja
summary: Author of the Tārkikarakṣā, a Nyāya manual with auto-commentary.

name: Varāha (the Boar avatāra)
summary: Viṣṇu's boar form, who appears to Ṛbhu after twelve divine years of austerity and teaches him the 96 tattvas and non-dual knowledge (Varāha 1–3).

name: Vardhamāna Upādhyāya
summary: Son of Gaṅgeśa; wrote Prakāśa commentaries on Udayana's works (Kusumāñjali, Kiraṇāvalī) and on his father's Tattvacintāmaṇi.

name: Vareṇya
summary: The king to whom Gajānana teaches the Gaṇeśa Gītā; in the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa Gaṇeśa had been born in his house.

name: Varṣāditya
summary: Son of Saṅgamāditya in Somānanda's lineage (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.119).

name: Vārṣagaṇya
alt_names: Vṛṣagaṇa (a related name in the Yuktidīpikā and in the Chinese Life of Vasubandhu)
summary: Early Sāṃkhya teacher. The Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 3.53) cites him by name: there is no difference at the root, since there is no difference of form, separation or kind. The Yuktidīpikā (on SK 22) reports his views that mahat arises directly from pradhāna and that the subtle elements are cumulative; it lists him among the teachers before Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71). Some scholars ascribe the Ṣaṣṭitantra to him.

name: Vārṣyāyaṇi
summary: Teacher cited by Yāska for the six modifications of being: is born, exists, changes, grows, declines, perishes (Nirukta 1.2).

name: Varuṇa (as teacher)
summary: The god Varuṇa as father-teacher of Bhṛgu: gives the definition of brahman as that from which beings are born, by which they live and into which they enter, and sends him to seek it by tapas (TU 3.1).

name: Varuṇaśiva
summary: Author of the Varuṇapaddhati, a Siddhānta ritual manual.

name: Vasiṣṭha
summary: In U06's texts: the family priest of the Ikṣvākus who, at Viśvāmitra's request, teaches the despondent young Rāma the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha / Mokṣopāya; within it he recounts his own learning from Brahmā, from the crow Bhuśuṇḍa and from Śiva.
alt_summary: Vasiṣṭha Maitrāvaruṇi, seer of Ṛgveda book 7: the hymns to Varuṇa in which he searches his conscience (7.86–89), the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya verse (7.59.12), the account of his birth from Mitra-Varuṇa and Urvaśī, 'born from mind' (7.33.11), and the victory of King Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings (7.18, 7.33). The tradition makes him the Ikṣvāku family priest and teacher of Rāma, rival and finally acknowledger of Viśvāmitra.

Ancient seer, family priest of the Ikṣvākus; in the Mokṣadharma he teaches Karāla Janaka the Sāṃkhya-Yoga doctrine of the 24 principles, the 25th and the 26th (12.291–296); in the Rāmāyaṇa he is Rāma's preceptor.
U02 contribution: the Vedic seer to whom the Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra is ascribed.

realization_account.text: Varuṇa took Vasiṣṭha into his boat and made him a seer by his powers (RV 7.88.3–4).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Ṛgveda)

notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). Parāśara is his grandson (through Śakti) in the tradition; 'students' here records that line of descent.
alt_notes: His teaching in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha is covered by U06.

name: Vāsudeva Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti on the whole Mīmāṃsā Sūtra.

name: Vāsudeva Sārvabhauma
summary: Navadvīpa scholar who, on the tradition's account, studied in Mithilā and brought the Tattvacintāmaṇi to Navadvīpa (by memory, since copying was not permitted); teacher of Raghunātha Śiromaṇi in the same account; later a court scholar at Puri, where the Gauḍīya hagiographies place his meeting with Caitanya.
notes: Most details are the tradition's account (low confidence).

name: Vāsudevāśrama
summary: Author of the Yatidharmaprakāśa, a digest of the renouncer's rules.

name: Vasugupta
summary: The Kashmiri teacher to whom the Śiva Sūtras were revealed and from whom the Spanda tradition descends; Kṣemarāja also makes him the author of the Spandakārikā.

realization_account.text: Paramaśiva, wishing the secret tradition not to be cut off, favoured him in a dream and told him of a secret on a great rock on Mahādeva mountain; on waking he found the rock, which turned over at the touch of his hand, and received the sūtras (Kṣemarāja). In Bhāskara's account the sūtras appeared to him 'by a siddha's command'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Vaṭakku Tiruvīti Piḷḷai
summary: Disciple of Nampiḷḷai who wrote down his teacher's lectures as the Īṭu Muppattāṟāyirappaṭi; father of Piḷḷai Lokācārya and Aḻagiya Maṇavāḷa Perumāḷ Nāyaṉār.

name: The Vātaraśana munis (seven wind-girdled sages)
summary: The seven 'wind-girdled' silent sages to whom the verses of the Keśin hymn (RV 10.136) are ascribed one each: Jūti, Vātajūti, Viprajūti, Vṛṣāṇaka, Karikrata, Etaśa and Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). A group entry.

name: Vātsyāyana
summary: Author of the Nyāyabhāṣya, the first extant commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra; criticized by Dignāga. Not to be identified (on the scholarly account) with Vātsyāyana Mallanāga of the Kāmasūtra.

name: Vātsyāyana Mallanāga
summary: Author of the Kāmasūtra; distinct from Vātsyāyana Pakṣilasvāmin of the Nyāyabhāṣya (tch:vatsyayana).

name: Vāyilā Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He worshipped Śiva in a temple built within his mind, with love as the offering.

realization_account.text: He worshipped Śiva in a temple built within his mind, with love as the offering.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Vedānta Deśika
summary: Veṅkaṭanātha of Tūppul near Kāñcī, poet, logician and theologian; the Vaṭakalai regard him as their doctrinal source. He wrote over a hundred works in Sanskrit, Maṇipravāḷa and Tamil — the Rahasyatrayasāra, Tattvamuktākalāpa, Śatadūṣaṇī, Nyāyasiddhāñjana, Nyāyapariśuddhi, Seśvaramīmāṃsā, Pādukāsahasra, Saṅkalpasūryodaya and many hymns — and lived through the sack of Śrīraṅgam.

realization_account.text: The tradition holds him an incarnation of the bell of Veṅkaṭeśvara; the titles Vedāntācārya and Sarvatantrasvatantra were conferred on him by Raṅganātha and Raṅganāyakī; Hayagrīva, whose mantra he received from Garuḍa, granted him knowledge; he declined royal patronage.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Contribution from U08.
alt_summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (Veṅkaṭanātha) whose Pāñcarātrarakṣā defends and expounds the Pāñcarātra.
Author of the Tātparyacandrikā on Rāmānuja's Gītābhāṣya.
For Mīmāṃsā: author of the Seśvaramīmāṃsā, a theistic commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, and the Mīmāṃsāpādukā.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Vena Bhārgava
summary: Seer of the Vena hymn RV 10.123; in the Atharvaveda (2.1) and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (32.8) Vena is the seer who 'saw that highest, hidden in secret, in which all becomes one nest'.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Veṅkaṭamādhava
summary: Author of the Ṛgarthadīpikā, a concise commentary on the whole Ṛgveda.

name: Vibhīṣaṇa
summary: Rāvaṇa's righteous brother who took refuge with Rāma; the Rāmcaritmānas's 'chariot of dharma' teaching is addressed to him.
alt_summary: Rāvaṇa's brother who leaves him and takes refuge with Rāma; Rāma accepts him with the vow to protect all who seek refuge (6.18.33).

name: Vicakhnu
summary: A king who, pitying the animals at a sacrifice, proclaims non-violence as the highest dharma (12.257).

name: Vidagdha Śākalya
summary: The last and most aggressive challenger at Janaka's court: questions Yājñavalkya on the number of gods and the persons and their abodes; unable to answer the question about the person of the Upaniṣads, his head shatters (BAU 3.9). In BAU 4.1.7 he holds that brahman is the heart.
alt_summary: Yājñavalkya's opponent at Janaka's court, who asks 'how many gods?' and loses his head (ŚB 11.6.3; BĀU 3.9).

name: Videgha Māthava
summary: King who carried Agni Vaiśvānara in his mouth eastward to the Sadānīrā with his priest Gotama Rāhūgaṇa (ŚB 1.4.1.10–17).

name: Vidura

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: An embodiment of Dharma; his death by yoga, entering Yudhiṣṭhira, is narrated at 15.33.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account
