summary: Half-brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, born of a śūdra woman; Dharma incarnate through Māṇḍavya's curse (1.100.28). He counsels Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Viduranīti, 5.33–40) and, declaring that as one born of a śūdra womb he will not speak beyond this, calls Sanatsujāta to teach the higher knowledge (5.41.5); consoles him after the war (11.2–7); dies in the forest by entering Yudhiṣṭhira's body limb by limb and breath by breath (15.33.25).

name: Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha
summary: Jayatīrtha's successor; the tradition dates the later division of the lines (towards the Uttarādi, Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas) from his disciples.

name: Vidyāguru
summary: Number 18 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Vidyāraṇya
notes: Identity with the minister Mādhava is the tradition's; scholars debate it.
summary: Pontiff of Śṛṅgeri (d. 1386), author of the Pañcadaśī, the Jīvanmuktiviveka, the Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha and the Anubhūtiprakāśa; in the tradition identified with Mādhava, minister of the founders of Vijayanagara and brother of Sāyaṇa, and so credited with the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha and the Śaṅkaradigvijaya.
alt_notes: The identification of Mādhava with the monk Vidyāraṇya is traditional and disputed; registry id used.
alt_summary: For Mīmāṃsā: Mādhava, minister and family preceptor of King Bukka of Vijayanagara, composed the Jaiminīya-nyāya-mālā with its prose Vistara, a verse digest of all the adhikaraṇas.
U04 contribution: the Jīvanmuktiviveka builds its account of the knower's renunciation and liberation while living on the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads and the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

In U06's context: his Jīvanmuktiviveka builds its account of liberation while living largely on quotations from the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (e.g. the weakening of latent tendencies and the dissolution of mind).
U02 contribution: tradition identifies the Vijayanagara scholar-minister Mādhava, author of the Parāśaramādhavīya and Kālanirṇaya, with Vidyāraṇya after renunciation; the identification is debated.

name: Vidyāśaṅkara (Vidyātīrtha)
summary: Śṛṅgeri pontiff of the 14th c., remembered in the Śṛṅgeri tradition as Vidyāraṇya's teacher; the Vidyāśaṅkara temple at Śṛṅgeri commemorates him.

name: Vijayadhvaja Tīrtha
summary: Pontiff of the Pejavara maṭha (Uḍupi) and author of the Padaratnāvalī, the standard Mādhva commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

name: Vijayīndra Tīrtha
summary: Pontiff at Kumbhakonam, trained by Vyāsatīrtha; a prolific polemicist (the tradition credits him with over a hundred works) who answered Appayya Dīkṣita's critiques of Madhva and commented on the Nyāyāmṛta.

name: Vijñānabhikṣu

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: (Yoga unit contribution) Vedāntin of 'non-separation' (avibhāga) who commented on Yoga, Sāṃkhya and the Brahma Sūtra. In the Yogavārttika he reads Yoga theistically, calls the bhāṣya 'the essence of all the Veda', argues for the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi (YV 1.7), gives his own account of the samprajñāta samādhis (YV 1.17) and holds that knowledge of the Supreme Lord is the swift cause of liberation (YV 1.51).
alt_summary: Commentator who revived Sāṃkhya-Yoga in a theistic, Vedānta-reconciling form: his Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, his manual Sāṃkhyasāra, and his Yogavārttika on the Yoga Bhāṣya; he also wrote a Vedānta commentary on the Brahma Sūtra (Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣya).

16th-c. Vārāṇasī scholar; in his Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣya he interprets the Brahma Sūtras as non-separation (avibhāga) of souls and prakṛti from Brahman — a difference-and-non-difference Vedānta integrating Sāṃkhya-Yoga and rejecting Śaṅkara's māyāvāda (which he calls a crypto-Buddhism, citing the Padma Purāṇa).

name: Vijñāneśvara
summary: Author of the Mitākṣarā at the court of Vikramāditya VI of Kalyāṇa.

name: Vikhanas

realization_account.text: Vikhanas is Nārāyaṇa himself (or the four-faced Brahmā born from him), so that his Sūtra is the first and best of sūtras.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Checked in sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/ebhAratI-sampat/AgamaH/vaikhAnasam/bhRgumaharShiH/kriyAdhikAraH.md (Kriyādhikāra, eBhāratī/NSU Tirupati) and sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/4_rellit/vaisn/srinivasamakhi_vedantadesika_dasavidhahetunirupana.md (GRETIL, input by U. Hüsken).
summary: Founding sage of the Vaikhānasas and author of their Sūtra; the tradition identifies him with Brahmā born of Nārāyaṇa, or with Nārāyaṇa himself, and salutes him as the one 'whose father is Nārāyaṇa, whose mother is Haripriyā, whose disciples are Bhṛgu and the other sages' (Kriyādhikāra 1.1).

name: Vimalaśiva
notes: From the Muktabodha catalogue description (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/muktabodha_metadata.json (Muktabodha catalogue descriptions)).
summary: Saiddhāntika author of the Vimalāvatī on ritual, who took a lifelong vow of residence in Vārāṇasī.

name: Vimuktātman
summary: Author of the Iṣṭasiddhi, defending indescribable ignorance and the self as pure experience.

name: Vindhyavāsin
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher whose distinctive views the Yuktidīpikā records: from mahat arise six non-specifics (ahaṃkāra and the five subtle elements); the organs are eleven and all-pervading; the functions of saṅkalpa, abhimāna and adhyavasāya are one; there is no subtle body — birth is the organs' functioning at the seed-place and death its abandonment; even the supreme sage's knowledge is acquired, not innate. Kumārila reports that he did not accept an intermediate body. Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu tells that the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa, pupil of Vṛṣagaṇa, defeated Vasubandhu's teacher Buddhamitra in debate before a king at Ayodhyā.
notes: Kumārila's report (Ślokavārttika, Ātmavāda section) and the Chinese biography details are recalled, not checked.

name: Vīrabhadra (Vīracandra)
summary: Son of Nityānanda and leader of his line at Khaḍadaha.

name: Viṟaṉmiṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A devotee who declared Cuntarar and even the Lord 'outside' the fold when Cuntarar passed the assembled devotees at Tiruvārūr without honouring them; this led Śiva to give Cuntarar the first line of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai.

realization_account.text: A devotee who declared Cuntarar and even the Lord 'outside' the fold when Cuntarar passed the assembled devotees at Tiruvārūr without honouring them; this led Śiva to give Cuntarar the first line of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Virocana
summary: Lord of the asuras who studies with Prajāpati alongside Indra, concludes that the body is the self and teaches the asuras this 'doctrine of the asuras' (ChU 8.8.4-5).

name: Virūpākṣanātha
summary: Author of the Virūpākṣapañcāśikā, probably South Indian.

name: Viṣṇu Tīrtha (Sode)
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Sode maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa. He was Madhva's younger brother; the tradition also derives the Subrahmaṇya maṭha from him and remembers his austerities.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Viṣṇucitta (Engaḷāḻvāṉ)
summary: Disciple of Rāmānuja and Piḷḷāṉ, author of the Viṣṇucittīya on the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, and teacher of Naḍādūr Ammāḷ in the line the Vaṭakalai follow. (Not to be confused with Periyāḻvār, also called Viṣṇucitta.)
alt_summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava author of the Viṣṇucittīya commentary on the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (dating not checked in this sweep).

name: Viṣṇusvāmin
summary: Vaiṣṇava teacher of uncertain date whom the Vallabha tradition counts as the founder of the Rudra Sampradāya in which Vallabha stands; cited by Śrīdhara Svāmin. His own works are lost.
notes: Tradition's account; the historical link to Vallabha is contested. No lineage id exists for a separate Viṣṇusvāmī school, so the tradition's attribution to the Puṣṭimārga is recorded.

name: Viśvakarman Bhauvana
summary: Seer (and deity) of the Viśvakarman hymns RV 10.81–82.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Viśvāmitra
summary: In U06's texts: the sage whose request for Rāma's help occasions the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and who is present throughout Vasiṣṭha's teaching.
alt_summary: Viśvāmitra Gāthina of the Kuśika clan, seer of Ṛgveda book 3, including the Gāyatrī (3.62.10) and the dialogue in which the rivers Vipāś and Śutudrī yield to his words (3.33; the rivers themselves are counted as seers of their verses). Priest of King Sudās in book 3; the tradition makes him the rival of Vasiṣṭha and, in the epics, a king who became a brahmarṣi through tapas.

Royal sage who takes the young Rāma to protect his sacrifice and teaches him (Bālakāṇḍa); in the Āpaddharma, during a famine, he takes a dog's haunch from an outcaste, arguing the case for survival (12.139).

realization_account.text: Born a kṣatriya king (son of Gādhi), he attained the status of brahmarṣi by long tapas and was at last acknowledged by Vasiṣṭha (Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (epic)

notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The Rāmāyaṇa episode is recalled at book level only.

name: Viśvanātha Cakravartin
summary: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Sārārthavarṣiṇī on the Gītā.

name: Viśvanātha Cakravartin
summary: Theologian of Vṛndāvana (late 17th–early 18th c.): commentaries on the Bhāgavata, Gītā and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi; Mādhuryakādambinī and Rāgavartmacandrikā on the stages and spontaneous devotion; defender of parakīyā.

name: Viśvanātha Nyāyapañcānana

scholarly.text: first half of the 17th c. CE

summary: Bengali Naiyāyika, author of the Bhāṣāpariccheda (Kārikāvalī) with its auto-commentary the Siddhāntamuktāvalī — opening with a salutation to Kṛṣṇa — and of a Nyāyasūtravṛtti.

name: Viśvārādhya
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Kāśī pīṭha (Jaṅgamavāḍī maṭha, Vārāṇasī).

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Emergence from the Viśvanātha liṅga at Kāśī and seat name Jñāna-siṃhāsana: low confidence.

name: Viśvarūpa
summary: Author of the Bālakrīḍā on Yājñavalkya; tradition identifies him with Sureśvara (tch:suresvara), which scholars doubt.

name: Viśvavārā Ātreyī
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 5.28, a hymn to Agni kindled at dawn as she offers to the gods.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Viśvāvasu
summary: A Gandharva, versed in Vedānta, who puts twenty-four questions and a twenty-fifth on reasoning to Yājñavalkya (12.306.27).

name: Viśveśa Tīrtha
summary: Pontiff of the Pejavara maṭha (Uḍupi) in the 20th and early 21st centuries, who presided over the Uḍupi Kṛṣṇa paryāya five times.

name: Viṭṭhalanātha (Gusāṃījī)
summary: Vallabha's younger son and the organiser of the Puṣṭimārga: completed the Aṇubhāṣya, wrote the Vidvanmaṇḍana and Śṛṅgārarasamaṇḍana, elaborated the eightfold daily service (aṣṭayāma sevā), founded the aṣṭachāp of eight poet-singers and emphasised Rādhā (Svāminī); his seven sons founded the seven 'houses'.

name: Vivasvat (the Sun)
summary: The first recipient of the imperishable yoga from Kṛṣṇa, who passed it to Manu (BhG 4.1).

name: Vivekananda
summary: In U06's context (recent reception): he often quoted the Avadhūta Gītā and the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā; Ramakrishna is remembered as having had him read the Aṣṭāvakra Saṃhitā.

name: Voḍhu
summary: One of the seven great sages, sons of Brahmā, in the verse quoted by Gauḍapāda on SK 1 (Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, Āsuri, Kapila, Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha).

name: Vopadeva
summary: Grammarian (Mugdhabodha) who wrote works on the Bhāgavata (the Muktāphala and the Harilīlāmṛta, the latter a summary of its contents); opponents of the Bhāgavata's status later claimed he composed the Bhāgavata itself, a claim its defenders reject (dsp:which-bhagavata-is-the-mahapurana).

name: Vṛndāvana Dāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Disciple of Nityānanda and author of the Caitanya Bhāgavata, called the Vyāsa of Caitanya's play.

name: Vṛtra
summary: The defeated asura whose equanimity is praised and who is taught by Sanatkumāra about Viṣṇu and the six colours of beings (12.270–271).

name: the Vṛttikāra (cited by Śabara)
notes: Identity disputed (Upavarṣa? Bodhāyana? Bhavadāsa?). Scholarly literature calls this passage the Vṛttikāragrantha.
summary: An earlier commentator whose exposition Śabara reproduces on MS 1.1.3–5 ('the Vṛttikāra explained this passage otherwise'): definitions of perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation and absence as means of knowledge, a refutation of the views that cognitions have no object and that all is empty, and a proof of the self.

name: Vyāḍi
summary: Ancient grammarian; the Vikṛtivallī on the eight modified recitations is ascribed to him.
notes: Ascription of the Vikṛtivallī recalled with low confidence.
alt_summary: Early grammarian, author by tradition of the lost Saṃgraha cited by Patañjali; the Vikṛtivallī on the modified recitations is also ascribed to him (low confidence).

name: Vyāghrapāda (Viyākkiramar, Puliyūr muṉi)
summary: The 'tiger-footed' sage who with Patañjali worshipped the Dance at Chidambaram (Puliyūr); named in TM 67 among Nandi's eight disciples.

name: Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: Presented as a seer who knows past, present and future, able to grant divine sight and to foresee the war's outcome; identified with the earlier Apāntaratamas (12.337.54).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Son of Parāśara and Satyavatī, in the tradition the arranger of the Vedas and author of the Mahābhārata; grandfather of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas; gives Sañjaya divine sight, teaches his son Śuka (12.224–247), and tells that in a former birth he was Apāntaratamas, the Veda-teacher born of Nārāyaṇa's word, reborn in Vasiṣṭha's line (12.337.38–54). The Gītā names him among those who proclaim Kṛṣṇa supreme (10.13) and 'among sages I am Vyāsa' (10.37).
alt_summary: Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, son of Parāśara, called Veda-vyāsa, 'arranger of the Veda': seeing the decline of the ages, he divided the one Veda into four for the continuity of the sacrifice and taught the Ṛg to Paila, the Sāma to Jaimini, the Yajus to Vaiśampāyana and the Atharva to Sumantu, who branched them into śākhās through their pupils (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.19–23; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4).

(Yoga unit contribution) For the Yoga tradition, the author of the Yogabhāṣya, the oldest commentary on the Yoga Sūtra. Vijñānabhikṣu calls him Vedavyāsa and Bādarāyaṇa and says he spoke 'the essence of all the Veda under the guise of the Yoga-bhāṣya'; Nārāyaṇatīrtha also names the bhāṣyakāra Bādarāyaṇa. Modern scholars doubt the identification; several ascribe the bhāṣya to Patañjali himself.

In the Purāṇic tradition the compiler of the eighteen Purāṇas (and Upapurāṇas through his disciples, KūP 1.1.280), who gave the Purāṇa-saṃhitā to his sūta disciple Romaharṣaṇa (VP 3.6.15-16) and the Bhāgavata to his son Śuka.

In U06's texts: the traditional author of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Uddhava and Kapila Gītās), the Devī Bhāgavata (Devī Gītā), the Kūrma Purāṇa and, as part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; the speaker of the Vyāsa Gītā.

In the Vedānta tradition, author of the Brahma Sūtras (as Bādarāyaṇa) and of the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas; in the Advaita guru-paramparā, son and disciple of Parāśara and teacher of his son Śuka; the Śaṅkaradigvijaya has him appear to Śaṅkara at Kāśī, test his commentary and extend his life.
U04 contribution: asks Śiva to instruct Śuka (Śukarahasya) and answers Śuka on Rudra (Rudrahṛdaya).
notes: U01 contribution: Vyāsa as divider of the Veda. Other units contribute Vyāsa as author of the Mahābhārata, Brahma Sūtras (as Bādarāyaṇa in some traditions) and Purāṇas.

name: Vyāsa Rāmācārya
summary: Mādhva scholar who wrote the Nyāyāmṛta-taraṅgiṇī defending Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta against Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi.
notes: A story that he first studied Advaita under Madhusūdana before refuting him circulates in modern accounts — low confidence, not verified.

name: Vyāsatīrtha

realization_account.text: The tradition regards Vyāsatīrtha as a rebirth of Prahlāda (after Bāhlīka of the Mahābhārata), later reborn as Rāghavendra; it tells that he sat on the Vijayanagara throne to avert an inauspicious conjunction (kuhu-yoga) that threatened the king, and that he installed 732 images of Hanumān.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The foremost dialectician of Dvaita and rājaguru of the Vijayanagara court (under Kṛṣṇadevarāya). His Nyāyāmṛta, Tarkatāṇḍava and Tātparyacandrikā ('the three of Vyāsa') attack Advaita, Navya-Nyāya and rival readings of the Brahmasūtras; the Nyāyāmṛta drew Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi in reply. A composer of Kannada songs, he was the teacher of the Haridāsas Purandara Dāsa and Kanaka Dāsa, and of Vijayīndra Tīrtha. His brindāvana is at Nava Brindāvana near Hampi.

name: Vyomaśiva

scholarly.text: c. 10th c. CE (some place him earlier)

summary: Author of the Vyomavatī, the oldest extant commentary on the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha; a Śaiva ācārya.

name: Yādavaprakāśa
summary: Advaita-leaning teacher of Kāñcīpuram under whom Rāmānuja first studied; taught svābhāvika bhedābheda (Brahman itself becomes Īśvara, souls and matter). His Brahma Sūtra commentary is lost; the Yatidharmasamuccaya and the lexicon Vaijayantī are attributed to him.

realization_account.text: Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography (Guruparamparāprabhāva) says he disagreed with Rāmānuja's readings, plotted against him on a pilgrimage, and later became his disciple as the renouncer Govinda Jīyar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Śrīvaiṣṇava)

tradition.text: 11th c.

alt_summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin, remembered in Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition as Rāmānuja's first teacher, later a tridaṇḍin renouncer; author of the Yatidharmasamuccaya on renouncers' rules.

Kāñcī teacher of bhedābheda Vedānta under whom Rāmānuja first studied; the tradition says they disagreed over Upaniṣadic readings and that he later became Rāmānuja's disciple as the renouncer Govinda Jīyar. (U16 owns his entry; this is U14's contribution.)

name: Yadu
summary: Ancestor-king of the Yādavas who questions a carefree young avadhūta brāhmaṇa about the source of his peace and hears of his twenty-four teachers (Bhāgavata 11.7.25-11.9.33).

realization_account.text: Hearing the avadhūta, Yadu became free of all attachment and even-minded (Bhāgavata 11.9.33).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Yājñavalkya

realization_account.text: BAU 6.5.3 says the white Yajus formulas come from the sun (Āditya) and are proclaimed by Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya; later Purāṇic accounts elaborate that he received them from the sun (not recorded here in detail).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The central teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: he teaches Maitreyī that the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated upon (BAU 2.4, 4.5), defeats the brahmins at Janaka's court (BAU 3) and teaches Janaka on light, dream, sleep, death and karma (BAU 4.3-4). BAU 6.5.3 names him Vājasaneya, through whom the white Yajus formulas received from the sun are proclaimed.
notes: Teacher of the mantha rite lineage: Uddālaka Āruṇi taught it to his pupil Yājñavalkya (BAU 6.3.7, moderate on the kaṇḍikā). The Yājñavalkya Smṛti and Yoga-Yājñavalkya are later works attributed to him (owned by other units).
alt_summary: U02 contribution: the authority of ŚB books 1–5 and 11–14, where he answers Janaka on the Agnihotra (11.3.1, 11.6.2), defeats Vidagdha Śākalya on the number of gods (11.6.3) and says he eats beef 'if it is tender' (3.1.2.21); tradition also makes him the lawgiver of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, which scholars date many centuries later.

Son of Brahmarāta, pupil of Vaiśampāyana. Told to give back what he had learned after offering to perform an expiation alone, he disgorged the Yajus; then, devoted to breath-control, he praised the Sun as the door of liberation and received from the Sun, in the form of a horse (vājin), Yajus unknown to his teacher — the White Yajurveda of the Vājasaneyins (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5).

In the Mokṣadharma (12.298–306) Yājñavalkya teaches king Daivarāti Janaka the evolution of the principles, the guṇas, yoga and dissolution, tells how he won the Yajus teaching from the Sun by austerity (12.306.3–22), and relates his answers to the Gandharva Viśvāvasu (12.306.27); he declares that knowledge may be received even from a śūdra (12.306.85).

U04 contribution: in the minor Upaniṣads Yājñavalkya teaches Bṛhaspati, Atri and Janaka on Avimukta, the tāraka and renunciation 'on the very day one becomes dispassionate' (Jābāla, Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad), is taught by the Person in the sun (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa), teaches Paiṅgala, and is named among the kuṭīcaka renouncers (Bhikṣuka).

tradition.text: the Vedic sage of Janaka's court; the Smṛti presents the same sage teaching in Mithilā

scholarly.text: the Vedic teacher c. 8th–6th c. BCE (if historical); the Yājñavalkyasmṛti c. 3rd–5th c. CE

alt_notes: U01 contribution: the White Yajurveda revelation. U03 contributes the Upaniṣadic teacher.
U05's contribution (the epic account); the Upaniṣadic Yājñavalkya is covered by U03.

name: Yama (Mṛtyu)
summary: Death, lord of the dead, as teacher of Naciketas: grants three boons, tests him with offers of long life, wealth and pleasures, and teaches the good and the pleasant, Om, the unborn self, the chariot, the ladder to the person and yoga (KU).
alt_summary: Lord of death; in U06's texts the speaker of the Yama Gītās (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.7; Narasiṃha Purāṇa 8; Agni Purāṇa 381, the last addressed to Naciketas).
Lord of the dead; in the Sāvitrī episode he takes Satyavat's life and, pleased by Sāvitrī's words, returns it (3.281); in the Jāpaka story he appears with Kāla and Mṛtyu (12.192–193).
notes: U05's contribution; Yama as Naciketas's teacher in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad is covered by U03.

name: Yama Vaivasvata
summary: Son of Vivasvant, the first mortal to die and find the path for many to the fathers; king of the dead in the highest heaven; seer of RV 10.14 and of his verses in the Yama–Yamī dialogue (10.10).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Yamī Vaivasvatī
summary: Yama's twin sister, speaker of her verses in RV 10.10 and ṛṣikā of 10.154 (on the departed who reached heaven by tapas).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Yāmunācārya
summary: Grandson of Nāthamuni and grand-teacher of Rāmānuja; author of the Siddhitraya, Āgamaprāmāṇya, Gītārthasaṅgraha, Stotraratna and Catuḥślokī, who laid the philosophical foundation of Viśiṣṭādvaita and defended the Pāñcarātra.

tradition.text: 916–1041 CE in one traditional reckoning

realization_account.text: As a boy he defeated the court scholar and won half a kingdom, hence 'Āḷavantār' ('he who came to rule'); Maṇakkāl Nambi led him to renounce it. At his death three fingers of his hand stayed folded, for three unfulfilled wishes, and unfolded when Rāmānuja vowed to fulfil them.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Contribution from U08 (Pāñcarātra defence); U14 owns his Vedānta.
alt_summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher (Āḷavantār), grand-teacher of Rāmānuja, whose Āgamaprāmāṇya defends the Pāñcarātra as valid scripture spoken by the Lord himself.
Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher, author of the Gītārthasaṅgraha summarizing the Gītā in 32 verses.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Yāska
summary: Author of the Nirukta, the etymological commentary on the Vedic word-lists (Nighaṇṭu). He defends the meaningfulness of the mantras against Kautsa (Nirukta 1.15–16), teaches that the seers had direct vision of dharma (1.20), that one who recites the Veda without knowing its meaning is a post bearing a load (1.18), and that because of the deity's greatness the one Self is praised in many ways (7.4).

scholarly.text: c. 6th–5th century BCE (before Pāṇini, low confidence)

notes: U01 contribution (Yāska as interpreter of the Saṃhitās); U02 owns the Nirukta.
alt_summary: Author of the Nirukta, the Vedāṅga of etymology; he reports the views of Nairuktas, Aitihāsikas, Yājñikas and grammarians and of many named predecessors (Śākaṭāyana, Gārgya, Aupamanyava, Aurṇavābha, Śākapūṇi, Kautsa and others).

name: Yogarāja
summary: Disciple of Kṣemarāja; author of the commentary (Vivṛti) on the Paramārthasāra.

name: Yudhiṣṭhira (Dharmarāja)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Eldest Pāṇḍava, son of Dharma; answers the Yakṣa (3.297) and Nahuṣa (3.177), defends acting righteously without seeking its fruit against Draupadī (3.32.4), wishes to renounce after the war and is persuaded to rule (12.7–36), receives Bhīṣma's instruction, and at the end refuses to enter heaven without the dog who was devoted to him (17.3).

name: Yūkimuṉi
summary: Physician-Siddhar to whom the Yūki vaittiya cintāmaṇi, a standard work on the classification of diseases, is ascribed.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400
